However, if you look at the amount that America spend s on research and development , its latest defence budget is extraordinary —t he one that is currently we nding its way through Congress , where I suspect the military w as surprised to receive substantially more tha n it had asked for. Would that the British military was in a similar position. It is hard to get a sense of where we stand in the middle of that.

On the UK and its issues, you asked specifically about DSTL . One of the challenges there is to know exactly as an outsider w hat is going on at DSTL and how effective its research is. There are a large number of scientists, a fairly big budget and l ots of it is classified . H ow do you go about discovering what is being done and how effective it is at translating basic research into applied functions ?

However, I would say that it is easier for me as an outsider to get a handle on the broader defence cultur al issues when it comes to innovation. The pattern there is one that I am sure you are all familiar with. We have a model that is predicated on developing exquisite technologies and a drive to be at the absolute cutting edge, which means incredibly low volumes, cost overruns, long lead times, a handful of suppliers specialising in making this kit and the challenge of keeping pace over extended procurement cycles with changing requirements so that you are designing and building the F35 at the same time.

That model , to me, is a world away from what I see when I look at DeepMind in Google and OpenAI and the very rapid innovation cycles that are going on there. That is the essential challenge for the MoD : how far does it, should it, and could it switch to a more disposable procurement cycle where it recognises the advantages of AI, for example , lie in scale and in mass , potentially disposable platforms with incredibly short shelf lives? How do you switch from a model where it takes you 30 to 40 years to develop an air superiority fighter? That is the challenge.

Q135 If you are to leverage this sort of innovative approach to research, experimentation and so on, failure and the acceptance of failure has to be a key element within that. How does that fit within an organisation that has accounting officers responsible to Parliament and Ministers who have to answer aggressive questions from across the aisle about expenditure?

I t is challenging. There is abundant failure on a large scale and money squandered ; you see that year on year. It is not easy . I do not mean to malign the efforts of people in the MoD and procurement and development to do an honest job, but you will be well aware of the various big-ticket items that are over budget and underperforming. You could say, where is the accountability for that? Who was the last person to lose their job over this —be yond a telling off in a c ommittee such as yours?

Again, it is the question of balance. I was very much taken by the recent and rapid cancellation of the RAF ’s Mosquito uncrewed Loyal Wingman project. It had not been kicking over for a long time and was abruptly halted. I take that as an encouraging sign , rather than a depressing one. I ha d my doubts about the whole Loyal Wingman concept anyway , but that is a separate issue. What I liked was that a li ne was drawn under it fairly rapidly . That is where you need to be : more like the aviation industry, whose enviable safety record relies on striking the right balance between owning up to your mistakes and being responsible for them , and not necessarily being publicly flogged for them. I think that is the trick.

Q136 So far , you are giving the MoD a relatively clean bill of health and certainly suggesting that in comparison with our European allies we have a better record in terms of innovation and meeting the challenges of new technology, AI and other changes.

However, there is a lot of criticism of the Ministry of Defence in terms of the need for cultural change. You have touched on this , but could you say a bit more about it , giving some illustrations of where you feel these comments are unfair or there is some merit in these criticisms ? If there is merit, what would you like to see the G overnment doing, not necessarily just at the MoD but across departments, in working more effectively, particularly with the private sector and businesses, but also with academia and other stakeholders?

I do not think I would give the MoD anywhere near a clean bill of health, but I certainly acknowledge the difficulty of the challenge. I would go so far as to say that the procurement process is hugely and extravagantly wasteful on many projects, and in doubling down on investing in sunk costs and chasing projects that are perhaps less relevant. I could name projects, such as W atchkeeper or the cost overruns on A stute . T he F35 programme itself is a success now , but it massively overran and was over budget . There was also the the cancellation of the W arrior infantry fighting vehicle .

T hat is not good, but what is the alternative? We have a wasteful process where we feed a lot of sausage meat into the sausage plant, and out the other end , after plenty of waste, emerges some useful military capabilities, some of which we are seeing being used in Ukraine now.

I do not think I would compare any of our European rivals favourably with the situation here; i t is always a slight finger in the air exercise to gauge military power , but I think we compare favourably with most of our European rivals w hen it comes to the procurement and weapons development process.

For me, the challenge s and the way that you improve it are in how you tackle those cultural issues in an organisation where people belong to a particular service stovepipe. They grow up through the ranks; there is no lateral entry and little outside influence. How do you tackle those cultural issues? That is the real challenge, and I do not think there is a n easy solution ; otherwise , it would have been reached many years ago . These are issues that this committee would have been talking about decades ago and will be talking about decades hence.

The challenge is to open the organisation up to the outside. That is why, in respect of AI , I am moderately encouraged by the MoD’s efforts to do so by engaging with academia and through things such as its partnership with the Alan Turing Institute and its engagement with UKRI. So there is no easy answer. You are right: I would probably give the MoD a soft pass.

I agree. I would not necessarily give the MoD a clean bill of health on the measures that it is implementing right now , but that does not mean one cannot recognise the steps that it has been implementing over the past years. When I said earlier that it is certainly better prepared to tackle some of the challenges and seize some of the opportunities that arise emerging and disruptive technologies, that only gets us so far towards the goal of leveraging that technological progress and putting it into our military capabilities.

There are many aspects that come into play when we talk about cultural change. One of them is the ability to evolve our approach to taking risk. Some risk is merited , especially when it comes to flexible and smart investment in emerging and disruptive technologies and proof s of concept early on. Others, on the more procedural side, are turning into obstacles to our ability to rapidly make use of these technologies and adopt them in defence. As Kenneth was saying earlier, with some specific technologies on the digital side in particular, that gap in procurement cannot be this long because we are going to end up with capabilities that are obsolescent or obsolete by the time they actually go into service. The reason why that is important, in my view, is that the technological development stage that we are at now allows technical performance in UK Armed Forces military equipment to be roughly at a scale that is met by our adversaries.

Like Kenneth, I think that one thing the MoD got right was threat assessment. It is very clear : we know who the opponents are and the UK understands better how those opponents are fighting and preparing to fight, both on the battlefield and below the threshold of armed conflict. It is attempting to channel its policies towards closing that vulnerability.

Russia is never as weak or as strong as it seems. The lesson that I take from the Ukraine war is that we need to get better at understanding the Russian challenge and Russia’s defence innovation pipeline, because we are now swinging from overestimating its moderni s ation towards underestimating the steps forward. That is a very challenging and dangerous swing.

There is another part of the cultural change that I see . You mentioned broadening our relations with the private sector and academia . T hat is probably one of the most challenging aspects of changing how we tackle emerging and disruptive technologies. It is about establishing new types of partnerships and new types of engagement with industry and academia, especially those that have not been active in the defence sector before and might have some apprehension about engaging with the MoD .

Key to that , in my analysis, is trying to lessen the bureaucratic burden for entry to MoD projects for all the start-ups and academic actors. Granted, that is happening to some degree. DSTL and DASA in particular are trying to do this —they are trying to shorten award times and to s horten the application forms — but , by comparison, our closest ally, the U S, has award times that are measured in weeks and its application forms are five to seven pages long. The UK ’ s are not. That is a really hard burden for a start - up which might develop a really exciting application for artificial intelligence, quantum or s pace debris clearing but has only five employees. It takes a long time to put together an application. That is definitely one of the challenges that I see. Procurement has already been well covered, and I acknowledge that that is also a big challenge.

Another challenge here is the fact that the MoD is still searching, and still on a learning curve , with respect to how to materialise that co - operation with the private sector and academia. Efforts are ongoing within the MoD more broadly to revamp the approach to R&D, shorten initial project cycles to 12 or 18 months , and foster more competition at these early stages. There are ongoing efforts to rethink contracting. For instance , the defence AI strategy m entions co - development, which is a big step. It lacks detail but it is definitely something worth pursuing.

A really big challenge in engaging with the private sector is being able to accurately communicate , and do so early , about what your goals and requirements are. That has been one of the big handicaps in how we were trying to engage with industry before . I see some encouraging signs with the newly launched defence capability frameworks. At least we have the promise of that early engagement and better communication, and we will see how that plays out in implementation.

Q137 You have cited a number of areas where you think there could be improvement . I f you were appointed as a consultant to provide some of the solutions — this question is for both of you — what would you come up with? You have identified problems such as overlong application forms, too much bureaucracy, very long timescales before contracts can be signed and not terribly accurate communication with the private sector. What needs to be done to make the department better at all this? Is it something about the skills of the people doing the job, something about their training or the fact that the department is to o closed and there are not enough secondments in and out of it? Could you tell us a bit more about what we should be recommending in order to solve the problems that you have cited?

The things you have mentioned there are entirely apposite. There is a skills challenge , particularly when it comes to AI , which is a fast - moving technology. The military is , broadly speaking , a generalist organisation , where officers rotate from post to post on a two- year basis, and those things work against the development of deep subject matter expertise and staying current in busy , high - tempo jobs with fast - moving technology. So there are real challenges , many of which are not easy to solve.

I would point to one good thing , the jHub , a unit within Strategic Command , as an example of a reasonably small - scale attempt to “ Dragon ’ s D en ”-ify engagement with technology actors for reasonably small projects, position ing yourself slightly at arm ’ s length from the mainstream military to allow yourself to do that. That is a good example of what the MoD is doing.

To mention o ne challenge , I was particularly struck by the contrast between Britain and the United States when it came to the latest DAR P A dogfighting challenge. This was a sensational breakthrough in simulators, in a competition between , first, automated pilots and eventually a human pilot . T he winner, Heron Systems , was not a prime contractor but somebody no one had heard of, yet it saw off Lockheed Martin in the earlier rounds of th e competition. When I saw that, I thought, “ Could I see the MoD doing that? I ’ d really like to see it doing that .” M y question for the PUS or whoever, if they were sat here, would be, “W here is your dogfighting challenge? Why isn’t it open to anybody to enter?”

I fully recognise the challenges you listed. I would start with the organisational challenge. While some analysts would say that innovation needs to be deregulated, that y ou cannot organise and plan for innovation, and that you certainly should not increase the organisational burden on innovation , successful examples of structures in the UK and abroad suggest that some level of planning and organisation is required. So we need to have the right process e s in place to know how quickly we can transition and how we can fast - track innovative solutions when they prove to be of significant added value, especially on the defence side, or when they can provide that immediate disruptive added value for defence. That is to do with procurement. That reform is slow in coming and that is one of the really tough nuts to crack.

The way I see it , the other solution is that we need to get better at communicating the effect s we want to achieve and our requirements for any kind of military capabilities that we are developing. That can be done through a number of platforms, both existing ones — DSTL, DASA and others— but also through new forms of engagement with start-up associations and putting out more frequent challenges that can help the MoD to have broader access and increase its tech - scouting capabilities more broadly.

T he skills challenge is very relevant and important. It is not one that the UK alone is confronted with; this is a general challenge, and not just for defence. It has some specificity to it . T he MoD seems to be aware of it . There are some plans, for instance , to implement tech - specific skills frameworks. The defence AI strategy at least goes into some detail about that and about how those skill sets would need to be adjusted based on the role s that different people in the organisation play ; one would not expect the same skill sets of an operator of military equipment and someone contracting in procurement.

There are also some potential challenges with that approach , because w e are not seeing the more fundamental changes that are require d. For example, the MoD and the Armed Forces rotate personnel depending on need; that is the modus operandi. T o better leverage the skill set that exists now with immediate effect , but also for the long term , with respect to bringing in new human talent and experts, that would need to be changed and adjusted so that specific skill sets were more prominently taken into consideration.

I shall add a concrete example of that skills challenge. The ministry recently a dvertised an ethics and AI job. This is a key job —perhaps the key job— in the Defence AI C entre, given public unease about the way lethal autonomous weapons will be used or , more broadly , the way society engages with artificial intelligence , surveillance and so on.

This job, which to me is extremely important , attracted a salary of £ 40,000 . I am fully aware that you are not going to get rich working for the G overnment, but the challenge is how to compete for people in an industry where salaries are extravagantly high. T he number of people who could credibly apply for that job is reasonably small, and that is a real bottleneck.
Thank you for that added information. It puts it all into context.

Q138 I am going to stick with the same area and look in more detail at the relationships in R&D for civilian versus defence purposes. With the Covid vaccinations, we saw the private sector come up trumps and then this became something owned by Governments. With the defence version of that, could we be more innovative? How do we share between the two? What are the drawbacks, especially in relation to IP theft?

The vaccines were a tremendous private sector triumph, as you say, but it is hard to disentangle that entirely from public sector funding, because a lot of those researchers will have been funded by UKRI during their career, including in work that is salient to developing those vaccines. Disentangling the two is a challenge.

In AI, you have an added problem. There is a loose analogy with the P ugwash conference of the 1950s. A lot of cutting-edge AI researchers are extremely uneasy about seeing their work used in a national security context. In fact, a lot of the leading private sector research corporations are explicit about their reluctance to do work that might contribute to national security issues, whether on facial recognition systems or, more broadly, any sort of decision-making technology.

So there is a real challenge about how the public sector in the modern age leverages the undoubted skills of the private and university sectors. It is a sea-change for AI. For most of AI’s history, the Governments here and in the US have played an outsized role in shaping the field, in large part with national security in mind.

The arrival of the big information companies—Amazon, Facebook, Google and so on—has changed that landscape. It is unavoidable that most of the bleeding - edge research will be done by corporations , DeepMind especially, that have h oovered up a large part of the talent in the field, including from the university sector. So that g ap is unavoidable . There are still very capable researchers working elsewhere and there are still plenty of companies that are happy to work in the defence sector. But it may be that the gap between basic research and applied research is wider in the AI field than it is in other technology fields.

I recognise that the relationship between civil and defence R&D is changing. While civilian R&D continues to be a much larger part of our spending , we as G overnments are increasingly outspent exponentially by the private sector . I agree with Dr Payne that better leveraging private sector R&D is very important moving forward. T hat is one of the challenges that we are currently seeing with adopting emerging and disruptive technologies in defence.

I will give you an example of th e scale that we are at now. This is not from the UK—u nfortunately , we do not have that data yet for the UK— but the US has established a Defen s e Innovation Unit, which has offices attached to all the major innovation hubs across the country. For every $1 billion that it contracts, that it award s contracts to the private sector for, it leverages on average $20 billion in private sector R&D.

I think someone mentioned the best practi c es of the private sector. The example of the Covid-19 vaccines is something that we also need to take into consideration. The fact that the vaccines could be developed and deployed so quickly is testimony to the quality of our research and development , but also to decades of R&D that were put to good use.

When one talks about leveraging R&D in the private sector, it is common that one would say, “ W e need to move as fast as private industry does”. That is not often associated with a detailed understanding of just how long it takes to pull through a technological breakthrough in the private sector t o o. Most of us carry phones in our pockets today and we get new software packages pushed through once or twice a year. That is the rate of technological moderni s ation and change , b ut it probably took th e company a decade to develop the product initially.

T here is an issue with leveraging civilian and private R&D better. There is also an issue o f p utting things in context more accurately —that innovation takes a long time to put through. We need to carefully manage expectations in investment in particular, about when solutions can actually become available.

DARPA is one of the successful examples that is usually referenced in the case of our American allies , but the return on investment for innovation in DARPA is nearly 15 years. That is a long-term approach. Yes, it is incredibly important when it comes through, but understanding that dimension and that challenge are also important.
You asked about espionage as well.

Q139 Yes, and that can be my follow-up. Obviously there is more scrutiny around inward investment with the NS&I Bill and its very broad non-definition of national security—let us put it that way. To what extent do you think there is enough safeguarding around IP between defence and non-defence, where they share the same IP?

It is a real challenge. Again, there is nothing new here. If you look at weapon systems fielded by our main competitors—China and Russia—they often bear an uncanny resemblance to technologies that were developed five years ago in the West. This is a long-standing issue, and, if anything, it is exacerbated by the extent to which AI especially is code—it is very pinchable. Also, the people who develop the basic research ofttimes have an interest in getting it out into the world. Their interest is not necessarily the same as the Government’s in safeguarding key technologies.

None the less, I am still reasonably confident, because my view is that the bleeding edge in AI technology— I spoke about the shift that is need ed in procurement to a more disposable , rapid cycling and fielding of technologies —conveys a disproportionate advantage when it comes to AI . Y ou do not get to the forefront of automated military technology by emulating; y ou have to innovate. It is not clear that the innovation ecosystems of our adversaries — particularly the Chinese model , where there are high levels of corruption and of centralised control , and with its very top - down , directed approach to R&D , as in other economic areas —are a better model. That is certainly not a better model than the very rich, multifaceted ecosystem that the Americans have developed.

I have a quick follow up to what Dr Payne sai d . The challenge with tackling or mitigating the risks from espionage and IPR theft a re double. One is that this sort of espionage, given the war in Ukraine and the comprehensive sanctions package against Russia, will likely intensify over the short and medium term. We have seen some signals from the US Administration that that might be the case. We know that Russia is actively looking for ways to bypass sanctions and continue to maintain access to foreign technology, particularly western technology.

This was one of the challenges that I flagged up at the beginning: protecting our technological innovation is increasingly important. Not everything will need to be protected. I see this coming through in the Government ’ s approach to S&T. I see it somehow resonated into the mechanisms for FDI monitoring. But there are some gaps that need filling.

I will start with foreign direct investment. In my own research, I have looked at what the capital markets are investing in, both in the UK and on the European continent. The UK is fortunate to have a robust capital market to invest in new technologies here. It is one of the biggest investors on the European continent. However, we also have to recognise that we have foreign funds residing in the I ndo - Pacific, and Russian venture capital funds that are still active on our markets right now , that are investing in critical technologies that have important security and defence applications.

I have looked recently , and one of the top 10 investors across Europe, including in the UK, is th e Skolkovo Foundation . The Skolkovo initiative in Russia is recognised for not producing much in terms of innovation in tern ally in Russia, but it is one of the top 10 investors by number of agreements and by the amount associated with those agreements, in ke y clusters of emerging and disruptive technologies that we are talking about. Other examples can also be brought to the fore. That is a very important pipeline that our adversaries have to access our science and technology and our technological base. The challenge with that is that investments often come in pre - seed and seed sessions, which are well below our FDI monitoring ceilings . P resumably an adversary, for £ 15,000, can get access to the cutting - edge orbital debris clearing technology, which one would argue is something that we need to protect .

Efforts are being made by the Government to close that gap , and I think the National Security and Investment Act will help with that, but ultimately one needs to expect an increase in espionage and trying to illegitimately and illegally get access to our technology. One would also expect us to better protect and monitor our own supply chains, especially the ones that are global in nature , to ensure that critical components , such as chips and semiconductors more broadly, do not end up in the wrong hands , becaus e they have contributed significantly to increasing the military capability and efficiency of our opponents.

Thank you for the cautionary note as part of your answer to that supplementary question. Clearly, at this stage, the enemy is time, let alone those outwith this country. So in the interests of time I invite Lord Anderson and Lord Teverson to ask their questions together for our witnesses to reply to, because they relate specifically to R&D spending and I am aware that we have covered some of that issue already; there has already been some contribution on that, particularly in Lord Teverson’s question, so it might be possible not only for the noble Lords to ask them together but for the answer to be cohesive.

Q140 As our Chair has said, R&D spending will invite a variation on several of the themes we have already touched on. You will be aware, of course, that in the Defence Command Paper the Government committed £ 6.6 billion t o research and development experimentation over the next four years. I quote from that document: “ This aims to implement a set of R&D pipelines which will address critical and enduring military capability challenges to deliver a decisive strategic edge ”. Can you say how effective and efficient the UK currently is in terms of defence and R&D expenditure? Is that £6.6 billion investment adequate to meet the goals?

If I may add to that, given the fear that much of the increased European defence expenditure will go to the US—the example cited is Germany, whose first major expenditure, of €100 billion, was on F35s—do you think that there is a danger of much of this R&D expenditure going outside of the UK, on collaboration, partnerships and so on?
Q141 My question is primarily about risk appetite, as they call it in the City. You have largely answered it in many ways but any extra comments would be useful.

I am aware that the Defence Command Paper talked about things called innovation hubs, which we do not have much information on. I would be interested to hear about them. I just want to put a bit of balance in there. One of the papers that was circulated was t he amazing House of Commons Select Committee report on the Ajax vehicle. We are told in it that it is a multi - platform , digitised , multi - domain vehicle that is extremely innovative, but the interesting thing to me is something that was not said . T here was no criticism of all the clever stuff. The fact was that they could not drive it because it made too much noise and vibrated too much — something that , in the old days , even British Leyland would have got right. In its solutions, t he one thing it did not mention was W D - 40, which is what I would have used and would have thought would solve it. We are useless . Did we get all that difficult stuff right but forget about the easy bit?

Thank you for all the questions. T hey are incredibly relevant to our conversation. I will start with R&D spending effectiveness. I welcome the fact that the G overnment ha ve decided to increased spending on defence R&D ; £ 6.6 billion is not to be discounted, and it is definitely the largest spending on the European continent right now. It puts the UK in a position to better use research and development and better leverage technological progress for its military capabilities for a country of its size.

However, I would also argue that £ 6.6 billion will ultimately not be sufficient to meet the G overnment ’ s ambitions when it comes to the next generation and the generation after next ’s capabilities. I would also argue that this R&D pot potentially should take into consideration retrofitting legacy capabilities. One cannot wait until 2038 to tackle urgent defence threats.

P erhaps one of the ways to increase capacity and capabilities in the short term is to deploy emerging and disruptive technologies to military equipment that we already have and we know works — with some exceptions, of course. That would be a good interim solution. However, to tackle all those threats, £ 6.6 b illion will probably not be sufficient, which is why it is so much more important that the G overnment are better at leveraging private R&D and the financially superior investments that our private sector makes.

Why not also leverage the technological strengths of investments that our close allies and partners are making? Keep in mind the fact that technological sovereignty is important. Close co - operation with allies and partners is important too, but there are certain technologies and use cases that one would strive to own and control on a sovereign basis . Perhaps the prioritisation within that pot of £ 6.6 billion i s very clear ; the need for prioritisation , along the lines of what we would need to ensure technological sovereignty with great priority, is important .

When it comes to risk appetite, we have probably missed the opportunity over the past four to six years to build up internally—within the Government— th e narrative about increasing our tolerance to risk, especially when it comes to adopting emerging and disruptive technologies. There are great challenges with respect to artificial intelligence; Dr Payne alluded to them. In many ways, they are unprecedented. However, that does not mean that we should not at least make an effort to better understand what potential use cases these technologies can be deployed for. W e are still at a level where we have not yet decided .

If I look at the evolution of strategic papers , from the Integrated Review, the Defence Command Paper and the defence , technology and industry strategy to the defence , s cience and technology strategy and the defence AI strategy, I see the same language with respect to emerging and disruptive technologies , in particular AI : that it poses both risks and opportunities. That is a generic way of framing things , but it also suggests that perhaps we are not as advanced as we should be in understanding what particular use cases these technologies have. This will be a significant limitation on our ability to scale successful models of artificial intelligence or other types of technologies rapidly . That is why , for instance, we currently have at the service level — this should be recognised — excellent pockets of innovation that none the less face significant challenges in scal ing up rapidly. That is important to mention .

The defence AI strategy in particular acknowledges this. W e will see how it goes with implementation, but it says that w e need to educate leadership at different levels within the MoD and the services to take risk and understand what the technology can do for them. That is a really good step in the right direction ; it should be reinforced really boldly in implementation.

With respect to innovation hubs, my understanding of open innovation systems is that innovation hubs happen organically as the ecosystem develops and matures. That is not to say that the G overnment do not have a role to play in them . Especially on the S &T approach, the G overnment have taken it upon themselves to intervene and support the development of these hubs.

We have examples . For instance, DASA has a hub with Imperial College here in London where it fosters engagement with the private sector and offers spaces for the private sector to come and work together on specific applications. There are many other examples at the service level which have put forward battle labs or accelerators in the context of specific innovation hubs. At least we see some encouraging movement

On the hubs, an example might be one that DSTL is standing up via the Alan Turing Institute in Septembe r, which was announced this month. My understanding is that it will be relatively small scale ; we are talking about eight to 10 permanent members of staff. If that is the scale of the ambition or representative of it, that would seem to be quite small beer.

On the R&D budget, I cannot get my head around the mismatch between the scale of our ambition and the way in which we unreflectively see ourselves bestriding the globe as a world-leading military, and the fact that , on the other hand , we have the smallest A rmy in a very long period of time and an armoured fighting vehicle that shakes and rattles a lot. There is a real mismatch . I f you look at the amount that the Americans are spending on their defence budget on R&D , it is $130 billion, which has gone up 9.5% in a year .

Unreflectively and in our heads, w e anchor ourselves to that. There is a moment whe re I catch myself and think , “ G et real , w hat do we think we are doing? ” What are the limits to what we can achieve as a military power that is still a large economy but one that faces some troubling headwinds more broadly and outside the world of national defence and security?

There needs to be a certain stocktaking moment where we need to th i nk . “ C an we really be at the cutting edge of hypersonics , quantum computing, AI and so forth?” Rather than a full - spectrum military — for various political reasons we find it hard to turn our heads to our European allies at the moment—w e might like to think more cannily about how we combine usefully with our allies to offset and complement o ne another’s strengths and weaknesses.

Without trying to sound na ive, one of the most successful civil R&D programmes is Horizon , which we are still trying to be a part of. Could there be an equivalent on the defence side , or is it just too dangerous in terms of secrecy? Why could we not combine that budget and do a heck of a lot better?
Members here will have much more experience than me , but the knitting together of the various national elements in European defence and security has a long track record of being problematic.

I jotted down that there are currently three sixth - generation fighter programmes around the world, but there is only one viable 5th generation fighter programme — the F35. So , somewhere between here and the next generation some head scratching is going to have to be done.

The European Union, if we are talking about H orizon, has an R&D budget for defence through the European Defence Fund. I think the committee knows much better some of the challenges with the UK having access to that —really with the willingness to have access to that. The European Union has a budget in place to support R&D for defence and it has really been one of the leading measures that the EU adopted starting in 2016 on revamping European defence .
Has it worked?

There are a number of projects in the pipeline that at least look interesting. There are some significant challenges and problems in the way it is being implemented. I t is a multinational instrument that depends on the will of the member states, so how fast it can run and what it can deliver are entirely up to the member states.
That is a very diplomatic answer.

Q142 Dr Payne, you said that when it comes to artificial intelligence there is a lot of aspiration but not a lot of detail, a point reiterated by Dr Soare. In inviting us to drill deeper, you said that we need a radical shift and to take a bet , because this is the way our allies and warfare are going. Last month, the MoD, as you reminded us, published the Defence Artificial Intelligence Strategy , setting out how it will “ adopt and exploit AI at pace and scale, transforming Defence into an ‘AI ready’ organisation and delivering cutting-edge capability ”.

Without giving either a public flogging or a soft pass, based on its track record how realistic is the strategy and its implementation? There is a Pro curement Bill before Parliament at the moment that was described by Professor Louth in evidence to us last week as being long on rhetoric, legalese and detail , but almost incomprehensible even to academics. What difference will that make to our procurement policies, not least in the area of AI?

That is a very difficult question to answer, because I have as much detail as was in the defence AI strategy and in conversations on the bazaars. You always want to be led into the secret rooms where th e plans set out in minute detail how the structures and processes are going to change.

There is a lot of ongoing experimentation work. The RAF has a swarming drones squadron. In Salisbury , the Army Futures directorate is experimenting with robotic warfare systems, and a lot of thought is going into the sort of concepts that might be applied to knit those bits of kit together. It is a bit like heavier-than-air aviation before the Great Wa r . It is a bit “ Wacky Races ” at the moment, and it feels very much—again this is slight ly finger in the air—as if it is a bolt-on to day-to-day business.

For me, the defence AI strategy is a clear signal of intent. When the chiefs were all in the running for the top job last year, every one of them gave a speech where AI was “the one ring to rule them all”—that is the one I remember from Patrick Sanders. Clearly there is a top - down aspiration, and the defence AI strategy is a statement of that . N ow i t encounters culture, “ business as usual ” , and what that actually means. How do you g o from 20 drones operating together in a s mall DSTL project to fielded systems at large scale? The answer is that there is still not a lot of detail about that.

In my evidence to the Integrated Review , I called for the creation of an AI stream operating b e t ween and betwixt the services as a specialist branch , in the same way that space and cyber might be developing their own domain expertise. That is touched on in the defence AI strategy , but what does it mean concretely? There is still no definitive answer to that.
And what difference will the Procurement Bill, which is now before the House of Lords , make to procurement and to AI in particular?
I am afraid I do not know . I would have to come back to you with a written answer , as I have not considered the Bill.

The AI strategy, at least in my analysis, strikes some good notes. It talks about the ne ed to build public and internal trust in this new stack of technologies and specific applications. It recognises really big problems with human talent in the organisation and the importance of organising for these kinds of technological adoption challenges .

W her e the strategy requires perhaps some careful management is expectations. The strategy talks very much in terms of ambition ; it places the UK as the leading AI power in its size group. However, in the short term, if we read the strategy, what it expects to deliver a r e the fairly low - hanging AI fruit . This is the back office uses, or what one would call the completion of digitali s ation or the digital transformation — the deployment of AI in back - office uses — and some limited use s when it comes to logistics and maintenance , for instance. It will n ot necessarily be in operational roles , deployed at the edge or deployed on the battlefield directly.

There is an implicit recognition, at least in the way I read the strategy, that that is a much higher challenge and will require more investment , experimentation and investing in verification , validation and c e rtification capacity . It is really important to recognise that about the strategy and to manage expectations about what it can do. I am expecting more detail to come through the implementation plan. This is a strategic document , of course , so one would not expect every detail to be included in it or else we would end up with a 400 - page document. That is not unprecedented but perhaps not necessarily conducive to the process. I hope the implementation plan will give that greater level of detail.

Another challenge with the implementation of the strategy is that there are no clear metrics for measuring progress that I can see . I am deliberately not saying “success ” here, in the light of the conversation we just had about failure and accepting greater risk of failure in R&D. My hope is that the implementation plan maps out some milestones and indicators that committees such as yours can use to measure progress, and to track progress in the adoption of those strategies. I hope that will be something that we can look forward to.

Q143 I want to ask about ARIA, which has come up in your earlier evidence, and how it compares to DARPA. Obviously the aim is to go after this high-risk, high-reward R&D, but we have seen a delay in its implementation until the end of the year, although I think it appointed its first chair and CEO yesterday. Its funding commitment is only £800 million and it is a little unclear how its relationship with defence will work. Do you think ARIA is best able to replicate DARPA’s successes, given those constraints? How can it work alongside the current R&D environment to make sure it complements rather than competes with existing defence R&D?

T here is always a challenge in looking at foreign examples of success in innovation. T he challenge, if we want to internalise that successful model, i s that it comes with a really high burden of adapting it to the UK ’ s innovation ecosystem. ARIA would not be the only body investing in high - risk, high - impact and high - reward i nnovation, one would assume, so I would expect some sort of synergy and collaboration , and more detail to develop on how it integrates with the rest of the ecosystem.

As always when developing a ne w structure for research and development , not just with ARIA , in my own research I am interested in look ing at how and where it is embedded in the ecosystem. Al though this is not necessarily the case with A R IA , because it will not be defence focused, t he tendency with defence innovation ecosystems in particular is to bring them out of the MoD because that will lower the organisational and bureaucratic burden on them within the MoD and set free the creative geniuses of innovation . A t the same time , it has to be recognised that there is also then a really big challenge to bring any innovation products from these structures back into the MoD . That deepens rather than bridg es the valley of death.

DARPA is making a success out of its activity by being outside the DoD’s immediate scope but being embedded at the high level of decision-making, which has the authority to rapidly transition innovation solutions that are feasible and disruptive and which can give a competitive edge rapidly in the hands of the end-user. My concern with this is with respect to the entire defence innovation ecosystem in the UK. ARIA will plug and play and find its place in this ecosystem. It might be more challenging than meets the eye at the beginning, but if there is no direct pipeline and channel in planning for how to transition its exciting innovation solutions towards the defence end-user, that will be a major limitation and it will impact whatever added value it has.

I have one final note on A RIA. You mentioned the budget. Part of the reason why DARPA is so successful is the methodology that it uses to implement projects, and its ability to take risks without being immediately held accountable for those decisions. DA RPA has a budget of $3.7 billion ; ARIA, to cover “innovation” writ large, will have a budget of £800 million. There has to be some deep consideration about that being a fundamental challenge to its success.

Q144 I want to come back to AI and machine learning. One of the few things I understand about machine learning is that you need to have lots of examples to see what goes on. T hat seems to be difficult for defence . I do not know whether it is possible to explain that to me.

The other think about AI comes back to the garbage in, garbage out thing from my university days on computers: you have to be very careful about biases and the way the information goes in. Although that might not be lethal in some of the civil AI applications that we talk about, it could be militarily. How do we guard against the real flaws we see elsewhere in that system?

Those are huge questions , but I will try to keep my answer brief. Unsupervised learning is a real growth area in AI research, where the machine, rather than looking at a bazillion pictures of a cat to learn how to identify a cat, can pick up salient aspects in its own environment and learn from those, as well as from small datasets. That is a growth area where there has been rapid progress in the last two to three years. But you are right: for a lot of problems in international relations, everything is particular un to the problem rather than being generalisable across them. That may be more relevant when you think about the use of AI in decision support at the more strategic level than when using AI to fly unmanned aircraft, for example, where presumably you can train it.

Biases are a subset of the bigger area of explainable and safe AI , and massively important. AI tends to do things from time to time that are wholly unexpected and not always advantageous. You certainly do not want to experience that in defence. So, again, it is a hugely important growth area which the MoD is actively interested in and I hope the committee engages with.

Q145 You made my day, Dr Payne, when you said, “Get real”. I have quite a long question, which I might send to you in writing. It seems to me that what you are both saying with great eloquence is that the strategy is inefficient, that in no way is it as far-reaching as it ought to be, and that the money that is ascribed to it will not be sufficient. My question, then, is: can we do all this out of 2% of GDP spending on defence?

There is a bidding war in the leadership contest for the Conservative Party at the moment, is there not, to see where we end up on that 2% figure? The answer is, n o, I do not believe that we can. I believe that this strategy is all about choices. You can do some things to offset that hard physical reality and the economic storm that is headed our way by working closely with friends , so, as I alluded to with regard to the six th - generation fighter programme , I would expect that to boil down to a smaller number of programmes.

Ultimately, you have to make those choices , and they are hard ones. Can you be good at everything? I do not mean to be declinist about it, but we have been telling ourselves for the p ast 70 years that we can be good at everything across the military spectrum, and I am not entirely sure that that is the case.

I have one quick follow-up to what Dr Payne said earlier. A function of how much we spend on defence is also how much we fear the threats and risks that are before us. That is as much the case with technology adoption as it is with preparedness for whatever threats we need to face. Necessity is a very good teacher.

W e have spent today talking about innovation and emerging and disruptive technologies, but I would not want to leave the committee with the impression that technology is the solution to everything . It is important to recognise that the UK has come out of two decades of operations in the Middle East where the challenge has not been to adapt to a foe who was technologically superior; t he challenge was a foe who was very good at using mature technologies, and fairly unsophisticated ones, extremely disruptive ly to the way the British A rmed F orces operate.

Moving forward, Russia and China are investing a lot of money and are aiming to be competitive technologically as well as militarily, but they , especially Russia , are looking for asymmetric advantage. In my reading, that is what the UK also wants to achieve. My understanding of the strategy is that the MoD does not pretend that it will invest in anything and everything . R ather , it will try to capitalise on innovation that will deliver an asymmetric advantage against these opponents rather than meeting the m head on , which might be impossible given the size of the force that we have now.
That depends on clear foreign policy objectives, none of which we have talked about this morning.

That may be for another inquiry. On this occasion, thank you both for taking us very deeply into the crucial areas of R&D, and, at the end, putting it into context; that when p eople say that they are bidding to become leader of—it happens to be my party, but it could be leader of any party—they would say that their p rime objective is to defend the country .

The question is defending against what , and you have been very clear about the challenges involved in defence. It is a question of the way in which threats develop —in the past, they developed over long periods of time, but now it seems they develop over very short periods of time —and being able to co - operate internationally where possible , particularly in non - military ways, and the risks in that. Thank you very much for making it clear throughout what those risks are, how they should be analysed and how we need to check the balances on that as against losing and winning the defence of the country in the future.

sessions.iT: Attitudes towards women and girls in educational settings
sessions.w: University of Exeter Law School; Dr Melanie McCarry (University of Strathclyde); Beyond Equality

segs.tx: Women and Equalities Committee
Oral evidence: Attitudes towards women and girls in educational settings, HC 331
Wednesday 7 September 2022
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 7 September 2022 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Jackie Doyle-Price; Kim Johnson; Kate Osborne; Bell Ribeiro-Addy.
In the absence of the Chair, Kate Osborne took the Chair.
Questions 26-6 4
Witnesses

I : Professor Cara Aitchison, Chair of Universities UK advisory group on addressing staff-to-student sexual misconduct; Ammaarah Faisal, Student Ambassador and Human Research for Higher Education, Our Streets Now; and John Edmonds, Co-author of “Unsafe Spaces: Ending Sexual Abuse in Universities”.

I I : Dr Rachel Fenton, Associate Professor in Law, Exeter University; Dr Melanie McCarry, Senior Lecturer at School of Social Work & Social Policy, University of Strathclyde; and Richie Benson, Universities Project Lead, Beyond Equality.
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Professor Cara Aitchison, Ammaarah Faisal and John Edmonds.

Q26 Good afternoon, everyone. This is the second oral evidence session of the Women and Equalities Committee inquiry into attitudes towards women and girls in educational settings. In this session we will look at higher education. For anyone looking online or in the room, the subject matter and the things discussed may be distressing. We have two panels of witnesses today.

Before we start, I want to make a brief comment on the appointment of our new Equalities Minister, replacing the previous Women and Equalities Minister. Women face huge issues of sexism and misogyny, not just around today’s discussion of attitudes towards women and girls, but in many other areas, such as the gender pay gap, gender health inequalities, menopause at work, and violence against women and girls. Women’s rights, as well as other inequality issues, must and will remain at the forefront of our work in this Committee.

One of our witnesses on our first panel, Professor Cara Aitchison, is appearing on Zoom—welcome. Will the first panel please introduce themselves and tell me how you would prefer to be addressed during the course of our meeting? Professor, will you go first, please?

Thank you, Chair, for the opportunity to attend today. I am Professor Cara Aitchison. I am president and vice-chancellor of Cardiff Metropolitan University. I am here representing Universities UK, which is the umbrella body for 140 universities across the UK. I am happy to be addressed as Cara, if that is appropriate, thank you.

I am Ammaarah Faisal. I am happy to be addressed as Ammaarah; my pronouns are she and her. I am from Our Streets Now, where I am head of research for the higher education team. We are campaigning to end public sexual harassment as a grassroots organisation. We define public sexual harassment as unwanted sexual advances and intimidating behaviour in public spaces in person and online, including higher education places. This is an intersectionality issue, so we would say that it is targeted mostly towards women and other oppressed groups in society, but can be experienced by everyone, including boys and men.

My name is John Edmonds. I am the co-author of a book, “U nsafe Spaces: Ending Sexual Abuse in Universities ”. My co-author, Eva Tutchell, is sitting behind me and might whisper in my ear if she is concerned about the parts she wrote. I am happy to be called John.

Q27 I will invite Members to put questions to you. Questions will normally be directed to one of the panel to answer. However, if a question is put forward that is not addressed to you but you would like to come in on it, please indicate and I will bring you in as well. I will ask Ammaarah the first question: how safe do female students feel on and off the university campus?

Not safe. It depends on the type of city as well—campus-based unis have different experiences. For city-based unis, we ran a survey in the autumn of 2021 with The Tab , which is a student-led newspaper in 80 different student cities. We surveyed just under 1,400 participants across 71 different institutions in the UK, and we found that 500 of those participants who were female students were feeling unsafe in clubs and bars, and on public transport, as well as in university campus areas like the library. They experienced public sexual harassment several times a month or more. That figure goes up when we survey non-binary participants and transgender students as well, with them experiencing greater rates of public sexual harassment and sexual violence generally. It is definitely a problem in the night-time economy and on public transport, but it is also happening on the way to lectures and online, with online lectures and things like that as well.
Q28 John, you estimated that at least 50,000 students are sexually abused in universities in England and Wales every year, possibly more. How did you get to that number?

We went through all the available pieces of information, some from individual universities and a lot from student union surveys that have been taken—a number of public organisations have done that—but the estimate is unsatisfactory. I am absolutely certain that it is more than 50,000, but we cannot say more because, for reasons that I do not understand, the universities will not carry out an authoritative survey to find out how many, where, who, why and all the other things that we need in order to develop a policy. The policies that have been developed in most universities are based on inadequate information, so we had to fill the gap as best we could. The best we could do—we explain it in great detail in the book—is 50,000 and more. We can find no information at all on the sexual abuse of men. The only information that we found was about the sexual abuse of women, and all the information is partial and, frankly, impossible to extrapolate from with absolute precision.
Q29 Why do you think it continues to be such a huge problem for the universities?

I have no idea. We have asked UUK several times. We asked the previous president of UUK. At one stage, we were told that UUK does not have enough money to carry out such a widespread survey, but of course we never suggested that UUK should fund it; the individual universities could. On the basis of a survey that took place in Australia, which was very complete and helpful, we reckoned a UK-wide survey would cost about £2,000 per university. We think that could be afforded.

Q30 This inquiry is mainly looking at women and girls, but what has your work revealed about men’s experiences dealing with sexual harassment and sexual violence? You have touched on it, but can you tell us a bit more?

I’m afraid it’s all guesstimates—not even estimates. We managed to set up a widespread network, getting to women victim-survivors, and many of them passed this on from hand to hand, so we could interview more. Although we went widespread, through a number of organisations, not one man came forward. Yet a lot of people said, when we interviewed them, we know there is a problem with male sexual abuse—usually male on male—but we don’t have any details of it, and it is even less well reported than the classically under-reported sexual abuse of women.
Q31 Cara, would you like to come in at that point?

Yes, I would. If I may, I will address some of the quantitative issues or the statistics briefly and then say why I think Universities UK and individual universities perhaps have not been focused on the quantitative issue and have instead turned their attention to some of the more qualitative or cultural issues.

Members may know that I was the chair of Universities UK’s advisory group developing guidance looking at staff-student sexual misconduct and making recommendations to universities. We published a report in March of this year. It was a fairly comprehensive strategic report and accompanying that was some operational guidance. We had long discussions at the beginning of that work, and that work took us a number of years to complete. Universities UK says it’s the most complex piece of work it has ever engaged in, because it involved fairly complex legal issues. But at the outset, we did have a discussion around the table, and around the table were groups representing all areas of universities, so we had the NUS, the staff trade unions, all the professional sector bodies, a number of experts in the field, Rape Crisis and a couple of vice-chancellors, including me. And we decided as a group we would not spend time or money undertaking what we called a prevalence survey. We were sufficiently persuaded that there had been enough small-scale surveys. There had been surveys conducted by, at that time, the NUS and Revolt Sexual Assault that had given rise to data that were small scale but sufficiently robust to persuade us that there was, in quantitative terms, a sizeable problem or challenge that we needed to address. Since that time, there have been a couple of other surveys, including some surveys of staff. So, at the outset of our work, we were all agreed that there is a problem, there is a challenge; we want to address it and we want to get on and do that.

To undertake a national, UK survey—it is probably not worth getting into the details, but it would certainly cost an awful lot more than £2,000 per university. I don’t think that is time or money well spent. There is now no dispute across universities in the UK, or across education more broadly, that we have an issue. Equally, I don’t think there is now any dispute that we all want to address this. For me and my colleagues, the real challenge is just getting on and doing that, and what we have tried to map out in our report is ways in which we think we can tackle this challenge, starting with—this is part of a wider series of Universities UK reports titled “Changing the culture”, and hopefully we will get on to talk about some of the wider cultural or systemic issues, because this is a multifaceted problem and universities have a very key role to play in changing the culture within their institutions and developing new policies and practices and then, going all the way back to data, in actually revealing and sharing some of the data.

So, we have made great strides in the ways in which we report and record data and we have recently produced new guidance on sharing data. One of the difficulties previously has been that these issues have not been transparent. They have not been shared across the sector. There has been, I think, a mistaken belief that reputations are protected by concealing some of these issues, rather than being transparent in the way in which we tackle them.

I think that we have actually gone beyond the need for a survey. No one disputes that there is an issue. The size of the issue is of some importance, but I, as a vice-chancellor, would be concerned if only one student was affected, and we know that there are many more than just single numbers of students affected.
Q32 Thank you, Cara. I’m going to bring John back in.

First of all, a survey would not just count the people who have said that they have been abused. It would identify which groups are most vulnerable; in which parts of the country, if there is a difference; in which universities, if there is a difference; and in what social circumstances in universities such things happen. It would produce, as it did in Australia, a mountain of material on which you could base a well-evidenced policy. That is one point.

The second point is that I have looked at every piece of evidence about numbers and the other issues that I raised. Not one piece is satisfactory. Believe me, if we had been able to put forward a combined result that would have been satisfactory, we would not have called it an estimate. This is very badly needed.
Q33 Thanks, John. I have to say that I agree with what Cara said about one being too many, but surely we need to know the scale of the problem. Ammaarah, did you want to come in?

Yes. I agree with John. The issues of intersectionality and all the different types of groups of people who are experiencing it are not really being considered in a lot of the surveys that have been done thus far. In order to create change in culture through education and policy changes that include the lived experiences of everyone, we need to be doing research that considers everyone’s experiences. Different groups in society face sexual violence in different ways, and it shows up in different ways. In the case of boys and men, it is often not reported, and we will not know how to address that until we take into account their experiences from a first-hand basis.
Q34 Good afternoon, panel. How widespread do you think staff-to-student sexual misconduct is at universities, and what are the challenges of successfully addressing that sexual misconduct?

Each university will have data on cases reported, but like all sexual crimes and sexual misconduct we know that this is vastly under-reported. In some senses, that is why I am a little sceptical about the quantitative data. There are other research methods that we can use to gain insight into these issues within universities or across universities, in specific geographical locations or mission groups of universities. I have yet to meet a vice-chancellor who does not think that this is a problem, so I think that we are all agreed that this is a problem. I think that we are all agreed that this happens within our universities. We have almost half of young people going to university. It is important to note that universities are, in a sense, microcosms of wider society, so we would probably be a bit surprised if this was not an issue in universities.

Student-on-student misconduct has been a huge and growing problem over recent years. The report and the group that I chaired was specifically concerned with staff-to-student misconduct, which I think all of us who have been in education for many years will recognise is a long-standing issue. Our work has really been part of that—the wider, changing the culture work. I think that we have made significant progress, in that we now have all vice-chancellors signed up to tackling this issue. If I go back 20 years, there were probably still elements of denial that this was an issue. There is a recognition that it is an issue. There is an acceptance of it. We are all on the same page, trying to tackle this.

What we have tried to do is map out a series of very pragmatic steps that will help organisations to tackle these issues, starting with the leadership at the top. This is about organisational culture. That culture is set at the top. One of the recommendations is that someone in the very top team— you are talking about someone in the top three to half dozen people in the organisation—has specific responsibility for this issue. So there is leadership from the top and then there is a whole series of systems and processes—new policies, new practices—put in place across the organisation that join up policy and practice areas that were previously quite separate.

They were separate because universities are often constructed into systems and processes, in HR terms, that deal with staff that have been completely divorced from student services. We would have different disciplinary processes, for example, relating to staff and students, that didn’t really speak to each other and didn’t align. We have done a lot of work on developing best practice in how to align these policies and how to enable students to report more readily, including anonymous reporting. There are all sorts of difficulties with that, but anonymous reporting helps us to do a little of what John was referring to, to identify areas and pockets, perhaps, where issues are perhaps a bit pronounced.

There is development of policies, new practices, support systems and a whole range of mechanisms right through from the point at which a student applies to university. We talk about the student journey and that first point of contact—students coming to open days, enrolling, going through a pre-enrolment period, going through a really robust induction that covers all sorts of issues around informed consent, sexual consent, what they can reasonably expect and reasonably not expect by way of behaviour within their organisation—and making all of this much clearer than perhaps it was previously.

Within my university, we talk about creating a sense of belonging and becoming. In these communities, people have to feel that they have protection under the law, but that is a fairly low bar. We want to create something much more encouraging—an environment in which people can grow and flourish. That is about the culture that we create from the top.

For me, this long series of work that we have engaged in goes right through from organisational culture, strategy and leadership to the detailed pragmatics of how policies are developed, implemented and communicated. One of the things that we have found is that students have previously been very unclear as to where they should go, who they should go to, what those routes for reporting are. Then, when they have reported, they have been less than satisfied with things like the timescale over which investigations take place, the way in which the outcomes of investigations are reported back to them, or worse still, never reported—that kind of reporting into a void and then just losing the student voice. We have tried to tackle all of this.

So, there have been these measures, combined with the slightly different initiatives across the four nations in terms of the use of NDAs—that has been a really significant step. In Wales, all universities have signed up to agreeing never to use a non-disclosure agreement, a settlement agreement, in cases of statutory sexual misconduct. That sounds like a small move, but I think it is a really significant one in terms of the position that universities are now adopting.

Q35 Thanks, Cara. You talk about trying to implement and make these policy changes. What evidence is there that there has been any change from what used to be? Who is responsible for ensuring that the policy changes you talk about are implemented effectively and that all universities have a consistent approach?

There is a challenge here, in that universities are autonomous institutions—we have the autonomy to develop our own approaches within the parameters set out through legislation, regulation and then also the different funding or regulatory bodies across the four nations—but I think the change I have noticed over the last few years is that there is now what I see as a very common approach across universities. I think there is a shared intent, aspiration and commitment to tackling these issues in a way that there probably wasn’t as recently as five years ago.

I mentioned the importance of senior leadership, and holding senior leaders to account. Boards of governors, university councils and courts now should be holding their vice-chancellors to account for these issues. We should be reporting the data internally; the mechanism for reporting or collecting that data across the sector, I think, is less well established.

It is important to note that I would not necessarily see an increase in reports as a short-term failing, because we know that when we get things right in terms of reporting sexual crime, the stats around reporting can sometimes go up. I have reports within my own university, which we deal with very robustly, and probably in a slightly different way than my predecessors of a decade or two ago dealt with them. It is all about transparency and accountability—not just up through the university’s executive, but through to boards of governors, councils and courts.
Q36 Thanks, Cara. I think John wanted to come in on that point.

Yes. We found a whole list of things that were going wrong. Most of all we found among people in universities, including some very senior people, a great cynicism about the level of commitment that is being given to driving through policies that have been developed. Let me make two points, very quickly.

First, we did a freedom of information inquiry of all England and Wales universities to establish their procedures for dealing with sexual abuse, and we found that a third of those procedures were obviously and deeply flawed. Most of the rest showed some cautious improvements—but very cautious. Many were still not fit for purpose, but some effort had been made, and of course there were some that had obviously done nothing at all.

Some of these procedures have review dates at the bottom and some review dates were 10 and 12 years ago, so that gives you everything you need to know. We need a separate procedure for sexual abuse. It should not be part of any other procedure. We saw procedures that put it in the same category as misusing library books. That is not an exaggeration, and it is quoted in the book.

The other thing is that Cara is quite right: the involvement of the vice-chancellor is essential. The power structures of universities mean that everybody notices if the vice-chancellor is committed to something and everybody notices if the vice-chancellor isn’t.

What happened in Leicester University, which is a good model for others, is that after a series of difficult cases, the student union managed to persuade the vice-chancellor to meet 15 victim-survivors. They sat around a table. It was not intended to be a “loud noise” type meeting, but they all told their story. At the end, the vice-chancellor had the sort of impression that Eva and I had when we interviewed victim-survivors—not detached or three paces back, but actually knowing the distress and upset. We met victim-survivors in railway buffets and on park benches because they did not want to be seen with us on campus. If vice-chancellors do the symbolic act of meeting victim-survivors, suddenly things change in the university. They certainly changed at Leicester.
Q37 Cara, you mentioned NDAs. How widespread is their use in cases of sexual harassment and abuse?

I cannot give you data, partly because of the nature of NDAs, but I can tell you that no university in Wales will ever use NDAs again, and we all have clear statements on our websites to that effect. That initiative in Wales came about partly on the back of Michelle Donelan’s initiative for universities in England to sign up to the pledge of not using NDAs.

As I understand it, around half of universities in England have signed that—perhaps more importantly than that, there seems to me to be a very different kind of peer pressure among vice-chancellors. No one would want to be on the wrong side of history, so I think there are many vice-chancellors who are actively committed to this and stand alongside many of the activists who have been looking for change for a long time. There are others who are perhaps less activist, less committed, but who none the less want to do the right thing, not just in terms of legislatory requirements but in terms of the moral standing of the right thing.

I would be surprised if we see many of these in future. That is not to say that we will not see any, but I think there will be more and more pressure as we move forward not to use them. The Wales example kind of sets a benchmark for other nations to say, “Can we do the same?”

Q38 Thank you so much, Cara. Ammaarah, you mentioned the impact of intersectionality and people reporting sexual abuse and misconduct. Can you say a little more about that in terms of the experience you have had and the work that you have been doing?

Yes. As we have found research-wise but also anecdotally, talking and getting text for news at Our Streets Now, students and people in society who face greater forces of oppression based on various different aspects of their identity are at greater risk of experiencing public sexual harassment and sexual violence.

For example, we found specifically in the survey we did with The Tab that 94% of the non-binary participants would not feel comfortable reporting incidences of sexual harassment or assault to their university, in comparison with 72% of male students who would not feel comfortable.

Other research has been done. The NUS carried out a survey and looked at the experiences of disabled students, and found that 24% of the disabled students surveyed had a decrease in academic performance after facing sexual misconduct in comparison with 12% of their non-disabled counterparts.

This is affecting students’ freedom of movement, right to education and their experiences of going out and socialising as well. Some 71% of our participants had their participation in student life affected based on things such as facing sexual assault on nights out as well as the shortening of daylight hours. Once it gets dark, a lot of the female students in our survey stop going out, including to lectures that might be in the evening in winter. Students’ experiences are affected both academically and socially at universities and in society as well.

Q39 Just out of interest, has your data been shared with universities so that they become aware of the impact and are able to put some support packages in place to help students—and staff, if they have experienced some of those issues?

Yes, we have a student ambassador scheme at Our Streets Now with a set of students, and it fluctuates in terms of numbers based on the year as they have to be students currently at university. They all had our report and disseminated it to their individual universities. We do it in that localised kind of way because at the end of the day the students are at the universities, they know the policies the best, they have their own experiences and they have their own contacts at the universities. We do not have contacts at all the different universities and, as I said, it fluctuates based on the academic year.

I absolutely endorse everything Ammaarah said and I also want to draw attention to international students. We now have more than 600,000 international students in the UK and there are specific challenges there, in part because some of those students are less clear about what they can and cannot rightfully expect or complain about. There are cultural differences. There are cultures among some of our international students with much more deference towards lecturers and less questioning of behaviour.

We need to be mindful of the diversity of our student population and also of the subjects we teach and the way we teach. Although we do not have comprehensive data, we know that there are certain subject areas where sexual misconduct is more prevalent. It tends to be those subject areas where there is closer proximity and more privacy between staff and students—so, with small tutorials, and applied subjects such as music, sport or small lab-based courses.

It is probably worth pointing out that perhaps slightly counterintuitively we believe—and all the surveys have shown—that this is a more significant issue for postgraduate students than for undergraduates. That might come as a slight surprise, but if we go back to that notion of proximity and small groups, that is more likely to happen at postgraduate level, particularly with PhD students. There is a real blurring of boundaries once you get to the level of PhD students, many of whom are also teaching while still being students who are subject to those same power relationships. So there are complexities.

Q40 Thank you, Kim. I will come to you in a minute Cara, but first I want to ask Ammaarah about the barriers around reporting incidents of sexual harassment and violent assault. Can you take us through what you see those barriers are and what might help break them down?

There is a huge issue with transparency and inclusivity. Lots of students from marginalised communities are less likely to report. As was said earlier, universities are a microcosm of society: those from more marginalised communities have lower levels of trust, as we have seen anecdotally in the media.

That is one big issue—there are low levels of trust. Only 16% of the nearly 1,400 students we surveyed would feel comfortable reporting and over half of them would not trust their university to handle a claim of public sexual harassment appropriately. In the short term, we need to improve reporting processes. Universities need to have full time accredited independent sexual violence advisers on hand to be able to support students.
