Q215 In regard to that perspective, the unions want compulsory redundancies completely off the table before negotiations recommence. Are you able to commit to that , or is it part of a wider conversation in the background before an offer is made?

It is part of the conversation we are currently having with particularly the RMT. It has less impact on ASLEF. It will not impact ASLEF in the same way. We are talking to the RMT about how we can try to avoid compulsory redundancies. I cannot give them that guarantee at this moment in time because I do not have an agreement from them on what modernisation will look like.

It is not quite chicken and egg. Let us agree the modernisation, and then we will have a better understanding of the potential impact. We can then work together to try to make sure that , if anybody wants to stay in the industry, hopefully we can keep them in the industry.

Q216 Finally, we have heard from the unions that the Government’s rhetoric has not been helpful. It is very much a wedge, a divisive issue, of “us versus them”. In their view, the Government should get out of the way and “let us have conversations”. What is the view from both of you as to Government intervention, or lack of it, so far in regard to the negotiation?

In terms of our position, it is better for us as the employers to be negotiating with the trade unions. We have worked in the industry for a long period of time. We understand it. It is not for politicians to be in a negotiating room. That is not what it is there for.

Do I have to work within a framework of funding? Of course, I do. The public sector pay increase is approximately 3% at this moment in time. If I am looking to go outside of that, I need to seek authority.

It will be something that we will create. It will be what I, and the negotiating team on my side, believe that the value of the modernisation is worth. We will then present that and say, “Can we be funded to this level?” Again, we have to make sure it is funded, obviously.

As I say, the biggest change we have had from the outset, when we started this, was that this was very much about how we reduce the cost of the industry while we have these challenges. Clearly, pay negotiations have become far more to the fore. That is making it harder to get a deal at this moment in time, but we continue to work with the trade unions to try to resolve that situation.

Q217 T o what extent do you think the current political narrative over the last couple of months has actually hindered rather than helped in terms of the negotiation position for both sides of the argument?

I think it depends which side of the fence you are on. For myself, it makes no difference to me. I have to go out and do a job and try and negotiate with the trade unions. As I say, we have carried that out in a very constructive manner. The political rhetoric between the trade unions and politicians is something that is not for m e to deal with at this moment in time.

I completely support that. G oing back to your previous question, as you can see we have made a pay offer that is outside the public sector guidelines. We have done that and it has proved effective. Indeed, we have had support from the Department for Transport to offer the travel offer, for example. That is not something that Network Rail can do on its own. We have had support from Government to enable us to do that. I think that does demonstrate in evidence the fact that there is a process that has been effective.

Q218 Notwithstanding what you have both just said, we heard compelling evidence from the trade union leaders about successful settlements having been made across the United Kingdom in companies not owned by the Department for Transport — in Scotland, Eurostar, Merseyside and so forth.
Is it not reasonable for the public to conclude that the problem is the Government , the Department for Transport and Ministers?
I do not recognise that.
Q219 It is true, is it not? They said that settlements have been reached in those areas.

All I can talk about is from my perspective. Let me be clear. The offer that we put on the table yesterday is what we can afford. Irrespective of any permission that anyone might give us, I cannot offer anything more than I can afford. We are not going to go back and ask passengers to pay more by putting fares up. We cannot ask for the Department and taxpayers to pay more into the industry than they are already doing. So, rightly, we are challenged to make this efficiency ourselves.

In the offer that we made yesterday, we said that the 4% offer was the maximum that we could afford. If there is more productivity forthcoming and more ways we can work together to save money, that creates opportunity to pay more. I do not think that their external factors are relevant.
Q220 What is your explanation for the fact that all those other organisations in the rail sector have managed to reach a settlement and you have not?

I do not know the economics of how Eurostar or some of those other companies work. What I am aware of from a rail perspective is that we have worked really hard to generate the cash to make the offer that we have made. The ability to go beyond that is entirely conditional upon the ability to generate more funds and more savings.

You have heard that , even with the 4% that we have offered against the productivity that has not yet been agreed with the union, they are still fighting some aspects of it. In that environment, that is the constraint and not any other influence.
Q221 Mr Montgomery, how come other rail companies have managed to settle and you have not?

Those other rail companies have different contracts from the contracts that are currently in place between the D F T franchises. I am not aware of what type of settlement, in terms of productivity, is included within those settlements. I do not have the detail of it.
Q222 Is it not your job to find out, so that you can get some baseline of where a settlement might be reached?

If we can get the details of it, yes. Mersey r ail is an example of where they have introduced a different form of working. It is a revenue-risk contract. There are different variants across the businesses. Again, those are funded by either devolved authorities or private-sector businesses. It is different variants and different contacts.

Q223 I will pick you both up on something you said earlier about intimidation. You both accept, I assume, the right to strike and the right to try to persuade people not to cross a picket line. I assume you both also accept that the strikes that we saw were overwhelmingly peaceful and, indeed, seemed to attract quite a lot of public support. All the opinion polls showed that the public have enormous sympathy for the strikers.
Why did you raise concerns about intimidation?
We did not raise concerns.
Q224 You talked about intimidation, I think.
We were asked a question about intimidation.
Q225 You gave examples of it. Do you recognise Ben’s point about the public support? What is your view on that? Again, I would agree with Ben that we seem to be hearing that.
I think it has been mixed across—
Q226 The polling suggests that 70% of the public support the strike and feel that the strikers have a case because everyone is suffering under a cost - of - living crisis.
I think there is another group here as well, which is the passengers and the people’s lives who are affected by it. I have seen different polls with different numbers.
Q227 That is a fair point, because obviously people who are not passengers are not as impacted. Have you polled passengers?

Network Rail has not polled passengers, but I have seen the feedback from passengers, and we have seen the impact that that has had on people’s lives. That was very well reported during the strikes. There is no doubt in my mind that the strikes were unnecessary. There was no need for the strikes to take place when they did. As I said, we have been working hard and we were near to making an offer to the RMT. What that strike did was to generate huge amounts of publicity, a huge loss to the industry’s reputation and income and made it harder to make the pay deal that we are trying to do.

I recognise the right to strike, but I do think it was inappropriate to strike when that strike was called. The only way we are going to solve this is by talking. The strike does not make that talking any easier. In fact, it made it harder to have those conversations.

What we have to bear in mind is that , when we talk, no one wins out of strikes, particularly when the RMT members, who probably have lower-paid members than ASLEF, potentially lost 10% of their monthly salary when they were on strike for three days. That is not fair on those individuals.
Q228 It shows how strongly they feel that the strike was so solidly supported, does it not?

It does not make it any better because the company picks some of that up later on. It is very much, how do we try and avoid the strikes and resolve this in a peaceful and sensible way ? That is how we move forward. That is the key area that we keep trying to bring the trade unions back to.
Q229 I have to move on because we are running out of time. What is your view on the Government’s response to these strikes by proposing to change the law on agency working?

We have been clear that that will have no effect in the short term, and it is likely to have limited effect in the long term because many of the most safety critical roles—signallers and what have you—have no agency market to be able to fill in for that sort of role.
Q230 Do you have the same view, Mr Montgomery?
Yes, very similar, but we will use agency staff where it is sensible. We will not compromise on safety.
Q231 It is a pointless political gesture by the Government , basically, is it not?

I would not say it is pointless. For example, if you have a number of different rail companies, at the moment one company would not lend its managers to another company to allow them to operate a strike service. That would be possible under this legislation. I do not think it is pointless. I think there is benefit to it, but the key point is that we have to avoid getting into this position in the first place.

It is a very sad thing, from the evidence that we have been hearing this morning, that strikes feature so strongly in the railway narrative. That really does not feel like a very helpful place to be. I would much rather put all our efforts into making sure that we create an industrial relations environment where a strike becomes irrelevant.
Q232 I take it you are aware that the national organisation that represents agency companies is strongly opposed to the change in the law?
Yes.
Yes.

Q233 Finally, do you understand, Mr Montgomery, the strength of feeling that was expressed earlier by the unions—and it is felt by a considerable proportion of the public—that on the continent, where the terms and conditions tend to be better, money is flowing back into rail companies, often s tate owned, from the profits made by rail companies here? They just do not see the justice in that.

The private sector has been involved in the rail industry, without giving you a history lesson because I am quite sure you are aware of it, since the private sector came in in 1997. It has doubled patronage of the rail industry. It has been a great success. Over the last number of years, we accept ed that the franchising system was not working as effectively as it could. During the pandemic the Government put us on to what are called emergency measures agreements and now will transition through to national rail concessions. Private operators who will take the risk in terms of operating these businesses are only paid at a very small margin. It is under 0.5%. They will have some performance payments as well.

That is probably not in line with most Government contracts. It is probably a lot less than most Government contracts, but the private sector stood behind the industry and continues to stand behind the industry, bringing the expertise that it does have, and will continue to try to use that expertise to recover the industry.

When the trade unions talk about taking vast sums of money out of the industry, I do not really see that. I do not see the numbers, particularly on the train operating companies’ side. I do not see where they get their numbers from.

Q234 T o finish off Ben’s theme of international comparisons, I believe Mr Whelan gave me the answer that basic contractual hours and pay for a train driver is 35 hours and £60,000. How does that compare to some of the European countries that Ben mentioned? Is it on the lower side, or is that regarded as quite generous?

I do not have it in front of me, but I think our drivers are probably on par or slightly ahead of some European countries. Again, a lot of it is really dependent on what their duties are in various companies. Some train drivers carry out far more than train driving. They do shunting, and almost maintain the trains as well at certain times. It is different comparators, and it is not an easy comparator to get—
I understand. If your organisation has any more detailed analysis on that, it would be very helpful if you sent it .

Q235 I have a question on Government intervention. Mr Shoveller, you said, almost understandably, that you can only pay what you can afford, when you were defending whether the Government should be getting involved or not. I assume you will be aware that the deal, which was just agreed this week, between ScotRail and ASLEF is 5% plus, and I will come on to the “plus” shortly. ScotRail are paying 2.8% of that because that is what they can afford, and Transport Scotland are paying 2.2% of that. Transport Scotland is obviously a Scottish Government agency. If it can be done in Scotland, why can it not be done down here?

I would not profess to understand how the funding mechanism works for the Scottish Government to enable them to do that. What I know is that as a result of the comprehensive spending review in this financial year, because of the fact that inflation was so low at the time, there was no provision made for inflationary pay awards. That is why we are in the position of funding this pay award ourselves through the productivity that is possible. It is horses for courses within different public administrations, I imagine. We are very clear that it is possible to fund a pay rise, and indeed that was the offer we made yesterday. It was 4% plus the travel.

Q236 The comprehensive spending review obviously affects Scottish budgets through Barnett, yet they have still found this money to pay the drivers. Have you made any representations to Government to subsidise any pay offers at all? I will come to you in a second, Mr Montgomery.
No. We have not gone back to Government to ask them to help us fund the pay this year.
Q237 Why not?
Because we believe we can fund the pay rise that we want to make this year, if we get agreement with the trade unions.
Q238 You can fund the pay rise that the staff want, or indeed deserve .

As I said, the offer we made yesterday is 4%, and based on the productivity that we have identified so far that is as much as we can afford. I think if we had a really collaborative relationship and we were able to work together effectively as employers and management, we could find much more savings than that and offer a bigger pay rise.
Q239 I will come back to that offer in a second. Mr Montgomery, do you have anything to add to the point I was making?

Not really. The train operating companies have an annual business plan that they agree with the Department for Transport. That gives them a percentage of pay increase. If they go outside that, it becomes what is deemed as disallowable. We have to go back to the Government and say, “We need further funding , ” where it is outside the budgeted figures that we have.

Q240 Part of the updated offer that has been made is a 2% unconsolidated cash lump sum that may well be consolidated into base pay on the delivery of specific working practice changes and productivity savings. Can you list what they are, please?

I will not list them. I will have to write to you because there is a number of them. I am happy to share that. They are fundamentally in the maintenance area, changing the way that people are rostered. Some of our staff are rostered. I have talked about them being currently rostered in groups. We want some of those staff to be rostered individually, which is common across the rest of the industry. Drivers are all rostered individually, so we want to do the same with some of our maintenance teams. That generates a significant amount of productivity.
There are other key things that enable that reduction for employers that I mentioned earlier. That is a significant saving, and that is one of the key things that helps to fund the pay rise.

There are a number of elements to it. I am happy to go into detail, but really this is about changes that allow us to operate rail more efficiently and safer. It also saves money, and that feels to me like a win-win.

Q241 Mr Montgomery, can you list what modernisation or efficiencies you are looking for from the workforce? We hear from the Secretary of State that he wants to modernise the rail industry. That is a very vague description. Could you list everything you are looking for in terms of modernisation?

They are probably the things I listed earlier. It is the multiskilling and the rationalisation of booking offices and making sure that we repurpose people in stations so that they can do greater things. It is how we make sure we can operate a Sunday service on the seven-day railway more consistently and guarantee it.
There are pension reforms. We are talking to the trade union regarding that. There are new entrants’ terms and conditions. That is an area that we want to look at.

We have very historical terms and conditions that go back, as the trade unions will tell you, to 1928. They are some of the dates that they quote to us. It is those types of areas that we are trying to modernise.

Q242 I am very conscious of the time, but I will come back to Mr Shoveller. You mentioned the updated offer to general grades. I think there is an updated offer to management grades being sent out today. Can you tell us if that offer, or the previous offer, was higher than the offer made to general grades?

Yesterday afternoon we also made an offer to our management teams. That offer is 3%. That is obviously lower than the general grades’ offer. There are other things which are relevant for managers. Obviously, the travel is also included. Indeed, we will make a payment from our normal performance-related pay arrangements. It is lower at 3% rather than 4%.
Q243 On the base pay . W hat is it worth overall in comparison to the general grades?

The percentage rise is 3% rather than the 4%. That is the simplest answer. It is worth a percentage point less. The reason for that is fundamentally affordability. For the general grades we have been able to identify the productivity that I talked about earlier. That is obviously much harder to do for management, but we believe it is still a good offer for management, albeit it is a little different.

Q244 I mentioned the deal with ASLEF. Whether it is in Scotland, England or anywhere in the UK, we all want to see an efficient train service that gets folks to their jobs around the country on time. It allows us to decarbonise transport as part of modal shift, etc.

I noticed that the Scottish deal is 5% plus. Obviously, there is a lot to it, and I mentioned some of the things earlier. Part of that is revenue sharing once various targets are reached on revenue and other things. Is it not a better way forward to look at some of these agreements and to try to work hand in glove between management and staff, giving staff a buy-in for the future of the railways? I have the details in front of me for the deal. It is not structured in the same way. Would that be something you could look at?

Ironically, of course, travel was the thing that our people had asked for most, and that is very fundamentally about getting employee engagement and buy-in, so that our employees can use the service that they provide. That has been asked for over a very long time, so I think that is a really important first step. It is the thing that they have asked for the most.
Q245 Perhaps it is a fair question to put , Mr Montgomery , in terms of revenue sharing. Obviously, you do not drive revenue yourself. What do you say to the points I was making on that?

Again, we have not discussed it in the current discussions with the trade unions. It is not something that we would definitely take off the table in any way, but again it has to be sensible measures that you can put in place , and how do people impact on growing revenue. That is back to your point about how we get people to work together. There are areas that we can look at. It is almost a performance-related pay increase that you are looking at here and key measures.

Again, the way that you can influence revenue is by the wider workforce reforms that we carry out. It may be something that we can bring into play, but at this moment in time we have not discussed it with the trade unions.
Q246 I have one very brief last question to you, Mr Montgomery. I think you mentioned ScotRail previously; is that correct?
That is correct, yes.

Q247 Do you notice any difference in the way that pay negotiations or issues between the unions and the operators are handled in Scotland, or anyone else, versus in England with the D F T responsible.

I think what you have to remember is that , when I was in charge of ScotRail and other train operators, until the pandemic each train operator was a private entity in its own right and had the revenue risk. Since the loss of the contracts under the old traditional train operating companies—the franchise model—it is a different set-up now. Their ability to be able to negotiate in previous ways and make those decisions is no longer available because you are now virtually a concession, on a management contract. You do not have those same control measures that you previously had.
I could go on and on with that, but I will pass back to the Chair.

Q248 Before I hand over to Grahame for the last questions, let me ask this. It is very difficult sometimes to distinguish between what is a working practice, which sounds quite bizarre, and what is not. Can we pick up on one that was referenced by one of the trade union reps ? It is this concept of someone on a break and their manager interrupts them to say hello ; then the break has to start all over again.

I have heard that said. In fact, someone wrote to me and said it is the case, and why not, because they are taking a break and should not be interrupted. It was also said by the union representatives that that was not the case. It seems a bizarre one to use, but it seems a bizarre rule. Is that the case? If anyone is interrupted during their break, does it start again, even with a greeting?
I am not aware of it. I have not heard it said, certainly by any of the train operating companies that I work with. I have not heard of it in any of my businesses.
Q249 It might be a Network Rail thing.

Many years ago I recall a similar incident where a manager tried to have a conversation about an incident that occurred when someone was on a break, but not in terms of saying hello. I do not recognise that whatsoever.

We have given an example about how some of our teams will not travel in the same van as a team with a different skills discipline. I think those are things that do not do the industry any credit, frankly. If they were ever right, it was in a different era. They are certainly not relevant to the way we need to work together now.

Q250 I agree, but I have a feeling that it was actually someone from Government who first mentioned that if a break is interrupted it starts all over again. I think I have used it on that basis as well. Grahame, I am looking at you. You have not.

My point comes back to some of the earlier questions. A lot of the rhetoric cannot have helped. One hopes that there is a political ding-dong going on, but then actually you are completely insulated, in a room making sensible decisions and having good, positive discussions. Surely, it cannot help your good, positive discussions if there is so much political noise and pie chucking.

My concern is actually for our employees. As I said, the negotiations have been frank, difficult and challenging at times, but professional. My concern is for our employees because most of our people are proud to work for the railway. They come to work and very often work on their own, unsupervised, day in and day out, all hours of the day and night. They do that job well if they are proud of what they are part of.

When they hear some of those examples being used readily around the industry in that way to discredit the job they do, of course that is an issue for them. I know that will genuinely upset people. It also generally upsets me because I know there is truth to some of these things. That upsets me because I think, “Crikey, is that the modern, efficient industry that we need to be ? ” Some of these practices go back 100 years or more and are still constraining how we run the railway today. That cannot be right. There is frustration, but the only way of resolving it is through dialogue.

It would appear to undermine their role and what they do, but it also undermines your ability to say, “This is a workplace practice which could be made more efficient.” Again, it is difficult to get the facts out there. Grahame will have the final word.

Q251 Thanks, Chair. I want to pick up on something that Mr Shoveller said and put a similar point to Mr Montgomery. I want to be positive because we believe that the dispute, with good will on all sides, can be resolved amicably in the interests of the whole of the industry, the travelling public and the workforce too.
It is a really important point about the operating contracts. In fact, Steve, you said that the railways were privatised in 1997. It was in 1993 that John Major did the franchises.
Yes; correct.

Q252 In the previous panel the trade union representatives—the general sec retaries—were talking about some of the costs in the industry. I particularly take your point about multidisciplinary teams, the people who maintain the track, the overhead cable and signalling. That is an obvious idea that could produce savings if it is done safety and you have the necessary skills.

Do you take their point about the additional costs that fall on the structure of our industry from the train operating companies, from the ROSCOs—the train leasing companies—which are needless costs in running an efficient industry? Perhaps similar industries in Germany and France would not face those. Maybe that is why Eurostar does not have these costs.
I do not know if that is better directed at Steve.
In terms of privatisation, the industry has probably had above-inflation pay increases right through the whole of privatisation for the majority of people.
Q253 The trade unions argued that that was paid for through increases in productivity, halving the workforce and working weekends and so on.

They may argue that that was the case. We could also say that the model and the structure that was created made it challenging for having industrial action during those times, so the trade unions, as is their place, extracted more from the private operators and tried to increase their overall conditions, not that anybody is against improved conditions.

The key thing is that we are now in a different operating model. The available money was there, going back to Gavin’s point, whereby you could reward people by higher pay increases where you were able to increase revenue. Now, we do not have that ability within the current contracts.

Q254 I was just looking at the press release from First Group. The TOCs paid a dividend of £51.5 million for the financial year 2021. The press release is really optimistic. It says, “As the UK passenger rail industry continues its evolution to a more successful and sustainable railway system that works better for all parties, we”—that is First Group—"are both well placed to drive increased patronage and to generate resilience and consistent return for shareholders.” So, your company thinks the future is rosy.

But that is more for my open-access operation because it is a fixed fee under the NRC-type contracts. I have open-access operations as well and other part s of First Rail that make it grow. It is how we can grow within the rail industry, but that is predominantly about our being open - access businesses, where I take revenue risk.
Q255 Tim?

I wanted to add that we have seen from the Williams - Shapps review, and indeed previous reviews such as McNulty, that there is opportunity to run the railway more efficiently. The biggest thing we can do to do that is to create the guiding mind that Great British Railways offers. That is the best way that we can make sure we maintain increased service levels whil e also reducing costs. It is about the benefit of having an organisation—a guiding mind, if you will—to lead the thinking and planning for the industry. There is no doubt in my mind that that is the thing which is going to do it. We have a very positive future and one, hopefully, where we can build much better industrial relations with our employees.
On that positive note, Chair, I will hand back to you.

Thank you, Grahame. I was also going to add a positive note. We are very grateful for the time that you have given us, and indeed we are grateful for the time given to us by the trade union representatives. We hope it has not taken you away from the negotiations. We wish both sides the very best in coming to an agreement that will be of benefit to our constituents, who are of course passengers as well as workers in the great rail industry. We wish you well, and we thank you for your time.

sessions.iT: Rail strikes
sessions.w: Mick Whelan (ASLEF); National Union of Rail, Maritime and Transport Workers (RMT)

segs.tx: Transport Committee
Oral evidence: Rail strikes , HC 581
Wednesday 13 July 2022
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 13 July 2022 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Huw Merriman (Chair); Mr Ben Bradshaw; Simon Jupp ; Chris Loder; Grahame Morris; Gavin Newlands; Christian Wakeford.
Questions 1 – 159
Witnesses
I : Eddie Dempsey, Senior Assistant General Secretary, Rail, Maritime and Transport Workers Union; and Mick Whelan, General Secretary, ASLEF, the train drivers ’ union.
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Eddie Dempsey and Mick Whelan.

Q1 This is the Transport Committee’s one-off evidence session talking about the rail strikes. We have two panels. The second panel will comprise Network Rail and a representative from the train operators. In the first panel , we have the rail trade unions. I ask them to introduce themselves for the record.
I am Senior Assistant General Secretary for the RMT union.
Good morning. I am General Secretary of the train drivers union, ASLEF.
Mr Dempsey and Mr Whelan, thank you very much indeed for being with us. We have an hour with you. Before I start, I had better ask whether Members have any interests they wish to declare.
I used to be a member of the RMT a little while ago. I have worked for both witnesses on the second panel at some point in my previous career.

I was a member of the RMT in the days when it was the NUR. I am a member of the RMT parliamentary group and the ASLEF parliamentary group. From time to time , we cross paths with interests of common cause.

Q2 Excellent. Thank you to both. Let us make a start. I will lead off and then I will bring in colleagues. By way of an opener and explainer, I would ask you to set out what the dispute is about. Where is the concern on behalf of your members in terms of their current pay and their current conditions?

In 2011 we had the McNulty report , which put forward a number of changes to the rail industry. We think that the industry and Government are using the health emergency at this moment, when we are supposed to be recovering from the pandemic, to bring forward a number of those plans which are detrimental to our members.

This is also at a time where many of our members are now in the third year of a pay freeze, so they have lost substantial amounts of their real - term s earnings over that period. Inflation is really high . We have the retail price s index at 11.7% and CPI is near 10%. Our members are feeling the pinch.

We have been speaking to industry for more than 18 months now, coming up to two years. We wrote to all the companies that are controlled by the DFT in January of this year, asking for a no compulsory redundancy guarantee for our people, for a substantial pay rise and for any changes in the industry to be negotiated and not imposed on our members.

We did not get a positive response. We had some very difficult conversations between January up to June, when we ended up taking three days of strike action. We have been in discussions since. We have had a couple of pay offers, but none of those ha s met the aspirations of our people at this time.
Q3 In terms of the factual information , with regard to RMT members have there been successful ballots on every single train operator, or just on some?

There have been successful ballots on every single train operator and Network Rail. It is all the companies that are direct ly contro lled by the DFT . Where the DFT is not in control , we have achieved pay awards; we have settlements; we are not in dispute; and we are making headway. It is all the companies that are controlled by the DFT .
Q4 Does that include Southern?
Yes.
Q5 Did your members vote for strike action on Southern?
Yes.
Q6 Not just on the Network Rail side, but on Southern?
On Southern, you are talking about the GTR franchise.
Yes.
They voted for strike action on GTR as well.
Q7 Before I come to Mr Whelan, in terms of the pay offer that you are demanding, what percentage is that?

We have not put a figure on it. In those companies , there is a range of anniversary dates for pay. We tend to use the retail price s index a couple of months prior to the anniversary pay date, if you like, for the new pay award. There is a range. They are all different, so we have not put a definite figure on it.
What we are seeking is a pay rise that reflects the fact that we have lost two years of real - terms increases and the current state of inflation in the country.

Q8 Mr Whelan, y our ASLEF members were on strike in East Anglia at the same time as the RMT members were on strike. You have now had ballots across the train operators. How many of those train operators has there been a successful ballot for, and what are you seeking on behalf of your members ?

We have currently had eight ballots returned this week. There will be a further three ballots returned on the 27 th of this month. We are currently running at 92% in favour on an 88% turnout. That shows a resounding willingness among the train drivers to stand up for their terms and conditions and for their pay at this moment in time.

As a membership-led organisation, we reflect the wishes of what our members want us to do. We are in a similar position to the RMT. Our members were out there, like all key workers during the pandemic. We were grateful for the Government stepping in. This idea, though, that the Government put £600 into every household to fund our wages and keep us employed is a fallacy. Basically, the Government funded the infrastructure for the two years of the pandemic when there was no footfall going through the turnstiles. Prior to that, they had already recognised that the privatised system was not working and were working to GBR through the Shapps - Williams report. I think that is accelerating slightly.

I do echo the concerns of my colleague that people are using the pandemic as an excuse to decimate terms and conditions and force things through on a less than opportunity - cost basis. We are in the same position. After three years our deferred pension and our wages have been significantly impacted.

We seem to be slightly demonised in the press because all I read about is train drivers’ wages and comparators with other workers. We do not believe it is a race to the bottom. We would also like to emphasise that throughout the privatised process everything we have gained has been paid for by flexibility and productivity. I would love to be able to walk into a room and say, “I demand this , ” and people just give it to me, but that is not the case. The idea that we should give up what we have earn ed or that it should be devalued because of the pandemic , as an excuse , we find incredibly wrong.
Q9 Thank you. Let me come back to Mr Dempsey. I understand that you have been the lead negotiator on the Network Rail side for the RMT. Is that correct?
Yes.

Q10 We were contacted by Network Rail —ob viously, you will be aware of this. You talked about your concern about compulsory redundancies. They appear to have put an offer in for a 4% uplift for 2022, backdated to 1 January; a further 2% in 2023; and a further 2% cash lump sum that is conditional on workplace reforms. There is also discounted leisure travel for your members, and their partners and depend a nts, with a guarantee of no compulsory redundancies.
You said you had not actually put a figure on what you were looking for on behalf of your members, but are we getting there with that type of offer?

We have made some progress with Network Rail, to be sure. This is in stark contrast to the position with the train operating companies. The difficulty we have is the proposal that is being made to us by Network Rail at this time. It is based on removing more than a third of the entire frontline maintenance workforce, which is massive, and also cutting planned maintenance on the maintenance side of Network Rail in half.

That is deeply concerning to us. They are plans that we have broadly discussed with people in maintenance, including senior engineers. They tell us that this cannot possibly work. We are going to end up with an industry that is overly reliant on overtime and massively reliant on subcontractors, which imports risk and has been recognised by the predecessor of this Committee as being one of the features in a number of disasters under Railtrack.

We are really concerned that we are going back to the days of Railtrack. There is an offer that has been made, but it is conditional upon cutting a third of the entire frontline maintenance workforce and half of all scheduled maintenance tasks.

Q11 But that would be done on a voluntary redundancy basis. I do not think we can get figures out, but my understanding is that when a voluntary redundancy scheme was put in place very recently it seems to have been oversubscribed two for one, I guess because there is an ageing workforce and the terms are attractive.
Are you not at least reassured that as compulsory is off the table with this offer, it will only be those who wish to go through natural attrition and those who wish to take the terms?
We recognise that is progress. We will be formally considering that this evening. Our executive is going to meet to inspect that offer in detail.

The problem we have, as I have said, is that this is based on drastic cuts that we have deep concerns about . You have to appreciate that the cost of living in this country has gone through the roof. If we are not keeping pace with that, we are losing and our people will be poorer in real terms.
We are definitely making progress, but whether or not it is enough progress at this point will be decided by my e xecutive later today.

Q12 Mr Whelan, you make the point about pay and about inflation. Obviously , that is recognised, but Office for National Statistics figures show that over the last 10 years train and tram drivers’ pay has gone up by 39% in comparison with that of coach drivers at 11%.

Recognising that this has been an incredibly tough couple of years and that there have not been any job losses in the rail industry, do you not feel that this is the time where perhaps you have had very good and generous pay rises when times have been good, but now that times are tough everything has to be viewed through that lens?

We might argue that they are not generous because we have paid for them. In some cases , we may have undersold the productivity; in other cases , we may have benefited from what people demanded. Most people do not understand the fractionalised industry.

We have several companies out there, because of the way the DFT continually carves up the franchise map, that have three sets of train drivers and three different sets of terms and conditions. Some are with Sundays in the working work; some are with Sundays outside; and some are with different rostering proposals.

Everything that has happened happens because of the way privatisation developed over that period of time , the devolved nature of the big sector companies that could afford to do certain things and protect performance by consolidating traditional things such as mileage payments, and other companies that had to deliver regional railways on a specific budget and could not afford to do things.

I would like to come back to the fact that I have about 2,000 train drivers that would like severance. They do not want to work in your new railway or the new vision. That is 10% of the workforce. They are the ones that we know about. I think if you opened severance up to train drivers at this moment in time, they would be rushing for it. When it was offered to the other grade groups and was not offered to us, we were getting many queries about why we were not involved. That tells you something of the nature of the industry. For us, it is a cradle to grave industry. It is not a transferable skill.
The only thing we have is that we sell our labour. I f somebody now wants us , under the guise of modernisation , to sell that for far less than it is worth, that is not going to happen.
Q13 So you would actively be seeking a voluntary redundancy scheme for your drivers as part of this .

The drivers would be. I think it would exacerbate the problems of the industry , and all the things that led to people, in recruitment and retention, competing against each other—as you intended when you privatised the industry—would get 100 times worse.

Q14 Thank you, Mr Whelan. I should put the same point to you, Mr Dempsey. Back in 2019 , there was an RMT press release that is still on your website. It congratulates the RMT on an inflating-busting pay rise for members back in 2019. There has been £16 billion - worth of taxpayer money put in to support the railway over a tou g h couple of years, and the passenger numbers just are not coming back.
Taking all of that into the round, is it reasonable to expect such a high pay rise for your members?

Absolutely. We exist to achieve pay rises for our people. We do not accept that times are tough. Times are pretty good if you are a private business in the industry. You are making extremely high profits. We have parts of our industry that do not make sense from the point of view of running a railway.

We have rolling stock leasing companies, which serve absolutely no purpose, buying trains and leasing them back to the railway industry. That is something we could do ourselves. These people are making billions. They made £3 billion in the worst pandemic year in terms of revenue. A sizeable chunk of that money left this country and went to tax havens in Guernsey, Luxembourg and the Cayman Islands. Our members are painfully aware of that.

We have the private companies that have made £500 million in the worst pandemic year in the train operating companies. We have these rolling stock leasing companies, which serve absolutely no purpose in the delivery of a railway—
Q15 It is the train operators and Network Rail that we are talking about here. They are the employers , not the ROSCOs.

No, but they are part of the system. They drive the costs up. They buy the trains and lease them to the train operating companies. The train operating companies have to pay over the odds to lease these trains. That is a huge part of their expenditure.

What we have is our people looking at pay at the top of the industry going up. Some people are on over £1 million pay packages. They are looking at the profits coming out of our industry, through outsourcing, through the train operating companies and through the rolling stock leasing companies, and everyone is having a very good time out of it except our people. They are being told, “You have to tighten your belt.” When the railway should be recovering — it is going to be vital to the future of the green economy in this country —w e have a Government decision to strip £2 billion out of the operational expenditure of the railway, which is crazy.

That is what is driving a lot of the cuts. The cuts in Network Rail, for example, are not driven by trying to design a better organisation to deliver the railway. The plans in Network Rail around workforce reform and cuts are purely about achieving the figures set for them by the Department for Transport in achieving efficiencies.

Our members are looking at all of this and do not believe that times are tough. They are doing very well if you are in the right part of the industry. We think it is right that people ought to be demanding that their wages keep up with the cost of living in this country.
Thank you. It is time to open it up to other Members.

Q16 I have a question to both witnesses. From you r perspective, how have the negotiations been conducted thus far? Obviously, we hear a lot in the press and we have heard it in the Chamber, but from your perspective how have they been going so far?

Thank you. That is an interesting question. I believe that the employers that we work for have been quite disingenuous and dishonourable, in the fact that to keep their profits and maintain their opportunities within the railway industry they signed up to contracts with the DFT , allowing the DFT and the Secretary of State to determine what percentage wages we get and what we can and cannot talk about.

We have free collective bargaining. We do not work for the DFT . We do not work for the Treasury. We do not work as public sector workers at this moment at time, because the primary legislation for GBR does not exist yet.

When we walk into a room, all we get from the employers is, “We can only offer you 2% unless it is funded . ” We are saying that that is not acceptable to us at this moment in time. Then they say, “Well, the Government will not let us do anything else.” Then we get statements from the Government saying that they are not getting involved in the negotiations.
I would love somebody to assist me in this Catch-22 situation so that we can have some sort of realistic dialogue. Whether it would achieve anything or not, it would break the dilemma that we are in.
Q17 From that perspective, it sounds very much like the companies are blaming the Government and Government are blaming the companies.
And the workers are being caught in the middle and being demonised for then standing up for their rights.

That is absolutely true . It is a shame Grant Shapps has not been called here to answer some questions about this. The people on the other side of the table that we are dealing with are telling us that they regard themselves as brokers and not negotiators. They have a mandate that they have to refresh. They often have to leave the room to go and have conversations with their m inisterial people before they can continue discussions with us.
As Mick has put it, we are in a room with people who are not making the decisions. That makes it extremely difficult to get towards a settlement.

I should just say for the record that we decided, as a Committee , not to have any politicians in this session. We wanted to keep the politics out of it, actually . I take your point, but we were trying to do it from a more grown-up perspective.
Q18 I will try to tone down my next question, Chair.
I was going to ask how involved the Government ha ve been in the negotiations. By the sound of it, I am assuming it is non-existent other than trying to scapegoat and blame the unions.
There is a lot of dialogue by the press.
Q19 What we have seen specifically through you, Mr Whel a n, is ASLEF in Scotland being able to come to a settlement. What is it that Scotland has done differently as opposed to England?

It is that horrible “N” word: nationalisation. The Scottish Government now control their own railways. They now ha ve the authority to deal directly, make their own decisions and take the shackles off that we currently have under the English system.
Q20 Do you think that is primarily down to nationalisation, or do you think it is very much a Government willing to engage?
If I am being incredibly honest, and I try to be, I think the Scottish Government saw the direction of travel and chose the option to take those shackles off and allow the negotiations to take place.
Q21 For the record, what is the settlement in Scotland for your members?
I believe it is 5%.
Q22 So that would be a good indicator of what you would be looking for in the rest of the network.

Again, agreeing with my colleague, we have not set a figure. As I say, because of privatisation we have 14 TOCs , many with up to three different sets of terms and conditions within them. It may vary. We have not said there is a set figure for it. What we have actually said to our negotiators is, “If you are allowed to negotiate and there is something you can recommend, we will put it to the members within that company , ” so it might vary.

Q23 We have also seen lots of interventions from the Government , whether it has been debates about condemning strike action or whatever. Has there been any intervention from Government that has been helpful in regard to the dispute, or has it been very much a one-sided scapegoating and trying to drive a wedge?
I would believe it is very much a ramping up and making things more difficult for everybody, in my opinion.

I think so. If you listen to the messaging that has been coming from the industry side—Tim Shoveller will be here later—and from the trade unions, it has been broadly measured. If you look at the sort of comments that have been coming from Mr Shapps and people in g overnment , it has been very hairy , unhelpful comments, incendiary comments and all the rest of it. It is a worry.

If you look across the piece, in London Underground we have got 8.4%. Eurostar, whose business was completely stopped with no Government support during the health emergency, had an 8% deal recently negotiated. Docklands Light Railway has 7.3%. Merseyrail had 7.1%. Everywhere the DFT is not involved we are managing to achieve settlements and avoid disputes, including the delivery of changes and productivity needed for the industry at the same time. It seems to be the case that where the DFT is in charge what we are getting is a very hard position with a very unpalatable set of demands on us in terms of making cuts and what is euphemistically called “modernisation ” , but is in fact winding back the clock on trade union rights and decent terms and conditions.

That is a real worry. That is where all the input from the Government has been unhelpful. By the way, they are also indemnifying the train operating companies from any losses they incurred during strike action, so they are hardly taking a neutral position in this.

Q24 Certainly from the Opposition’s perspective, we have been saying that the Government should be getting a round the table. By the sounds of it, where you have been able to get a settlement it has been without DFT or Government intervention. With the rhetoric that is being put out, would Government representation be helpful in regard to some of the conversation, or do you think we have gone past the point of no return and a lot of good will will need to be regenerated?

If they are going to take a leading and directing role in all of these disputes, they ought to be at the table to negotiate a settlement. It is either that or they need to just get out of the way entirely and allow us to bargain freely with our employers and reach settlements , as we have always done.

I could add to that. Some of what they are asking for is counterintuitive. We have seen our employers generate profits throughout the pandemic. We have seen the forecast profits under the new contracts that they have, yet we are expected to fund the productivity for these employers, where 85% of the money goes to support state railways elsewhere. We find that rather difficult. Rather than the employers paying us, we are paying the employers , which I do not think is the way it traditionally works.

Q25 With regard to the rhetoric that has come from Government , I would imagine there is quite a lot that both unions would dispute strongly. Is there any particular message that you would like to get on record?

We believe we have free collective bargaining. Please let us bargain. Traditionally within the industry, it finds its level and we find a solution. We are being driven into strife by the Government not allowing the companies to talk to us. One contract has 22 clauses that they have to refer back to the Government on issues relating to pay and conditions before they can make an agreement with us.

I would say that people ought to be aware that right now Network Rail spends more servicing its debts from the privatised era than it does on delivering maintenance to the railway infrastructure of this country. That is extremely worrying. Their whole plans are based on Government -set cuts to the operational expenditure of the railway. In order to achieve that they need to rip out one third of the frontline workforce in maintenance and half of the scheduled maintenance work in the industry. That is not a recipe for success in a railway that needs to expand and be part of the green future of this country.

On the other side of it, we have had a lot of very hairy rhetoric from the Government . It seems that the answer the Government ha ve to the cost - of - living crisis is to criminalise dissent against poverty. They are talking about bringing in laws to further restrict trade unions. It is worth noting that the global index on trade union freedom, done every year by TUC International, rates us as No. 3 . That means there are regular violations in this country of trade union freedoms, such as the right to collectively bargain, the right to strike and the right to organise and build a trade union and have your civil liberties defended.

I would urge people to look at that list. We have some very interesting company on rating No. 3 . It is really worrying that the Government ’s answer to the cost - of - living crisis is to criminalise dissent against poverty in this country.

Q26 A final question. Mr Whelan, you have highlighted one of the arguments and , unfortunately , the unhelpful political atmosphere where it seems to be train drivers versus the rest of the world and how they are paid more than nurses and teachers. What message would you like to send out to correct that? It does not sound fair. If it is a race to the bottom—
Christian, ask the question. They are here to give the evidence.
It does sound, as you said, like a race to the bottom. What can we do to counter the narrative?

We have publicly stated, and have for 140 years, that we believe all workers deserve decent pay. We believe that nurses, firefighters and shop workers are all currently valued by society and should be financially rewarded for what they do. We do not believe that anybody is going to automatically give it to them if we do not fight for our own rights at the same time. We will not engage in a race to the bottom.

Q27 I want to pick up on an earlier response. The Chair indicated that the object of this session is to interview you as representatives of the trade unions and the workforce, and then interview the employers to see whether there is a workable solution that could resolve the current disputes.

It seems to me that the main actor—the Wizard of Oz who is pulling the levers behind the scenes—is not here. A convenient smokescreen is being put up that this is not an issue for the Secretary of State. You mention the Department for Transport, but it is clearly m inisterial direction. It is set out in the terms and conditions of the train operating companies and Network Rail.
In your opinion, should the Secretary of State be here to give an account of his actions if he is indemnifying the train operating companies and Network Rail from any losses they may suffer?

I would say that is down to the Chair of the Select Committee to decide whether they want him to give evidence. My view, quite simply, is that there should be no interference in free collective bargaining. As has been highlighted, quite rightly, we are employed by people who are making profits out of our industry and who we were forced to deal with for the last two-and-a-half decades. We have done that in good faith. That good faith element has now been damaged by third-party interference that has set out what can be paid, what cannot be paid and what must be dealt with.
Where is our wish list in this? Where are our aspirations? Where are our demands? There are not any, strangely enough, in this post-pandemic world.

I would also like to correct something. We are not seeking pay rises. We are seeking not to go further behind. We are not seeking a backdating of the two years that we did not get a pay rise during the pandemic. As you saw in Scotland, we are seeking to achieve something that takes us towards the cost - of - living crisis. We have not asked for more than RPI. We do not want to gain in a post-pandemic world. It is about not deteriorating; it is about not being degraded; it is about not falling further behind.

Q28 Mr Dempsey, on this point the Secretary of State has consistently raised, both in interviews and in response to questions and in debates in the House of Commons, that this is a dispute about modernisation and the trade unions resisting modernisation.

Some years ago, prior to privatisation when I worked on the railways, there were over 400,000 people employed on the railways. I do not know what the figure is currently. Examples were given about the use of modern technology cameras fitted on trains to identify cracked rails and so on , and not working at night time in dangerous conditions.
What is the trade union view on that? Perhaps I could ask Mr Dempsey in relation to maintenance about this modernisation argument.

We are absolutely in favour of modernisation and technology that keeps our people safe. It is an extremely dangerous industry and an extremely dangerous role that our members perform. We have heard an awful lot of us being opposed, for example, to drones. We have been to two demonstrations of drones in operation. On one occasion the weather was not quite right, so they could not get the drones to fly. On another occasion they landed a drone in someone’s garden. We were due to go back for a further demonstration on 21 June, but unfortunately we were on strike that day.

Where drones can be used to improve inspection work, we are in favour of it. We use lineside early warning systems and remote disconnection devices. We use telematics and ultrasonics. We have plain-line pattern recognition trains—those yellow trains you see—and an entire department of people responsible for analysing the data that comes back from that in a department called Asset Information. We are in favour of using technology.

We have assisted in the bringing in of a couple of particular pieces of technology that allow Network Rail to meet its improvement notice under the ORR. We are in favour of technology. What we are not in favour of is technology being brought in on a cliff edge that makes people unemployed. Our opinion has always been that , if you have a new spanner that does the job better than the old spanner, you do not sack the bloke who used the old spanner but teach him how to use the new one. Our expectation is that , where technology is brought in, workers are upskilled so that they can be modernised along with the industry.

Q29 Is that not going to be the case if there are no compulsory redundancies? A camera sensor can take 70,000 pictures per minute to check on cracks . When that comes in, it will displace labour. Every industry works on that basis. When technology comes in , humans are not needed as much. Notwithstanding that, this offer that we were talking about actually takes compulsory redundancies off the table. Everyone who wants a job within Network Rail will still have one, notwithstanding the advances in technology. In other parts of industry that gift is not there, and they lose their jobs. So, you have got your assurance on that basis.

No compulsory redundancies is a definite improvement and we are very pleased to see that finally come forward, because up to now it has only been offered to the press by Ministers and not by anyone in the room negotiating. We are very relieved to finally see that written down on a piece of paper.

At the bottom of it, you have to appreciate it is not just the people who are being removed. One third of the entire frontline maintenance organisation is being taken out, and one half of all scheduled maintenance tasks are being removed. That does not seem to me to be a modern idea, when what we need is an expanded and efficient railway to look after the needs of the country. It seems to me, and is reflected in opinion we have had back from people right across Network Rail’s organisation, including senior people, that we are going back to the bad old days of Railtrack here. We are going back to a reliance on contractors and overtime in an industry that is safety critical. We think that poses its own questions and its own problems outside of the context of a no compulsory redundancy agreement, which we are pleased to see finally down on a piece of paper.

Q30 I want to ask about the changes to working practices. The Committee recently visited Manchester as part of our inquiry into the integrated rail plan . We had discussions at Piccadilly station about the number of upgrades and major schemes that are happening. There is the TransPennine upgrade , the integrated rail plan, east - west links, as well as HS2.

There is a difficulty in recruiting skilled people in order to undertake this quite demanding engineering work. Is not one of the changes that are being proposed by Network Rail to change the rostering ? Is it 39 weeks that people will be required to commit to? How is that going to attract the thousands of people that we want into the industry? Are you opposing that or are you prepared to negotiate on it ? Is it a legitimate area of contention?

We are happy to accept what is known in the industry as the higher rostering principles. This means you can work 39 weeks of night shifts, 39 whole weekend turns or 65 weekend shifts in the course of a year. We have had that in place since 2012. Lots of our people work to those higher rostering principles now. We are happy to continue to agree to those arrangements going forward.

What you have to appreciate is that our members work 24/7 around the clock. There are all kinds of shifts. Their shifts can be moved. Their shifts can be amended in order to fit the needs of the business. The real problem in Network Rail is planning. They have a problem in delivering the right number of people to undertake tasks as they are needed. We have people being sent out to do tasks that are not required. We have an over-reliance on contractors, which ramps up the cost of delivering maintenance.

Our members are some of the most flexible workers in any industry. It is absolute nonsense to say that we are not working in ways that are flexible. They have a problem with planning in Network Rail, not with flexible workers.

Q31 T o correct one thing, Mr Whelan—I will explain again, though I thought I had tried to state this—we agreed as a Committee who would be here. We agreed as a Committee that we would not have any politicians. It is not down to the Chair to decide who comes. The reason you are here, Mr Whelan, is that on Monday night I messaged Members and said, “I think Mick Whelan should be invited because ASLEF are now taking action , ” and they agreed with me. If they had disagreed, you would not have been here. We are a bit more democratic than you may think.
Q32 Gentlemen, it sounds from what you have been saying that you think the Government ha ve deliberately picked this dispute. Why would they do that?

If you ask me, I think the Government were a bit shaky recently and probably felt it was a good opportunity to pick a fight, particularly with the RMT, and to paint us as the enemy within. I think they have bitten off more than they can chew because it has clearly demonstrated that the public is on our side and not the side of the Government . They support our efforts to achieve protection for our people in a cost - of - living crisis. They do not support the massive cuts that are being proposed and they do not support the Government bringing in more authoritarian legislation to take away the right of the working people to dissent against poverty.

I think they have picked a fight with us. If you listen to some of the rhetoric coming out of the Government , it is pretty clear that that is what they were after. Some of the stuff they were saying was so crazy, such as if a manager says hello to a railway worker , it means you have to start your break over from scratch. The industry could not run. They are saying that there are too many people in the industry, but the whole industry runs on overtime. How does it make sense, if you have an industry that runs on overtime, to slash thousands of jobs out of it? That is not going to improve the situation, is it? I think they have picked a fight with us.

Q33 Do you see a lack of engagement across Government , or would you blame a particular Department such as the Treasury, the Department for Transport or the Prime Minister — though not for much longer? Where do you think the blockage or the real problem is?

I do not know. I suspect it is the Department for Transport, but I do not really know what goes on over here if I am honest with you. It is just pretty clear that the people we are dealing with in the room have a mandate from the DFT . The DFT writes the contracts. Part of the arrangement for the train operating companies to be indemnified against losses occurring from strike action is that they have to carry out the DFT ’s mandate. We estimate that £65 million of taxpayers’ money was given to the train operating companies so that they did not lose any profits during our strike action. The Minister has at least admitted that he is responsible for those mandates and will have to sign off any deal. It is pretty clear that this dispute is in the hands of the Department for Transport and Grant Shapps . I think that is obvious to everyone. I think he has even admitted that really at this point, which is useful , I suppose.

Q34 What do you think the impact is likely to be of the fact we now have eight weeks of Conservative party leadership campaigning ? Will that allow those Ministers the capacity to engage and change their approach to solve this crisis?

I do not really know how that is going to affect things. What I do know is that a lot of our members were very upset to see their livelihoods and their industry used as a political football in that session in Parliament. Lots of our members saw that and were deeply hurt and upset by it. That was a real shame.

Q35 Mr Whelan, you reminded the Committee that quite a lot of the profits that are made by companies here are channelled back often into s tate-run organisations on the continent. Can you give us a picture—and you too, Mr Dempsey—of what your equivalent members in countries like Germany, Sweden and France enjoy in terms of working conditions and how that generally compares with here? I often find these international comparisons very instructive.

In most countries , train drivers retire far earlier on far better pensions. Most of them have 35-hour, four-day weeks. Most of them are in countries where the infrastructure is seen as a national asset and generates for the local GDP and the national GDP. It is not expected to make a profit per se. I think we saw that during the pandemic. The cost of running the infrastructure was the cost of running the infrastructure, but before the pandemic for every £1 invested in transport, £5 was coming back to the country. Post pandemic, it is £2 for every £1 invested in transport. We do believe that transport washes its face.

T hose countries have nationalised railways. They have integrated transport. Germany recently created a € 9 ticket anywhere i n Germany for a month. Ireland dropped train and bus fares to encourage people back on to public transport and to get people back out there.

What did we do in the last three years? We introduced a 10-ticket carnet when the nature of work changed. You had to use it within a month. The disadvantage of that was that with traditional season tickets you paid for five days and you got the weekends free, whether they were weekly, monthly, quarterly or annually. People psychologically believed that they were getting something out of it, even if they did not use that ticket travelling to their place of work at weekends. We introduced the 10-ticket carnet where, if you broke it down, it was cheaper to buy a ticket on the day. That has not encouraged people back.

At the same time, we did go to the Government mutually as trade unions and say, “Annual fare rises are within your gift.” They put fares up by 3.8% while cutting the duty on short - haul air traffic. If you look at France, if there is a train that can get you between cities in four hours, they have stopped short - haul flights. There is a totally different political dynamic to what people do and how they see transport on the continent, and how they value their workers.
Q36 Mr Dempsey, is that a similar picture for your people?

It is a similar picture, yes. The main feature is the level of profiteering in our transport sector compared to countries elsewhere. That leads to better investment in the transport networks and to broadly decent terms and conditions.
Q37 Most European countries invest more and put more public money into the railways.
They do.

Q38 The Government seem to be assuming that passenger numbers will be permanently reduced post pandemic, largely as a result of the growth in homeworking and flexible working. Is that something you accept? Does that not have to have some impact on your aspirations for your members and the amount of money that can come into the industry?

The changing nature of the industry is something that we will all have to live with and adapt to. At this moment in time , recent figures in recent weeks have seen passenger numbers com ing back to 92% of previous footfall. That does not offset the amount of fare revenue that we lost in the previous couple of years.

We are seeing horrendous pictures of overcrowded trains. We have seen the shift from Monday to Friday to Tuesday to Thursday. The word “ TW a Ts ” is now being used for the commuters: Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursdays only. We have seen a massive increase in footfall at weekends. How do we sustain that and grow it? The real problem is still slightly counterintuitive by putting up fares and reducing services.

There are areas in the north-west where , I believe, currently they get one train every three hours. That is not going to encourage people back on to our lines for commuters, tourism or other purposes. We would much rather have seen a railway that ran as it did, and then reduce your services to the demand once you see what that demand is when it comes back over a period of time .

Commuter railways will still run on Monday to Friday, regardless of whether there are full numbers on a Monday and Friday. Therefore, I think we would like to see a greater period of time before massive change within the industry, so that any change we do make recognises the long-term changes. At this moment , it is still quite reactive.

There definitely are changes, but how they will bed in in the long term is yet to be seen. What we are seeing at the moment is the railway industry being talked down. What we are hearing and the rhetoric around it is almost like a managed decline of the industry. Putting out flashy adverts to offer a few cheap fares for leisure travel on a weekend does not help us because we have seen the leisure travel come back really strongly .

At the moment , it seems that the Government want everybody to travel on the weekend. They want to do all the major maintenance on the infrastructure at the weekend at the same time. That does not make sense. If you have a high volume of traffic on the weekend, then you pick a quieter time to do the engineering work.

We have to incentivise people to come back to the railway industry. We want to get people out of cars. It is part of the green future for the economy. You cannot do that while talking about a managed decline of the railway industry. It needs to be encouraged, supported and helped to recover properly and grow rather than talking about a managed decline because we have had a temporary fall in passenger numbers due to a global health emergency.
Q39 Thank you. Finally, Chair, forgive me if I missed this right at the beginning , but is there a date for the next industrial action?
We meet tomorrow to discuss our recent results.

Q40 You talk about the need to focus on the leisure market and weekends, which actually has shown signs of growth , unlike the weekdays. On that basis, are you very much of the view that we will have to change the voluntary working on a Sunday practice and, like other parts of industry across the UK, that will become a normal working day?
For 25 days we have been saying that you cannot run a performance-driven industry on voluntary overtime. The companies that, at privatisation, had the resources to protect their performance did so.

There was a cost to that. Anybody can have Sundays in the working week. It can be negotiated. It is our aspiration. We want to have it, but the opportunity costs of that cannot be devalued just because we are in a post-pandemic world. If you want people to work additionally over and above their contracted week, we are not going to force people into indentured work at weekends. It has to be part of the overarching contract.
Q41 How many TOCs have Sunday as a normal working day, if I can call it that, where your members are rostered?
Over 50%.
Q42 What would it take to get the other 50% working to the same degree? Your members must be comfortable with it.

It comes back to my colleague’s point. You need the staff to do it. If you put Sundays in the working week , it drives your establishment up by 20%, but you have enough staff there to cover your three-shift, seven-day-a-week railway as required.

At the moment , you have certain days relying on overtime working. You lose the flexibility that is within your contracts to get people to do their day job. If you are forever robbing Peter to pay Paul because someone will work a Sunday, then they are not available for everything they might do on a Monday, or if you are already working other rest days.

Q43 Let me put this to you. Yes, I take the point that you would then need more drivers, but if the number of services daily has gone down from 24,000 to 20,000 timetabled because of the pandemic, so the timetable has not been fully restored, then surely you have that bandwidth to give you what you need.

I have had people working 13 days out of 14 for the last 23 years. They are working their quality time off. We gave massive productivity to generate quality time off. Unfortunately, many of our people never got the advantage of it because they work their rest days. Some choose to work a Wednesday as their day off rather than work the Sunday because it is not in their working week.

As we have said, we have a high overtime culture within the railway industry. The reduction of services should then reflect the fact of the number of people required to do it. It does not necessarily mean that because you reduce the services during the week you have enough people to cover a seven-day-a-week service. It does not work that way.

Q44 But if the employers were in charge of when they actually wanted the staff to work, which at the moment they cannot on a Sunday because it is voluntary, then they could look at the reduction from 24,000 to 20,000 and say, “Now I can spread the workforce across a seven-day week . ” That is what most employers have the ability to do, but not in this industry. That is why some think, “Look, this is a very antiquated way of trying to run a service.”

Even in companies where we have Sundays in the working week, there is a requirement for overtime working. Unfortunately, the tradition in a railway, because it is a three-shift system—people seem to forget that it is a 24-hour railway and trains do need to be maintained, cleaned and whatever else outside the running hours and whatever else, and staff on the train you get at 8 o’clock in the morning have generally got on at 3.20 am to get it to the point where it starts or departs, or whatever else—is that people do 11-hour days. We are living in an industry that is not particularly modern. We have five or six-hour turns with no breaks, where our people are using Tena products to survive in their cabs. It is not particularly pretty.

This vision of the railway is not quite the one. Traditionally on the railway, the shift change takes place on a Sunday. There is a three-shift system: mornings, afternoons and nights. The shift change takes place on a Sunday. If you increase Sunday turns, your ability to get people back from when they are finished on a night shift on a Sunday to a Monday afternoon or a Monday morning or another shift becomes impacted. It is not just as simple as the juggling of days.
Q45 I have a last question before I hand over to Simon. What are the contracted hours for train drivers?
In most cases an average of 35 hours for a four-day week, but in some places it is still a five-day week.
Q46 A 35-hour, four-day week and yet your previous answer suggested that actually it was an almost 24-hour process. Obviously, it is for the train drivers as a whole, but —

The day before a train driver or critical safety member of staff goes to work is no good to them because they cannot enjoy the rest of things that society enjoy. They have to rest. They have to be responsible. They have to be whatever they do. Most of them are working their days off currently, or have been working their days off.
Q47 But then getting paid overtime for working their days off.

They get paid for that, and that is voluntary as well. Our view has always been that we do not want people living on voluntary overtime or working voluntary overtime. We would much rather have full employment.
