You need to let the railway run, get back to its levels of where the future demand or GDP drives it, because privatisation drove nothing, and then determine the levels of establishments and what you need and the timetables you require. You then determine how many people you need to run it. You cannot arbitrarily change people’s contracts and their shift systems and say, “You are going to work every Sunday for the next 24 years.”
I would not disagree with that. Let me hand over to Simon Jupp , and then we are going to Chris Loder.
Q48 Simon Jupp : Thank you, Chair. Good morning, gentlemen.

Consumer confidence is really important in the railway industry. My colleague Ben Bradshaw mentioned passenger numbers. You , Mr Whelan, mentioned that it is 92% —that, obviously , is not across the board. I do not think it is as high as that in the south-west, wh ich I represent.

I am really worried about the car-led recovery from the pandemic. Understandably, the Government put out some warning signs at the start of the pandemic about using public transport. We now know that we probably did not need to do that, but we have learnt lessons from that. Passenger numbers have not come back.
Do you think that strike action hurts confidence among consumers, when we want to get people back?

Look, the underlying deceit here—it is a strong word I am using—was the employers entering into a contract that allowed someone else to dictate what we would be paid and what our terms and conditions would be without the free collective bargaining process that we enjoyed with our privatised employers—
Q49 Simon Jupp : I am not talking about that—
Hold on. The confidence—
Q50 Simon Jupp : I am not talking about that. You have diverted my question. My question is about—
I am answering your question.

Q51 Simon Jupp : It was a long time coming. Passenger numbers are down. Confidence in public transport is down. Strike action does not help that, does it? How does that bring people back and make sure that we have a greener future?

Strangely enough, the polling that we do—and I do not believe it is just the railways that are going on strike currently; there are barristers, postal workers, teachers and all sorts of people—shows that there is an underlying feeling from workers everywhere in this post-pandemic world that the cost - of - living crisis is driving them to do things. It is exacerbated in the railway because we cannot talk to our employers or the people pulling the strings.
The strike action is the fault of this G overnment and the fault of the employers, and not the workers who have been disadvantaged.
Q52 Simon Jupp : You are here to serve passengers. Passengers are—
Why are we here to serve passengers?
Q53 Simon Jupp : Without passengers you would not have a job, would you?
I would.
Q54 Simon Jupp : What would your members be doing?

That is not the point. You asked what I would do. I do not serve the passengers. I have spent my whole career trying to grow this industry, trying to make it safer, trying to make it greener and trying to make it cheaper. Most of the time in previous years I would have been on many platforms with many people in this room and elsewhere trying to do that. At this moment in time—
Q55 Simon Jupp : No one doubts that your members work really hard . During the pandemic it was a dreadful time to work on the railways—
We work in partnership.

Q56 Simon Jupp : —and it was really difficult with all the different regulations and restrictions that were placed on you. Now, as we try to build back confidence in the railway sector, people need to use public transport again, whether it is branch lines, main railway lines or rural lines wherever they may be. If you go on strike, you are cutting people off from going to work, going to school —they are missing exams and everything else. That is just hurting confidence.

Part of that confidence is the confidence of people within the industry to be treated equitably and to come and work fairly for their employer. Nobody goes on strike lightly. We see it as a failure when we have to do so. We do not want to be on strike. Our people do not want to lose money, but when you get the level of mandates that we are receiving of 98% in favour on an 88% turnout, I think it is the strength of feeling of the members that I work for which is telling me it is their only option at this moment in time.

It does resonate with the public because the public have a great deal of sympathy at this moment in time. It is strange that we have more sympathy now than we have ever had in the past for rail workers or transport workers going on strike.

Q57 Simon Jupp : I have a great deal of sympathy for your railway workers. I also have a great deal of sympathy for passengers who were stranded for days during the strike action in parts of the south-west, who I represent.

Mr Dempsey, I have the same question to you. We all want passenger numbers to go back to what they were, and to increase. How can we make sure that we do that if you are going to interrupt their service?

I do not think confidence in railways and public transport is helped by the Government stripping £2 billion out of the operational expenditure of the railways and talking about a managed decline of our transport system. That is not going to increase confidence in getting people out of their cars and back on the trains.
Q58 Simon Jupp : That is your wording. “Managed decline” is not a phrase used by the Government .
They are talking about having a smaller, cheaper railway that has less services on it. That is a decline, not an expansion or a growth.
Q59 Mr Dempsey, we have finished an inquiry into the £96 billion integrated rail plan . What you have just said does not quite equate with what is being spen t and planned over the decades.

That is a different type of expenditure. I am talking about the operational expenditure of the railway, which now has a £2 billion black hole in it, thanks to the Government . That is not going to increase any passenger confidence in using the railway. If you are talking about having a cheaper, smaller railway with less services and you want to achieve that by cutting back on people’s wages and cutting jobs out of the industry, that does not achieve confidence in transport, does it?

Q60 Simon Jupp : Can you not see that by interrupting services and people being forced to use their car and not being able to work, it is actually counterproductive for your members, who rely on those passenger numbers to survive and keep their jobs ?

If we had a way of achieving a settlement without taking strike action, we would do it, but we have been forced into this position. We have had the operational expenditure stripped. We have had demands put on us by the industry, mandated by Government , to decimate our jobs. We have been told, “You will accept a pay cut , ” as part of that package, for the pleasure of having jobs taken out, members of my trade union thrown on the dole and having terms and conditions we have achieved over many years stripped out. “You will have a pay cut for that as a reward.”
What do you expect from a trade union under those circumstances? Do you want us to just doff our caps and say, “Thank you very much, governor”? That is not going to happen.
Simon Jupp : I think it is about the bigger picture, but I will leave it there because I know that other people want to come in.

Q61 I want to come back on that. Again, it is trying to match the rhetoric of what you have just said with what we have on a piece of paper — that being either the contracted hours that Mr Whelan gave us or what you have just said about taking workers out and , using the rhetoric that you have , about not getting any increases. There is an 8% increase over the two-year period and no compulsory redundancies. That is what we have been emailed from Network Rail, and you recognise that as an offer as well.

I recognise that as progress, but you have to appreciate 8% out of five years , over two years , represents a real - term s pay cut. You will be poorer with that offer than if you got one that reflected where you are in terms of earnings in the economy as it is. That does not answer the question on the cost - of - living crisis, to give somebody a real - term s pay cut.

Q62 Do you not take into account any comparator? We have done a lot of work on aviation. Five thousand workers lost their job. There was no Government support. They got furlough ed and nothing else. Do you not take that into account? There has been an insulated period. Yes, inflation is high , but, to come back to Mr Whelan’s stated aim of always wanting the railway to be cheaper and the concern about rail price increases of just over 3% putting people off, ultimately you are going to have to put the prices up even further to pay for the pay rises that you want—
That is not what is happening.
Q63 —otherwise where does the money come from?

Let us have a look at this. Grant Shapps and Andrew Haines, who runs Network Rail, modernised the CAA. Look at the state of it. Now they are going to modernise the railway. There is plenty of money in my industry, and it is going out of it in the form of profits. It is leaving this country and going to tax havens.
Q64 The taxpayer has put £16 billion into supporting the railway over the last number of years.

It ran the infrastructure during the pandemic—during a national crisis—to get key workers to work and to move food and medicine around this country. The cost of running that railway was £16 billion. The £!6 billion did not go directly into the pockets of train drivers or other rail workers—
Q65 Mr Whelan, no one is saying—
—but £102 million went in profits to First Group alone.

Q66 Mr Whelan, no one is saying that. What is being said is that it used to be the case that, by and large, train operators , through passenger ticket receipts , used to pay for themselves , but that fell off a cliff because people were not using the rail—
Eddie Dempsey : It has never paid for itself.
Q67 —the taxpayer had to step in with £16 billion.
Eddie Dempsey : The railway has been subsidised since privatisation.
Q68 But are you disputing the fact that basically it used to wipe its face—
No, it did not wipe its face. That is a falsehood, unfortunately.
Q69 I put it to you that it is not because—
Okay, let me put my rationale first, please.

Q70 Both Labour and Conservative Governments have gone with above - inflation increases in rail ticket prices to make sure that it does, largely, pay for itself. The numbers fell off a cliff, which is why the taxpayers’ subsidy had to continue to run it and then not make redundancies. Are you disputing that is the case?

Yes. I will send two reports to you that we had done previously, “ The Great Rail Rip Off ” , and others. To service the excess charges of the operators, £7 billion went into the industry , of which they paid £3.5 billion back and then were allowed to take their services over and above it. They never paid their full costs, and they never made their money out of fares.
Write to me with all of that, and I will look forward to looking at it. The Library will research it and we will write back.

Q71 Good morning, chaps. Nice to see you. I want to concentrate my questions on the TOCs side of things because we have talked plenty about Network Rail. I think we should just think about the TOCs a bit more.

I would like to ask both of you—and I will come to you first, Mick—about terms and conditions , which we mentioned earlier. Which are the specific terms and conditions that give you cause for concern that either the train operators want to negotiate out or you want to stand particularly firm on?
One of the things that we seem to be seeing is an indication that they want to introduce DOO across the board.
Q72 Introduce DOO across the board?
Driver-only operation.
Q73 You have supported that on many occasions, have you not, as a union?

We have 50% of the TOCs that are DOO. As you know from the last time that we might have been in front of you, which was the Southern dispute, we do not believe it is a safe way of operation currently. Prior to the pandemic the rate of sexual assaults on our railway ha d gone up dramatically. I think that has been recognised by this body in the past, and county lines and all the other things that were going on. We are very much against that.
Q74 Can I be clear? Is ASLEF’s position that—
No DOO.
Q75 —that driver - only operation is not safe?
It always has been, yes, for the last few years.
Q76 Any other terms and conditions?
Well, I am answering loads of questions about modernisation. The last time I was asked this question by Philip Hammond—that is how far it goes back—about train drivers demanding time to change ends.
Q77 I am not really worried about what Philip Hammond had to say.
I know, but it is on the list of all the things. Reduction in training time for train drivers.
Q78 Reduction in training time?
Yes, and forcing people to work over and above their contract at weekends.
Q79 What is the training time at the moment ?
It is roughly a year, but it depends on which company you are in because of the geographical nature.
Q80 A year?
Yes. It takes about 34 weeks to train a train driver, and then to get competent on various tractions and routes. It depends what company you are in.
Q81 What about Sundays?
We want Sundays in the working week, but we are not doing it for nothing.
Q82 What are you saying you want for Sundays to be in the working week?

It will be down to our membership and what is offered, but it is a difficulty for us that everything that we do when we change our members’ terms and conditions goes to them for their decision. If the deal is inequitable, they will not vote for it.
Q83 Eddie, can I ask you the same questions about T&Cs ?
In the train operating companies we are concerned about new contracts being brought into the industry on far inferior terms than currently exist. We are worried about new contracts being—
Q84 I am thinking more about the current ones. I appreciate it is another debate, but—

There are three key areas, I suppose. N o. 1 is the reintroduction of DOO. It is something that has been the subject of disputes for many years in the railway industry. They want that across the board, which we do not.
They want to shut almost 1,000 ticket offices in the country.

Q85 Let me ask you about that. I have your press release that you sent to the national media dated 9 May. You have listed in excess of probably 1,000 ticket offices. I am afraid I have not been through to count them all. Can you tell me where you got that information from?
From Transport Focus.
Q86 How are they involved in this?
I would have to write to you on that, because that was done in our policy department. The people in the industry have told us that the number now is 980.

Q87 You have made the point about ticket office closures, but you have not really been able to substantiate from within your negotiations that that is actually true and accurate. Suggesting, for example—
I have not finished speaking.
Q88 Please do. Where does it come from?
If you will give me a second, I will substantiate it . The industry have told us—the people who negotiate—that they want to close 980 ticket offices.

Q89 And they particularly want to close Clapham Junction ticket office and London Waterloo . There is a list. The reason I am asking the question is because I have a list of them here. I am just unclear as to how—
My understanding is that that was a list from Transport Focus, who are expecting a flurry of applications for the closure of those ticket offices.
Q90 So, the RMT has basically made that statement—
Based on the information we had at the time, is my understanding.
Q91 Chris Loder: — based on something from Transport Focus and not from the train operators.
The point has been clarified since by industry. They have told us it is 980 ticket offices that they want to close.

That is one area. We are concerned about across-the-board degradation of terms and conditions in introducing new contracts of employment with longer working hours and lower pay for everyone in the industry.

We are also concerned about the Sunday question. We have quite a mixed picture on Sunday working. We have people who work committed Sundays. I think you probably will have heard the same terms when you were on the railway. You have Sundays that are voluntary, but you are obligated to work them , so you might as well have them.
Q92 So they are inside the working week, as it happens.

So are many of our members. We are quite relaxed about that point. What we are not prepared to do is have our working weeks extended from the hours that we have by five hours to accommodate that without an increase in pay.
Q93 Is your position that you would like Sundays in the working week, subject to negotiation?

We do not mind. I have recently done a deal with Network Rail, funnily enough, where we said to them, “You can have Sundays inside the working week or outside the working week, committed or not committed, any way you want, as long as the pay is right for them.” They were quite content to have them outside of the working week.

I think this is one of those points there is a lot of heat around, but it does not make sense when you drill into it. We are quite content to accommodate Sunday working. We know the industry wants to have improved services on the weekends, and we support that, but what we are not prepared to do is work hours for free to accommodate that. If we are going to work longer hours, we expect to be paid for those hours.
Q94 Mick, w hat was ASLEF’s policy on trainee drivers during the pandemic?

On trainee drivers, there are an awful lot of functions that require two people in a cab. What we put forward was quite creative in partnership. We created bubbles within the industry. For those that needed to go out to do signal sighting or those who needed to go on the front of a train, we extended that process. If you had an instructor and a trainee, they would go into a bubble. They would be tested. Once they were both clear , they would be tested every week. They would work together for that period of time to make sure that the trainees could be trained.
Q95 So, for the whole period ASLEF’s position was that provided the instructor and the trainee were bubbled together, they could continue throughout that period .

And then, for the classroom-based training, we put in social distancing, cleansing and lower numbers in the classroom. We tried to do everything we could to protect those roles and those jobs, and to ensure that the throughput happened.

Q96 For any train operators that may or may not tell me that trainees had to stay at home because the union said they would not allow a trainee with an instructor/driver in the cab, is it incorrect of them to say that?
There was the opportunity for them to put processes in place along the guidelines in the agreements that were agreed at the RICF. During the pandemic the joint trade union—
Q97 Is it incorrect for them to say that?
It is incorrect because there was a process, if they chose to follow it.
Q98 What you are saying is that , if the TOCs wanted to have trainee drivers during the pandemic, they would have had to come to you to ask you to endorse it for that to happen. Is that correct?

No; that was not what happened. What happened was that at the height of the pandemic we could not force them. You cannot wear masks in a driving cab. Most drivers wear spectacles and they fog up and whatever. Because of that, and because of cleaning regimes, the driver/instructors or the trainees could do it on a voluntary basis, initially. We could not force or coerce people to do it. We put a system in place where it could happen.
Q99 On a local basis your representatives have interpreted that.
Not really. I think most of the things that came out of the industry body at that time worked as a standard practice across all the TOCs.
Q100 Do you know what percentage of trainee drivers actually did train during the pandemic and those who sat at home—

I do not know. You also factor in that an awful lot of train drivers would have been driving trains normally because of the amount of people impacted by the pandemic, safeguarding or else. Not all instructors were available. The ability to do it as you would normally do it and the numbers who would normally do it would not have existed.

Q101 Gavin is here. I hope I am not going to steal your thunder, Gavin, but I wanted to ask about the situation in Scotland. You have agreed with ScotRail, as I understand it, a 5% pay deal over what period?
I believe it is a one-year deal.
Q102 A one-year deal.
I will confirm that for you.
Q103 Were there any efficiencies or productivities associated with that?
Nothing substantial to my knowledge, but I can get you a copy of the deal and send it to you.
Can I make a point about ScotRail, though? ScotRail was different from the other TOCs because they had had pay rises in the intervening two years.
Q104 Thank you. Is the unofficial overtime ban in Scotland now off for drivers?
I would not know. I did not know there was an unofficial overtime ban. Thank you for apprising me.
Q105 That is not what I think most people would understand. I just wanted to check with you on that one.
I do believe that people do vote with their feet when they are unhappy , but let me reassure you that we were not behind it.
Q106 Will you be entering into further conversations with ScotRail about next year?
Yes.
Q107 When will that be?

It normally happens traditionally in the industry about two months after the anniversary date, so every year in most TOCs we tend to be around this time of the year. The reason most of our ballots have been this week is that we wait for the anniversary dates with all the TOCs to see if they make a substantial offer. We advise them that we require a substantial offer . When it is not forthcoming , w e make a decision to ballot.
Q108 You told us that eight train operators had balloted for strike action, and action including short of a strike .
Yes.
Q109 On what basis did those ballots get returned like that?
It was on the basis that we had not had a pay rise. “Do you want a pay rise, and are you willing to take strike action ” —
Q110 So, it is all about pay .
It is all about pay.
Q111 And terms and conditions did not feature as part of that .

There has been no offer on terms and conditions, so basically we have not had a pay rise through the three years. Even if we get a deal, it will not be a pay rise because we will still be behind the curve because of the cost - of - living crisis.
Q112 Have the train operators said they are not going to enter into pay—

What train operators have said is that they are unable to negotiate with us because the G overnment have said they cannot offer more than 2%, and unless we give up a raft of productivity for less than it is worth—
Q113 So you have had no negotiations so far with respective employers .

We have exhausted the negotiation with the employers because the employers have said they cannot give us above 2% unless we give rafts of productivity that they are undervaluing. We have said that we would not do that until we have a reasonable pay rise.
Q114 What is the average salary for a train driver in your—
I keep reading it is £59,000 to £60,000.
Q115 I am asking you for the facts.
I believe it is £59,000 to £60,000.
Yes.
Q117 I think the Chair asked you about the hours and the days of the week. The majority, you said, were on 35 hours a week. Is that right?
The majority are on a 35-hour, average four-day week.
Q118 And roughly half with Sundays in .
Yes.
Q119 Where will your starting point be in this in order to achieve a further pay rise?
Our starting point?
Q120 Let me rephrase it. What is on the table for you in order to —

I have 14 negotiating teams in there that know their companies and know their districts better than I do. They come and make recommendations to us based upon the negotiations that take place. As I answered the question earlier, we could end up with different solutions in different companies. That is down to the massive vagaries of privatisation.

We have many companies with many people in the same grade on different terms and conditions. You might be varying it for one set of them or two sets of them, and that might impact upon how the negotiations go and what is received. The complexity of it is not just simply saying, “What do all train drivers want across the board?”
Q121 If you instruct your members to go on strike as a result of this ballot, will you pay your members strike pay?
No.
Q122 Nothing at all?
No.
Q123 Eddie, can I ask you the same question? If your members go on strike, do you pay strike pay to members?

We do in some cases, but in the context of this national dispute, no. We have been known, where we have cleaners out on strike trying to get offered a minimum wage, to pay them strike pay because they are very low paid. They are relatively small in number . In a national dispute, no, but the Government are paying the industry side to make sure that their profits are not damaged by any strike action that occurs.

Q124 I appreciate that you have a number of grades that you are dealing with, and it is not as straightforward as just the train drivers. In terms of the working week and the days per week, with Sundays in and out, would I be right to say that it is too straightforward just to say it is average this and average that? Is there a grey group? Is there a particular average?

In the train operators we are generally 35-hour weeks. There are some examples where that is higher. In the train operating companies, again, we have quite a wide range of conditions around Sunday working. I think we have probably got more people with Sundays in the working week than you find in the drivers’ grade, for example, but we also have a lot of people who work obligated or committed Sundays.

When I was on the railway, I had 17 Sundays I was obligated to work through the course of the year. They were outside of my working week and paid at an overtime rate for doing them, but it was my obligated duty to work those turns. There are a lot of people on arrangements like that. It is similar in Network Rail. We have a range of hours between 35 and probably up to 40. There are different arrangements for Sundays as well.
Q125 Thank you. Mick, you mentioned working 13 out of 14 days. Just so we are clear, that is optional, is it not?
It is optional.
Q126 Will that attract a further rate of overtime? If you are paid regular time, is overtime paid at time and a half or time and—
Yes, it is generally paid at varying rates. There are different agreements in different companies.
Thank you. I think that is it from me for the moment.
Thank you, Chris. Gavin has just joined us and asked if we had covered one matter. I was not sure whether we had. There is only one way to find out. We will get it on the record.

Q127 Very briefly, Chris asked a question about the deal in Scotland and what it asked of drivers. Essentially, it is going to bring Sunday into the working week in Scotland. It is going to have more flexible rostering as well. It has the 5% pay rise , but it also has a five-year , no compulsory redundancy agreement.
There are many more aspects to it, but they are the main ones. I just wanted to put that on the record, given that Chris asked a question.
I think the question was whether we were going to have productivity for it. There are talks on Sundays in the working week as part of the deal.
And flexibilities, but obviously there is lots for the drivers to gain as well. Anyway, I just wanted to put that on the record.

Q128 Thank you, Gavin. Grahame wants me to cover one point as well. Before I do so, Mr Whelan, you touched on driver - only operation. You said that was a real safety concern for your members. Can you perhaps explain a little more about why you are concerned about that?

Unfortunately, we do not live in the most polite of societies. All the figures prior to the pandemic were going in the wrong direction for us. It was everything from sexual assaults on our railways and people talking about women-only coaches on our railways , to county lines. That was a big and prevalent problem. In areas of Scotland, you will know that we had drivers not wanting to drive on certain lines after a certain time at night because of youths and no other people being on the platforms or in the booking offices.
Recently, train drivers have been designated as lone workers, so we now have to recalibrate where we put them. We have a nasty habit of dumping people in sidings—
Q129 But specific to driver only—

We do not believe, particularly in intensive areas where we can have 12 coaches and up to 1,300 people on there, or nobody on there at certain times of day and night, that we should be the only visible presence. We do not think it is safe.
Q130 You are completely opposed to the practice .
Yes.
Q131 You went on strike on Southern on that basis.
Yes.

Q132 The strike was started by the RMT because it was your members who would lose their jobs, but the technology was already in place so it was basically down to your drivers not to drive it, and that would have stopped the practice — and indeed it did whil e the strikes were on.
We came to an agreement to keep a visible presence and the safety - critical aspect of those people to retain their knowledge. The frightening thing—
Q133 That is going to be my question. Given that it is so unsafe from your perspective, why did your drivers then agree to go back to work and drive those unsafe trains?

Because we are honourable. We agreed those things in the dim and distant, and where we made agreements, strangely enough, we do keep to them. The number of strikes that have happened because we have broken an agreement is zero. The number of strikes or industrial action that has happened because other people are dishonourable or break agreements is vast. That is a factor of the world in which we live. We have systems of work. It is hard to explain the technical aspect to you.
A train driver with a 12-coach train, with 1,300 people on it and 30 people deep on the platform at London Bridge, is given less than two seconds to look at 12 pictures to see that it is safe and—

Q134 I was very fortunate indeed to drive in the carriage with one of your train drivers, who was explaining to me how it all worked. He was absolutely fine with it. Again , my point is, if it is so unsafe, why did your drivers agree to drive the train that you have just described?
Because that was a pre-existing agreement based upon when we only had three-car trains and different systems of work.
Q135 Your members went out on strike on Southern because it was not safe. You said it is not a safe practice, but then they ended their action and agreed to drive the unsafe trains.

Y ou know the legislation . Our disputes have to be specific. It was specific to the three coastal depots where they currently had the second person on the train, and they were trying to remove them. We went on strike because of those three depots.

Q136 You and I both know that there was a 28.5% pay offer in the end because Southern caved. I doff my cap to you for actually negotiating that. That is why your members agreed to go back and drive those unsafe trains.

The reason they went back was that in those three Southern depots the people were allowed to remain upon the train and keep their safety - critical locality. Nothing changed on those trains. They were not paid the 28% because they took the people off those trains. Those people were allowed to stay on those trains and keep their competency if they required. That was the agreement. I wrote it.
Q137 It was done for the safety principle, and then , for the money , you will take it.
No—
Q138 I want to ask Mr Dempsey—
Excuse me, I want to correct the record.

Q139 —what he thought about that. I remember RMT members were absolutely furious because, effectively, that was their strike guarantee : that if the train did not operate because the conductor was not operating it, then it would not move. But, as soon as the drivers took that control over , that power was lost. How did you feel about that? Your members did not get the 28.5% pay rise. In fact, they may have lost their job.

No, what happened to our members is that they were faced with a version of fire and rehire. It was nothing to do with what the drivers did or did not do. Our members were told, “Here is a new contract of employment. That means you will work in a different role. You will sign that new contract of employment or you will leave the industry.” That is what happened to our people, and that is how that dispute ended.
Q140 But the dispute ended because the drivers ended up driving the trains, and your members were the first to take action .
The dispute ended for our members when they were issued with new contracts of employment and told, “You will sign that new contract or you will be unemployed.” That is how the dispute ended.
Q141 I am a southern MP, so I remember it very well.
I remember it , too.
Q142 The dispute ended because ASLEF drivers drove the trains. If they had not, then the dispute would have carried on and the trains would not have run.
The agreement was that those trains were manned with safety - critical staff.
We would have continued the strike action, but what we faced there—
Q143 It would not have made any difference because they would have driven the trains.

You might say so, but we would think differently. What happened then and what is happening now is that people in my industry are facing fire and rehire. Everyone in this place condemned it when it was P&O. Now it is being done to railway workers, all we seem to hear is people talking about bringing more laws in and criminalising the act of dissent against low wages and against being made unemployed. That is what happened to us on Southern. It was fire and rehire. We were given new contracts and told, “Sign that or go and sign on at the dole.”
Q144 Which is why I was amazed that you were so supportive of how it came to an end, because I felt that your members got taken out by ASLEF.
I think fire and rehire should be illegal in this country.
Hear , hear.
I was not happy about how it ended. It was disgraceful.

Q145 I want to put one other thing to you. Touching on the Southern train dispute, it was a big dispute. People could not get to work. It had a massive impact, but it was effective because there was a very generous pay rise that Mr Whelan was able to negotiate.

Are you concerned now that you will not have the same bargaining power over passengers? Take the first day of strikes, when there were also strikes on London Underground as well as rail—so you would think that things would be really paralysed . TfL wrote to us and said that bus patronage was 92% of pre-Covid levels. You would think that the buses would be absolutely crowded, but people worked from home. It does not impact them as much. It impacts certain people — key workers , perhaps — but not others. Do you feel there is a danger that this strike will carry on running because it does not actually bring the workforce to its knees ? P eople can work from home and have learnt how to do that from the pandemic .

I am not so certain about that. The money that has been spent on protecting the profits of private companies during strike action could easily have been put into resolving this dispute, and the money that it has cost the economy more broadly. I accept that it has been difficult, but our strike action is effective. On the run-up to a strike people say it is going to be Armageddon, we are going to shut the country down and there will not be food on the shelves. When we take the strike action, people say that it was not effective at all. Everyone was on the trains and no one is using it—

Q146 That is a very fair point. I am tending more to the latter in terms of not having the power to stop the economy in the way that you did, so is there a danger that you have rather over - chanced your arm?

We will see, but wages have been falling in this country for 30 years. They have not kept up with inflation. At the same time, private profits have rarely not exceeded inflation. There was some research done by Unite that said the FTSE 350 companies’ profits are up 73% since 2019.
Q147 I gave the figures for train drivers, which was a 39% pay rise over the last 10 years—
Let me tell you something. At the same time—
Q148 —when inflation has run at 20%, so that is double inflation.
—there has been a 73% increase in private profits for people at the top—
Q149 How many are specific to rail?

The point I am making is that everyone in this country is feeling the pinch. Enough is enough, and it is about time people made it clear where they stand on this. I think people across the economy—nurses, postal workers and railway workers—are all about to stand together and say, “We deserve a pay rise in this country.” That is coming. It is not about whether or not we are just as effective as we were three years ago. There is a bigger thing happening in this country that people do not seem to realise. That is, people are not prepared to accept any longer that they have to continue to be made poorer so that people at the top can continue to rake in profits. That is over. That is going to change over the next period.
Q150 The last point that Mr Morris wanted to make sure—
Can I respond?
Q151 You can perhaps shoehorn it in, Mr Whelan. I want to ask about the legislative changes that have either been brought in or are being proposed.

On the agency side of things, as you have said—and I think I have said this before—I cannot see how that will make any difference to replacing highly skilled workers who work on the railway, because you cannot bring an agency worker in. Do you feel it would be ineffective as a change?

I think it will be ineffective, but I think it is shocking that the answer to the cost - of - living crisis coming from Government is to criminalise dissent. I think that is outrageous. We rank No. 3 on the TUC i nternational global index for freedoms for trade unions. We have got some interesting compan y in that bracket, let me tell you.
Q152 You have mentioned that before.

That says we have regular violations of trade union freedoms in this country. That is a disgrace. We are meant to be a democracy. We are meant to be a free country. We are meant to have the right to bargain freely for our members in a free market with employers. Instead, as soon as people stand up and say they want a decent shake in a deal for working people, we have a Government that want to criminalise that. That is wrong. Do not worry about whether it is going to be effective. It is just outrageous that that is the answer to the cost - of - living crisis.
Q153 Mr Whelan, I am going to give you the chance to put your views.
I have three brief points. In relation to your statement that we took 28% for DOO, no, we did not. That was settled separately. Go and look at the agreement; I will send it to you.

On top of that, this is not about power. This is about the people who we represent and what they want us to do, and how they feel impacted. No worker rushes to go on strike. No worker wants to lose money. No worker wants to receive the levels of abuse that we receive, particularly in the transport sector, when we go on strike. Therefore, it is a last resort.

The trouble is that these issues happen when they happen. It is not because you are at the height of your power or the weakness of your leverage at a point in time. It is about when the situation happens that drives that dispute to occur. I am making that quite clear.

As for the scab charter that the Government ha ve created and passed recently, that is what it will be. The real problem in an industry like ours is that there are still people not being spoken to who were scabbed in 1955 and 1982. Of course, scabbed labour can only work for scabbed management. What it will do is impact and destroy the industrial relations of this industry going forward when 97% of the time we work in partnership with our employers, which is what people seem to forget.

Anybody who employs any scab labour, if it is unsafe, we will not be working with them. I will make that quite clear. I will put that on the record. Afterwards, anybody who has employed any scab labour, we will look on them as our employers in a different way.
Q154 You have used the word “scab”—
How do you define “scab”?
It is anybody who breaks a strike and crosses the picket line.
Simon Jupp : We are not in school.

Q155 Let me just finish up. You have obviously used quite an emotive term to call them “scabs”. It is quite an intimidating term as well. Are you saying it is not just a question of not working alongside them but that there will be intimidation to ensure they do not take—
We do not intimidate anybody. We are not advising or advocating that. I said the difficulties will be—
Q156 I think if anyone has heard—
—where it is unsafe, we will not work with them. That is what I have said. That was my actual statement.
Q157 If any reasonable person heard what you just said, and you used the word “scab” about four or five times, I would take it as quite intimidatory myself.
I think if you look at the newspapers and how it has been defined and reported, it has been called a “scab’s charter”. I am reflecting the terminology that has been used elsewhere.

Q158 I have never heard the term used on the agency workforce. Let us also ask about minimum service levels and the proposal to bring those in. They are widely used on the continent. Is that something that you would feel as emotive about as you do with regard to the agency legislation, or do you think that if it is good enough for Europe it is good enough for the UK?

I am not sure how it can practically work, if I am honest, logistically or otherwise. Do people still have the right to protest in the UK? That has been diminished recently by certain legislation that has been passed. If there was a picket line and somebody who was obligated to work refused to work that picket line, what would happen to them? I have no knowledge of how this could operate in a realistic way. Would it end up exacerbating strife and making it longer and more difficult? Quite possibly.
Q159 Mr Dempsey, again I should give you the chance to state your views on that.

I do not think minimum service legislation will work here. We will not co-operate with it in any event as a trade union. I think these laws that are being talked about are to further weaken the ability of trade unions. What we are really talking about here is taking power away from working-class people to address what is already an imbalance of power where they work. We have all seen what happens when powerful people in companies want to take liberties with working-class people. It happens all the time. We are here to address that imbalance. If we have our ability to do that taken away, we will have to find other ways to do that.

I do regard people who cross the picket line and break a strike as scabs. You have to appreciate that working-class people have a different morality around stuff like this. My father was a seafarer. His father was a railway worker. None of us ha s ever crossed a picket line. None of us ever will cross a picket line. That carries with it all kinds of connotations.

There are only two sides in a dispute, and you have to pick which one you are on. You either stand with people who are struggling to get a fair deal, or you are on the side of people taking a kicking and being made unemployed. There is no middle ground in this. There is no sitting on the fence. If you sit on the fence, you only get splinters where you do not want them.

My view is that the legislation is uncalled for. There is no need for it. It is the wrong thing to try and further weaken trade unions in a country where we probably have the worst anti-trade union legislation in western Europe. It is authoritarian nonsense. If you really want to stop people taking strike action, what you need to do is put money in their pockets in a cost - of - living crisis. That is what is causing strike action. It is not that trade unions have the ability to strike.

I have just listed a whole range of companies where we have made settlements, and everything is fine. In these companies , we were having operational expenditure slashed, jobs being taken out of the industry, wages being attacked , and terms and conditions being torn up. That is where you have strike action. If you want to solve this, you need to have a fair settlement for people in the industry, not bring more laws in to criminalise dissent.

Thank you. The last word to you. I am very grateful for all the time you have given us. We have gone way over time, but you have given us a lot of evidence, so we are grateful for that. We hope that negotiations will continue. There is an offer on the table. You have given a hint as to where that could go. We will now find out from the next panel where they think it will go for themselves. Mr Whelan and Mr Dempsey, thank you and very best wishes.

Q1 T his is a one- off session on unlocking the potential of agricultural science and technology. Welcome this morning t o our two witnesses: P rofessor Alistair Griffiths and P rofessor Malcolm H awkesford.

If any members of the C ommittee have relevant interests they would like to declare, I ask that they do that now. If not, perhaps I may start with P rofessor Malcolm H awkesford, head of the D esigning F uture W heat I nstitute S trategic P rogramme at Ro thamsted R esearch . W hat are the major challenges that currently fac e UK agriculture and food production?

T he first one , which has always been the case, is producing enough quality food for UK markets and beyond . That has always been the case, but currently farming production —I speak mostly with experience in the wheat sector —has particular issues with regard to pressure to have a low environmental footprint. This brings all sorts of additional complications. It can probably be summarised by having efficient farming . E fficiency has always been important for profitability and it is even more important now to have this low environmental footprint.

Why is there a need for that , a part from public opinion? I t is because of certain impacts in contributing to climate change , for which farming is well known. T hose climate change issues directly impact production, for example currently with a lot of extreme weather conditions , but also long-term changing conditions , so the kinds of varieties grown and the agronomy used need to adapt to these changes. There are lots of other specific issues, not small ones, that come alongside tha t — perhaps increased problems with diseases and the ir control and limitations with regard to inputs , particularly chemical inputs for the control of such diseases .
Q2 A re the issues you have just been describing becoming more acute?

P eople are acutely aware of them . Some of the issues certainly are. It is definitely the case with some of the control s of pesticide use and with the increasing awareness of the importance of the right fertiliser inputs . P reviously , we were not quite so aware of some of the detrimental effects that farming could have . Now we are much more aware of them , so there is increased pressure to adopt methodologies for farming, which include inputs but also the management of soils , for example . T hat is also a key issue . T hey have always been there and farmers have always been aware of them , but now there is increasing pressure on them to adapt their methodologies .

I t is all about being efficient, as t hey have always wanted to be. I am a big promoter of the farming community . They have always wanted to look after their l a nd . They have always needed to be profitable because they are businesses and they need to live . A lot of the pressures now upo n them are about being efficient and , therefore, profitable , but the one overriding issue which we cannot do much about or which is extremely difficult to do , thinking about it , is climate change . That is definitely an increasing problem . W e have a classic example at the moment with these very hot conditions .

Q3 S ome of my colleagues will ask about this in a bit more detail. If I may turn to P rofessor Griffiths, who is director of science and collections at the Royal Horticultural Society, is horticulture in the UK facing the same s ort s of challenges as agriculture, or are there some different issues that you would like to make us aware of?

There are significant challenges. One is looking at the potential of cultiva ted plants and landscapes in the UK and the ornamental and horticultural landscape industry, which is often the Cinderella of agriculture but has a major potential , particularly with in cities , to help more people in those cities in dealing with climate and biodiversity crises .

T he fundamental challenge is that, even in the 2021 UK plant science research strategy, there was little mention of the ho rticultural industry or ho rticultural and cultivated plants, yet we use more cultiva ted plants in our daily lives th a n we use food or medicinal plants . F ood agricultural ist organisations talk about 50,000 different types of plants. There are 32,500 medicinal plants . I n this country alone , through the RHS plant find er we have 88,000 different types of cultiv ated plants .

T he challenges we face are similar. There are big challenges in how we accelerate th e transition, which we have to, to P3 with new growing media technolog ies . How do we deal with water , which will be critically e ssential in cooling our cities on days like today ? How do we mak e sure we have more water - use efficient plants? The re is the pest and disease increase element s . To take ash dieback, for example, there is an estimated cost of £15 billion in not developing good UK plant scientists . W e have good ones, but we need to invest and build on all of these things .

T he industry has worked with DEFRA on an ornamental horti cultural roundtable growth strategy . What it is really about is the right plant in the right place with the right purpose , and how they all interact . It is critical to get f undamental investment in understanding that we need to look at more than just spe cie s and the natural and farming environment, which are critically important . W e also need to look at this no man ’ s land which is our cultivated landscape s .

There are 30 million domestic gardens . There are 700,000 hectares of domestic gardens , of which 25.9% are within cities . What role can we play to optimise these cultivat ed plant genetic resource s and landscapes to maximise the health and environmental benefits ? W e need landscapes to adapt to climate change . W e need to know how to grow them so they can perform to their best capabilities. We also need to have good biosecurity in plant health so they can maximise those benefits . W hile doing that, we need to minimise resource use and waste to maximise those genetic resources .

T he industry is valued by Oxford E conomics at £ 28.8 billion to the UK economy. We believe in investment in the ho rti cultural and landscape industry and deliver y of many of the 25-year environmental plan issues, including mental health . C ovid -19 shows you that seeing is believing in terms of domestic gardens . T hank you, G overnment, for keeping open garden centres during lock down, because you averted quite a number of mental health challenges . T here is overwhelming evidence about mental health and our cultivated landscapes, our habitat . W e could grow with this strategy. I f you look at the unlocking green growth strategy, it is £ 13.2 billion by 2030 to put the green back into green infrastructure, but we have the same challenges of pests , diseases, nutrition, water , labour and a whole bunch of other things that need support.
Q4 Professor Griffiths, do you think there is enough public and G overnment understanding of the importance of ho rti culture ?

I do not think there is enough G overnment understanding. I have been talking about this for eight years . I am pleased to be invited here to talk about this missing link and the opportunity for growth , but also a win-win situation in helping to get to net zero. The general public are seeing these elements more and more : plants for flood mitigation; plants for noise reduction ; plants for cooling; and plants for water-use efficiency.

A good example of that where the public ha ve seen what we can do is linked to biodiversity. Cultivated b iodiversity is not even recognised in G overnment measures o f biodiversity in this country , but plants for pollinators , underpinned by research , have been ad opted by the public . T hey are buying plants with the plant pollinator logo and put ting them in their gardens. We are getting economic growth and helping to contribute to biodiversity .

A study in Leicestershire showed that in one domestic garden there were 2 , 600 different species of organisms within that garden, a nd a quarter of ladybirds, bees and butterflies resided within that single garden . We need m ore to be done in how to unlock the UK ’ s garde ning capital of the world and shine globally . Nowhere else in the world understands the cultivar . “Ornamental” is a bad word and does not help; it should be “environmental horticulture”.

These challenges face us, particularly the recent loss of the AHDB levy fund for research and development. There is a loss of almost £2 million R&D for horticulture. That investment is critically needed so that we can do what is needed right now for th e climate and biodiversity crisis. W e need to follow the road map , which is fabulous . There are many great things in that road map and it is a great piece of work, but we also need to look at how we do applied research on the ground to understand how these plants will adapt to climate change , and how we can use them to optimise the plant genetic resource s—the 400,000 domesticated and cultivated plants in this country — to provide those health and environmental benefits.
Thank you, Professor Griffiths. I have to say that p robably 25% of the living organisms in my garden at the moment are midges. I will now turn to my colleagues.
You have made me forget what I was going to say.
Apologies.
Q5 P rofessor Hawkesford, most things in this area are a balance and a trade - off ; y ou improve one thing and do not improve the other . A s a priority, should we still be producing biofuel s?

T hat is a tricky one. F ood production is the primary role of agriculture , but in certain areas, perhaps areas of lower productivit y , why not produce biofuel s ? It all comes down to appropriate land use . O ne argument is that we might want to reduce the amount of land we use for agriculture so that we can have more diverse uses for the countryside . T hen we might be focused on increasing yield s on the land we do use for food production , and any land that is then put aside for biofuels will impact on such a strategy. We can produce biofuels or food. You cannot produce both to the maximum . It is a tricky one to answer , and I apologise.
Q6 That was partly why I asked you. It is useful to know , because land use for biofuels is a matter of some debate at the present time .
I t depends on the profitability of the biofuels and the demand within the UK for supplies of such fuels.
Q7 That is probably a regulatory issue as well , is it not?
Professor Hawkesford : Indeed.
Q8 In terms of other trade - offs and balances, can you talk us through how you make choices between crop yields and the reduction in pesticides ?
P esticides specifically , or inputs generally?
Q9 You can certainly widen it, but , if you prefer, chemicals on the land.

All farmers want yield ; t hat is what they get paid for . A lot of plant and crop science research is focused on inputs and efficiency, be it fertiliser inputs , water - use efficiency , which my colleague has already mentioned , or the use of agr i chemicals to control pests .

A better solution to the use of inputs such as chemicals is to have varieties which can cope with lower inputs, including agrichemicals . T here is a huge amount of research looking for resistant varieties both within the academic sector and the plant - breeding industry . B y far the best solution is to have the appropriate varieties , and that is where the major focus of research certainly lies. Having said that, at the moment in some cases there are no alternatives to using some pesticides.
Q10 A t the present time are we maximising the nutrients in the UK ecosystem and avoiding as much as we can chemical inputs? Where are we in that debate ?

T he UK is in a fantastic position , and UK farming is really good about this . There are some instances where it can still be improved . T here is a lot of work going on at the level of agricultural research to improve both management and the kinds of varieties we use , but we are pretty good in terms of fertiliser use efficiency within the UK system compared with many areas of the world. Globally, it is a completely different issue in terms of how well fertilisers are used. Of course , a big driver is the cost of all agr i chemicals and fertilisers, which currently has really rocketed.

Q11 Professor Griffiths, you mentioned in your opening remarks ash dieback . I took from your comments that you do not think the G overnment ha ve the right policies on ash dieback. What do you think th ose polic ies should be?

It is not about the policies that are in place around that; i t is about how we may tackle the plant health side of things in relation to those industries and the opportunities for saving around those aspects . T here are a number of areas in relation to plant health . There is already some very good work with both industry and G overnment, in particular the plant health y assurance scheme created by both industry and G overnment.

As to the key element , in New Zealand—I know the Government are working on this—every New Zealander is a biosecurity person . They look after the ir sites, which is probably why —I cannot prove it —Covid ‑ 19 worked quite effectively there , because they had an understanding of disease and issue s . W e need to look not only at improved monitoring and surveillance of plant pests , but at further improvement of our supply chains — not removing genetic resources into this country that we will need for resilience against pests and climate change , but look ing at how we can better bring them into the country through that.

We also need to reduce risk s that we know of already . W here there are challenges , we need to look abroad but also in the UK to undertake research on existing pests and diseases , and also to do horizon scanning for the top 10 that we think may be coming in . F or example , rose rosette virus in the US is a significant issue . I t is our national flower and it earns quite a lot of money .

W e have to look at that , but, most of all, we have to work on that. The G overnment are beginning to work on that, but we need to advance this element of engagement and link that to how we look at behavioural change , providing information and knowledge for practitioners on the ground — foresters and horticulturalist s —a bout effective control and management strategies of existing problems.

Q12 Do the Government have their priorities correct in what plant science supports ? W ould you in any sense recommend a change of focus in terms of which particular approaches and technologies are supported?

In that the planet and human resilience is utterly dependent on plant diversity and will be more critically needed going forward , we need to invest significantly more i n plant sciences, full stop, across the board. It is a small amount compared with other areas of research . W e also need to go back a little bit.

If you look at Wageningen, Cornell in America , the Academy of Sciences and so on, we need to continue what the road map is saying , because it is very good, but we also need to take stock and understand what genetic diversity we have in th is country , which is basic applied research, but applied - oriented scienc e , strategic ally applied , specifically applied an d experimental development research . T he G overnment paper that talks about the types of research that have happened does not match the offer in the research strategy .

I will give you an example of t he reason why we need to understand what these plants are . One shrub that we have looked at —we have looked at its morphology—can capture 10 times more particulate pollution th a n another shrub , and that is due to its features and t he basic fundamental s of botany. We need to understand what we have with those genetic resource s so that we c an then understand them and test them in the field linked to climate change . We can then marry that up. For m any of the good research projects , first they have gathered all the cultivars and all the species— not species. W e need to think about the cultivar more , bring them together and then look at the new technologies out there , because that will speed up things . We need to act within five or 10 years , so we need to learn and do . While doing that , we need to do the other long-term strategic work th at may take 10 to 20 years.

Q13 G entlemen, I do not know whether the following two points are formal declarations of interest . One is that I was honoured to be an undergraduate at R othamsted for a very short p eriod asking stupid questions . S econdly , the horticultural grow er s in my patch will not forgive me if I do not put the marvellous ness of west Lancashire on the map for that kind of stuff.

We have just had quite an interesting overview of where we are. I want to turn to solutions . I n doing so, I may just pick up a couple of the points you raise. Both of you have been talking about developing different cultivar or specie s lines for specific purposes: reduced water co nsumption in agricultural settings , or reduced water consumption in a garden setting that will allow for a city to manage itself.

The Genetic Technology (Precision Breeding) Bill is going through Parliament at the moment. I have served on the Committee. I believe it has just gone off to the Lords. For the purposes of the tape and general public, that is using scientific techniques to look within species for positive traits and consolidate them. Professor H awk e sford, what do you think gene editing can offer for some of the issues we have just been talking a bout , as well as t he opportunities?

As f or improving any of those key traits , those are incredibly complex , and they are built up of multiple complex traits. Genome editing, or even GM technology , usually focuses on single genes . All of these processes probably involve hundreds of genes. The trick is to have enough knowledge to know exactly where one should be focusing. That is the basic goal of some quite good plant science research in the UK, but it is incredibly difficult to pin down. Scientists have been working in this area for, dare I say, 50 years or more . M ore recently, it has been possible to identify some key targets . Once you have identified a key target you can start using these technologies. G enome - editing technology is also in its infancy relatively .
Q14 CRISPR .

CRISPR i s one approach you can use within genome editing. There are several ways in which you can do this editing . I t is very precise editing . I t is very clean technology and does not leave anything that you would not want, so you end up with a plant, crop or whatever , which is pretty much indistinguishable from the original, because all you have done is literally to make a few precise edits . That is completely different from all other forms of gene modification and a lot of plant breeding technologies. This is definitely the way forward , but the trick is to find out exactly what to do that will really work. I fear that we still have a long way to go for a lot of these big traits : w ater-use e fficiency , i nput use and climate resilience.
Q15 F ertiliser s and pesticides .

Yes. In some cases there are specific examples where there are claims and good evidence, but they are fairly restricted because of the complexity of the system , not the technology , and knowing exactly what to change .
Q16 K atherine, for clarification, could you explain what CRISPR is, for anybody , including myself, who doe s not know what it is ?

T here are various ways to do genome editing . It is basically about taking DNA, cutting it and changing individual bas e s within the DNA. The CRISPR / C as technology is one way you can do this . There are several different ways in which you can do it , but it is about introducing enzymes to cut the DNA , edit the DNA and then repair it . CRISPR is just one method of several .

If I paraphrase what you are saying, gen e editing has a role to play, for example , in generating a w heat that barely requires fertiliser in most UK conditions, but that nirvana requires an enormous amount of research input to make sure you are e diting correctly . Before I come to Professor Griffiths with the same question, w hat c an we do to accelerate that understanding? Q18 W hat can we do to make sure we understand the car better so we can use the spanner properly?

T his comes back to the question of how we fund science and the s cience that we should be funding. We fund basic plant science to a reasonable extent in t his country. Q19 W e will return to that because it is very interesting and ties into some of the research we hear d about DARPA and orienti ng science around missions . Before I get over - excited, P rofessor Griffiths, what is your view on gene editing and that big, very technical spanner?

It goes back to what I said previously. A paper has been published this week about the demise of botany and botanical people who look at whole - plant systems , and also the ecolog i cal elements of interaction . I do not think we know fully what we have , or perhaps we do not have people within the institutes that are doing some of this fundamental translational research who have a full understanding of the genetic diversity that is already apparent . F or example , there are 60 different varieties of heritage purple tomatoes in this country; t here are 26,000 different types of daffodil s , one of which, Carlton, is the produc er of galantamine. I do not think we ha ve that expertise and knowledge .

I am not saying we should not be supporting th at kind of research . I f we want to accelerate this , we have to increase both sides of research so we can work together in understanding that car a little better to match what we think these character traits are like. Are they arachnoid hairs, stellate hairs or lepido t e hairs that will capture more pollution, or different types of hair shapes , or is it the p hysiology that will link to that ? That plant -based system and ecological-based approach will be critical. A bit like green energy, we probably know that electric cars are not the solution, but in the meantime we need to use the green plant stuff in the best way we possibly can and learn as we are going .

Q20 I think I am following you, but I just want to make sure. When we were in the C hair ’ s home town of Glasgow we saw some very exciting stuff in the space satellite industry. Professor H awkesford, is t here technology there that can also accelerate us while we are on this pure science journey?

Yes, 100% . I mproving agronomy is just as important as improving the genetic basis of the crops that we grow . B oth have massive roles to play and the increasing use of such technology is definitely coming to farmers. Farmers have GPS; t hey know exactly where they are , and all of this additional information , however it is generated —from satellites or elsewhere —is definitely a way forward to improving the efficiency of farming .
Q25 P rofessor Griffiths , do you agree with that?

I think there is some really interesting technology o n pheno typing , which means basically going over a plant and measuring all the different character istics that may be there. That will be p ossible . T here are still some challenges with phenotyping. You cannot necessarily get everything, but literally there is technology out there ; there are drones that will fly over a plant and measure certain parameters that will help us better understand those systems.

The other really interesting technology is twinning whereby we can do digital twins of real - life situations, say cultivated landscapes in cities , and put in the parameters —it is early days —and understand how th ey might behave according to different climate predictions with different types of plants. It is fascinating stuff that could be adopted and needs to be developed further.

Q26 If we have a series of mission-oriented actions, be they reducing inputs in the land , leaving more land for nature or using the l and we do use in a more efficient and effective way , this kind of technology will provide information that allows us to start to address those challenges more quickly . W here is the UK on that?

I think we are among the leaders , but there are plenty of other countries in Europe and further afield —A ustralia , the US and China —which have big activities in remote sensing and agriculture , and also in the area of phenotyping, which m y colleague mentioned. We are good in the UK , but we are a relatively small country. I come back to the point I made previously about needing to assemble big teams to be competitive internationally .
Q27 In that context—w e cannot be five-star at everything—where would you want to see us foc us the science and technology of agriculture in the future?

In my opinion, we need to look at different option s ; we should not have a single focus. The one option is genetic improvement and breeding, where there is a big industry push , and a big academic link to that, but also the whole science of technology around improving a gronomy and using technology tools . B oth of these areas are critical for UK farming . W e have industr y support and innovation in both of those areas and plenty of academic experts .
Q28 P rofessor Griffiths, would you add anything? What do we need to do?

I t is all about understanding and realising that we have a wealth of knowledge and information on cultivated plant genetic diversity , particularly ornamentals , many of which are in our daily lives in cities . W hat we need to do is ramp up and create climate-smart cities and landscapes that will deal with and tolerate climate changes . I am afraid that the way to do that goes back to two basics and the adoption of technologies by knowing wh at we actually have and how those different character traits and different things can benefit us so that we can go into breeding , plant selection , growing and testing .
Q29 I n your earlier comments you were talking about improving our ability to get genetics into this country. Were you talking effectively about sanitary and phytosanitary che ck s ?

T here is concern in some instances that we get to a point where we do not enable genetic resources from around the world to come into the UK. I believe there are two fundamental reasons why that should not happen and also to make sure that when it does come in it comes in very safely.

The two fundamental reasons are these. I f we are looking at 4° to 5° increases in temperature and extremes of flooding and drought by 2030 , we need more diversity . A s with people , we need more plant genetic diversity so we have more tools in the box that we can call on. The other one is that the majority of plant resistance will often come from these collections . A sh dieback and e lm came from overseas ; it came from genetic resource institutes that had many cultivars . W e need those things to come in . We have to look at making sure that is as easy as possible to bring i n while making sure that we are plant healthy in the country.

Q30 The counter to that would be the introduction of alien invasives . G enetic modification was talked about and dropped. It is something on which I have done some work . I s there a role for genetic modification in terms of different species being combined , as opposed to gene editing, to play in the solution to moving forward ?

As to t he technology of genetic modification to produce a final product , we are to an extent looking at that in the past , because g enome editing can do so much more and leave a much cleaner final product . H owever , there are some things which are quite difficult to imagine do ing through just using genome editing , which is just editing some of the DNA in that plant . Y ou could transfer things with in the same species or modify how things are working within a species, but there are still some things where it might be better to bring in a trait from, say, a tomato into a cucumber or something like that. There could be different reasons for wanting to do that transfer between spe cie s, but the basic technology of GM is an older one and has been superseded . I think that genome editing will also continue to evolve and give us much better tools.

Q31 P rofessor Griffiths, you mentioned in response to Katherine a second ago the use of technology to enable our better understanding of what we have around us and why and what it means. I assume that, like me, you are o bsessed with the New York City tree map. Do you think that something like that should happen here , especially in urban areas ? Would that be a really good use of investment?

M apping our trees and understanding the benefits of that has been clearly demonstrated through some of the i-Tree work that has happened in relation to the UK , valuing the economics of carbon se questration , pollution capture and all the leisure activities that they provide. W hat is important is that you need long - term sustainability for a map like that . A gain , it is about working with a consortium of different groups with perhaps different audiences on where those trees are and making sure you have long - term stability of that . Y ou will also get a good understanding of what trees are doing well plant health - wise .

I also know there is Treezilla —a nother app —that has a focus on plant health . Our forest research look s at those things . It is helpful to have that. The RHS also has My Garden. There are 126,000 people on there and 80,000 different types of plant in their gardens are already o n that mapping system. It is about understanding what we have.

As to where some of the challenges lie , particularly in relation to net zero , trees have been grossly underestimated , as have landscape s, for their potential carbon sequestration and storage, because the underground part of it has not been measured , particularly in urban systems , and also their optimal growth.

Q32 My brief talks about the bush y , hairy-leafed c otoneaster, which the RHS is looking at in terms of its ability to trap harmful airborne particles. I spent a significant amount of my time supporting a school on a main road in my constituency to get an ivy screen. Through the scientific research that you are doing , do you see that in the future plan t s like c otoneaster could, if the price comes down, be more effective in protecting particularly young , v ulnerable lungs from harmful particles?

W e currently have a two-year research project with the 1851 R oyal Commission which is looking at exactly pollution capture. W e have also looked at all the ivies . It cools; i t provides green for wellbeing; i t provides food for birds ; and it captures particulate pollution. I believe multiple -service provision will be very critical . We also need to look again at water - use effectiveness . T here are a lot of plants out there already in th ose 400,000 that can be repurposed and used , but we just n eed to understand which ones are better than others , and what those traits are.

Q33 If I may follow up K atherine ’ s question, at the present time gene editing is covered by the same legislation as genetic modification. The G overnment say they want to go step by step and move to genetic editing because they will change the genome only in a way that it would change in nature ; there would not be cross - species change. When I listen ed to the evidence given to the G enetic T echnology (P recision B reeding ) B ill , we seem ed to be being told that that is not the case . T he plants are not that pure and there is already exchange between different species and plants, so the legislative basis on which the G overnment are proceeding is not a scientific one . Would that be your opinion?

I think we are going forward in a very cautious way and that is probably quite important for public acceptance , which is fairly critical. There are always different caveats one can make and all sorts of things do happen in nature in terms of transfers of gene s, but the whole concept and technology of genome editing is really a clean way of doing what we want to do and would be achieved via lots of different ways of traditional breeding methods , but in a precise and rapid way w ithout going as far as doing GM technology , where you have a lot of other parts of the machinery — for example , antibiotic resistance , et c.— carried forward . It is definitely a clean way of doing it. You could say that we could go further, but in terms of public acceptability , world markets and acceptability of products it is definitely a sensible and cautious way forward . I do not have anything against that as an a pproach.
I th a nk both P rofessor Griffiths and Pr ofessor Hawke sford for the ir evidence this morning .
Thank you, gentlemen.
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Dr Bastow and Dr Flanders .

Q34 W elcome to our session this morning. We have Dr David Flanders, chief executive officer at A grimetrics, and Dr Ruth B astow, innovation director at Crop H ealth and P rotection , or CHAP . Thank you for joining us this morning.
I f I may turn first to Dr B astow, what are the key problems facing UK agriculture at the moment, and how would you prioritise the m in terms of solutions?

As we heard from Malcolm this morning, there is always a challenge in producing enough nutritious and safe food in a way that reduces your impact an d environmental footprint , remembering that it needs to be economically viable as well . F arming , agri culture , is a business. That is the big picture we have heard about . C ertainly , thinking about what is happening at the moment out there, farming and agriculture , like any other industrial sector , is facing inflationary input and energy price s . Fertiliser has gone up by at least 150% in the past 12 months . T hose are the sorts of things we need to think about . That means we are seeing difficulties . P eople are thinking about how to make ends meet , deciding how much fertiliser to put on and whether they will reach the yield at the end of the day.

You have probably all heard about the labour shortages that agriculture is currently facing . They are massive. There are 50% vacancies, maybe even more at the mome nt. We need to think about that .
