T hey want to make sure that their ro utes match what will be offered when we have CPTPP accession hopefully, because those are the sorts of practical tools that help businesses to be able to reach new markets, which is where we can see that growth com ing as quickly as possible.
Fantastic. Last but not least , Tony Lloyd.

Q345 Secretary of State, the FTA has similarities with parts of the Australia and UK digital economy agreement s with Singapore. Those digital economy agreement s go a little bit further in some areas —for example, on online har m and so on—but where do you draw the line in negoti ating what goes into a free trade agreement and what goes into a digital economy agreement? T his is not meant as a philosophical question. Are there practical reasons for making that differentiation?
The digital chapter , which , as you say, is b road and extensive , is what we negotiated with them. The DEA with Singapore is, if you like, a new layer . W e have an existing FTA with Singapore .
It is a stand-alone.

It is a stand-alone. In the nicest possible way , it is not the most exciting F T A in the world , but under WTO rules you cannot do what I call extra agreements unless you have an FTA . T he digital area is very important to Singapore and they are also world leaders on it too. We have c reated this agreement and what is in it is genuinely world-leading. This is effectively the UK ’s poster child of what a digital economy would look like .

I would be very content — Crawford probably would be too ; it means less work—to put that into every F T A we ever negotiated. That would be fantastic. All of that digital economy thinking in an FTA would be great . T he reality is that , when you are doing a bilateral agreement with a particular country , they will not always be in a place where you can have that sort of n egotiat ed position which w ould cover all those areas . E very F T A will be negotiated within the limits of each countr y’s mandate and capacity to move toward s that stage.

A ustralia is pretty good and we have negotiated something that is great . It might lead to your point about doing more later , thinking, “There is some stuff in the U K - Singapore digital economy agreement that is good .” At the time, 2021 , that seemed too far, but by the time we get to 2025 —I do not know—in those areas that their businesses want to develop we would be open to doing that .

I n my ideal world , from an efficiency perspective , every UK FTA—name a country —could have as much as is in the DEA in their digital data chapter, but the realities are the limitations of negotiation that each country has at any point .

At the moment w e are talking to Ukraine , with which we have an FTA—it has a very digitally savvy environment , a very extensive , young population and it is very keen on digital development —on whether we can do a d igital economy agreement of the type that we have with Singapore . It is very keen to leapfrog with a lot of these technologies and use those tools and work with the UK to help grow those economi es . As you know , we are very keen to support them in every way we can , not only militarily but in helping them sustain and grow their economy.

The DEA in its present form is there to use as a template for other countries that already have FTAs with us and that might want to take this step . For us as the UK, driving as we did the digital trade principles through the G7 last year , we are absolutely of the view that this is so important to helping businesses , particularly SME s, to move forward , jump to that next generation and strip away cost by using those digital tools in their business activities. This is in a way our poster child . T his is the ultimate that we have with Singapore . It came into force just last week , so we are excited to see how businesses make use of it and take those opportunities.

Fantastic. Secretary of State and Crawford Falcon er , thank you very much indeed. It has been a mammoth session combining one and a half hours this morning and two hours this afternoon. So it is quite something. Sadly, I suspect the L iaison C ommittee will probably occupy more space on the news w ires tonight th a n this C ommittee. We appreciate you r coming to see us . Such a long session is hard work ; it certainly is for us and almost certainly for you as well . W ith that, we will draw this to a close .

sessions.w: Government Equalities Office

segs.tx: Women and Equalities Committee
Oral evidence: Work of the Minister for Equalities on LGBT+ matters , HC 545
Wednesday 6 July 2022
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 6 July 2022 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Kate Osborne (Chair); Elliott Colburn; Jackie Doyle-Price; Carolyn Harris and Caroline Dinenage.
Questions 1 - 44
Witnes ses

I : Mike Freer MP, Minister for Equalities and Equality Hub at Government Equalities Office ; Anna Thompson, Deputy Director LGBT domestic policy, International and Communications, Equality Hub an d Marcus Bell, Director, Equality Hub .
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Mike Freer, Anna Thompson and Marcus Bell .

Q1 Welcome to you all to this one-off session looking at the work of the Minister for E qualities on LGBT+ matters. If you would briefly like to introduce yourselves and , I understand, Minister, that at the beginning of the meeting the C hair gave permission for y ou to speak for no more than two minutes, please. Thank you.

I do not recall they gave me such a strict time limit, but I will do my best. T hank you, Chair , for the opportunity to reassure the C ommittee that there is a cross - g overnment piece of work to address some of the day - to - day issues facing the LGBT + community. We have the HIV action plan . L ater this year w e will have the women's health strategy , which should address the imbalance on access to IVF for lesbian couples. We are already expanding the Gender Identity Service . T he former S ecretary of S tate for Health had agreed there was more work to be done on trans healthcare. The ban on conversion practi c es is underway and the draft B ill is imminent, and we hope to get that before Parliament in the autumn ; and t here is the victim support scheme in place for victims of conversion practi c es.

Minister Hughes and I are meeting to discuss LGBT homelessness and the link with sex work. We are looking at the money that has gone into the education sector to tackle homophobic, biphobic, transphobic bullying. We are looking at targeted support , particularly at the university sector looking at student mental healt h . I n terms of data gathering , where we believe there is still work to be done , t he census included new questions. We have digiti sed the G ender R ecognition C ertificate. The armed forces have already addressed some historic al convictions and expunged them. There is now more work being done by Lord E ther ton. The Home Office is continuing to publicise the disregard s and pardon s scheme . Lord Herbert is continuing to do his work overseas, and there is an extra £2.7 million to address — particularly through NGOs — historic al criminalisation to see if we can get those laws overturned.

J ust 10 days ago, I led the first ever LGBT+ trade delegation to the S tates , where they were exposed to a variety of businesses with a variety of tech expertise . M ore importantly, we were able to look in some detail at a supplier chain diversity programme that I hope to be able to replicate . The programme, which is quite systematic in America, looks at under-represented groups like LGBT , women , race , veterans , and I think that i s something we can learn from. That is a quick canter through some of the work going on across G overnment.

Q2 Chair : Thanks very much . T hat was well within two minutes s o thanks for that. I am sure we wi ll be touching on some of those areas in today's session . I f I can start off , t he G overnment ha ve clearly stated the independence of clinicians providing gender identity healthcare services to adults, young people and c hildren will not be affected by a conversion therapy ban, and that legislation will not impact the existing professional frameworks that guide clinicians ’ ability to support people.

Similarly, Dr H ilary Cass, who i s running the i ndependent Cass Review on c hildren and y oung p eople's g ender i dentity s ervices, explained that the r eview’s terms of reference do not include consideration of the proposed legislation to ban conversion therapy. The G overnment ha ve also been consistently clear that clinicians utilising outcome-neutral explorative approaches will not be impacted by a ban. Robust exploratory and challenging conversions, which are part of regulated care, do not fall within the scope of the ban. This should, therefore, also apply if the G overnment include transgender conversion practices in the B ill, should it not?
I agree.

Q3 Ca n you tell us which clinical groups have expressed concerns about the C onversion T herapy Bill including the issue of transgender identity , and the progress of the additional scoping work on conversion therapy, which would protect clinicians in exploring gender identity with clients ?

I n terms of the specific clinical stakeholders , that i s a matter for Dr C ass . I ha ve spoken to Dr Ca ss and , as you say , Chair, s he ha s been extremely clear — she did this in a frequently asked q uestions section on the interim report — that the work on banning conversion practice s is not dependent on her review, whether the interim review , the full review , or the G overnment's response to it .

We have made it abundantly clear that the B ill is a narrow - scope B ill which w ill clearly s tate what conversion practice s are and what are not conversion practice s, and that should provide clarity . S ome of the professional bodies have talked about the “ chilling effect ” , b ut they have been reassured . W e believe we can present a workable B ill that ensures a clinician who starts from the point of believing that their clients are suffering from gender distress , and then pursuing and probing all the possible reasons why somebody is in gender distress , is not a conversion practice . Under t he rules of the clinical guidance , a s I understand it , it is only if a cli nician is absolutely sure, having explored all the possible reasons for gender distress, that there is a clinical diagnosis of gender dysphoria w ould they recommend a clinical outcome for transitioning . That is the situation , b ut it has been caught up in a lot of misinformation . I believe the B ill can protect c linicians, parents and teachers from having proper robust conversations so t hey do not stray into conversion practice s.

I would g o so far as to say that I have had conversations with people who have said people are being forced to be t rans . I do not share that view , b ut if you genuinely believe that people are being forced to be t rans, then that i s a reason to back the conversion therapy ban , not to oppose it , because the B ill is symmetrical. S orry, I will c alm down now.
Q4 T hank you. W ill the scoping work be ready in time to include transgender conversion practice s in the B ill ? Will that work be done by then?

T he exact scope of the work has yet to be signed off, but it is certainly the F oreign Secretary ’s intention . She has been very clear on her intentions on this matter, and we hope the work w ill be able to inform the passage of the B ill through Parliament.

Q5 Chair : Thank you. T he G overnment's own commissioned research tells us that most people volunteer for conversion therapy, yet it is my belief that it is mostly done under duress. Non - physical conversion therapies will protect under - 18 s regardless of circumstances, and over - 18 s who do not consent and who are coerced. This flawed concept of consent will leave some adult victims of conversion practice s at risk, and the law is clear that personal autonomy must be restricted when there is an imbalance of power or where there is a real risk of a large number of vulnerable people giving consent through coercion or manipulation, which is not true consent. Wh y is it necessary to allow adults to consent to conversion practice s?

T he G overnment position is very clear that , in a free and open society, adults should be able to make an informed choice . T here are two aspects to consent. One is informed choice : w e would expect anybody thinking of consenting to conversion practice to be clearly and explicitly informed that the practice they are about to embark on not only does not work , but it can cause lasting psychological harm. I n terms of where the law would kick in , the level of the bar on harm would be set similar to other legislation . I think “ serious harm ” is the threshold . T here are checks and balances within consent , b ut I appreciate it is a thorny issue which I look forward to exploring in more depth as the B ill progresses .
Q6 I think the question is, can you consent to something th at some would deem to be abuse ?
Th e legal framework is that people can consent. The threshold at which you cannot consent is “ serious harm ” . I am hopi ng t hat i s the correct l egal definition.

Q7 In a policy paper published on 10 May, which lists briefing notes on the announcements made in the 2022 Queen's S peech, it states that , “R ecognising the complexity of issues and need for further careful thought , w e will carry out separate work to consider the issue of transgender conversion therapy further ” . C an you tell us what these complexities are? W ill you agree to publishing the B ill in d raft so that it can be scrutinised by this C ommittee and others?

M ike Free r : I made it plain that I do not believe pre - legislative scrutiny is necessary for a variety of reasons. T he B ill will be narrow in scope, and the opportunity for pre - legislative scrutiny to delay the passage of the B ill is not one I would wish to take. We have taken long enough to get to this stage on a narrow B ill that I would seek to ensure is very clearly defined .

I n terms of the complexities , t he F oreign S ecretary and I are very clear there may be a legitimate debate on other issues regarding trans people in the UK, provided those debates are dealt with in a balanced and respectful way. However, we believe that the issues, the complexities if you like, of how to protect clinicians, parents and teachers can be deal t with by a short, sharp review , a nd that i s our submission to the P rime M inister.

Q8 You said it has taken a long time for us to get this far. Would it not be the case that, regardless of the narrowness in scope of the B ill , it would be better to take a little bit longer to make sure th at consultation an d other input is in there before publishing?

In normal circumstances I believe that is a reasonable argument . I recall having, if not the fi rst , one of the first debates on banning conversion practice s in 2015. I accept that i f it was easy, G overnment would have done it before now. Having said that, this debate has been raging for decades and I am not sure pre - legislative scrutiny would add anything to the debate or the B ill . My fear is i t would simply be an exercise in both sides of the argument, just repeating the arguments we a re already aware of. I am not sure it would provide any new information. W e are very conscious of the issues and concerns people have on both sides of the debate, and I think we are now in a good place to be able to address those issues during the passage of the B ill .

I am the deputy director for LGBT policy in the Equality Hub. J ust to add that , o f course, we have already carried out an extensive public consultation . We wi ll be publishing the results of the analysis of that consultation along with the Government response ahead of the introduction of the B ill .
Q9 Minister , c an I begin by asking you a very open question ? D o you think the Government ha ve a problem with trans people?

No . I think there are elements of Parliament that have issues with trans people. Some of that I cannot get to the root of . M uch of it is due to misinformation or lack of knowledge. My fundamental belief is that Parliament is rightly an accepting place , a questioning place , and I have no problems with those colleagues who do not understand or have genuine concerns. M any of the concerns I have discussed with colleagues are very genuine concerns, often from a position of lack of knowledge.

C an I , hand on heart , say that everybody in P arliament is not transphobic? No , I cannot . C learly , we have a very heated debate going on within P arliament. Some people may have their own agenda , but on the whole P arliament is not transphobic . None the less, w e have a lot more work to do t o educate and also to ensure that colleagues have their concerns respectfully listened to and , hopefully , addressed.

Q10 I would be the first to agree with you that we need to take the heat out of this debate. A cross Government , there are many colleagues who are simply getting on with trying to address day - to - day issues. The sadness is that m any of the toxic elements of the debate drown out m uch of the good work going on behind the scenes in Government .

Q12 There is one D epartment in particular you did not mention there that was being helpful and constructive, and that is N o. 10. Would you say N o. 10 is preventing the G EO and other G overnment D epartments from , in your words , “ getting on ” with that job?

Y ou are tempting me down a route I do not particularly want to go down . L ike any G overnment D epartment t here are a variety of views in that D epartment , b ut if you look at the work programme that I have outlined across Government that , clearly , has N o. 10 ’s seal of approval .

Q13 Thank you, Minister . Y ou a re absolutely right, in my opinion . T here are really serious questions to be addressed when it comes to trans issues, not least of which are the concerns around the protection of single sex spaces and violence against women and girls. I t seems like every other day there is another media story, another announcement about how we are going to scale back the rights of trans people or use that as , you might call it , a wedge issue or weaponise the issue. Is that really a good use of g overnment t ime to put so much effort obsessing about what the best estimate gives us is 1% of the population ?

Is it the best use of g overnment resources when we have so much to do? C ertainly , t here are bigger issues to deal with and I think we can address many of the concerns women feel they have in terms of dealing with transition . I understand the concern. I t ha s been said to me , “But you are not a woman; you can’t possibly under stand, ” and I accept that. I believe , if we sit down in a respectful way, we can try to iron it out , because I think the disagreements are possibly not as wide as people would think.

Some people are , perhaps, trying to use d ifferences for whatever reason, but we could address those issues on a day-to-day basis without making it a major policy announcement. I f we are trying to illustrate what the Government are doing to tackle the cost of living crisis, w hat we are doing for the economy and what we are doing for the h ealth s ervice, etc, then some of these issues can be addressed on a day-to-day basis. Sometimes I do not think we need to make a massive hoo-hah out of it. I s it a waste of resources? Perhaps.

Q14 Elliott Colburn: T hank you, Minister, and I totally agree with your point, and I would be the first to say that I think the majority of colleagues across Parliament are not transphobic in any way, shape or form. I believe there is a much narrower gap of opinion tha n might be played out in the media .

W hat I have seen in the last six months is the number of people with complete opposition has diminished dramatically to the B ill . M any people are now realising the B ill is not what they thought it was, and they say, “ Yes, you are right to stop the hurt and the damage being done by conversion practice s , provided our concerns and safeguards that we have already discussed are in the B ill ” .

Q15 Thank you. C ould I move on to ask a bit more about some of the day-to-day specifics ? Starting with the recent announcement that the GRC process is now available online, could you talk me through some of the assessment the D epartment ha s done of the potential increase in the number of applications you may now have as a result of it being available online and whether or not that process is, by its very nature of being digital, easier, harder, or no different than the process it is there to replace?

Q16 Thank you, Anna. A 75% increase on the previous year is an absolutely whopping great increase. We are c onfident about the capacity at their end , and our liaison with M OJ and HMCT S. F orgive me , I think there was a further point that I have forgotten.
Q17 Yes. As well as assessing the reasons for the increase, i s there confidence the system can cope with the numbers ?

Our close liaison with MOJ and HMCTS deals with that . I think you were also interested in what the reasons for the increase might be. I would flip it the other way round and say the reasons we identified the reduction in the fee and the digitisation as the key elements we were going to take forward was off the back of some of the intelligence from the previous consultation — people pointing out that financial burden , because the fee previously was £140 , and the clunky administrative process via the post . Those things were getting in the way. Those we re two of the key barriers we identified through that consultation and have therefore tackled .

Q18 Eric Colburn : G oing over some of the more day - to - day issues, M inister , in the Westminster Hall debate we had on GR A reform there w ere t w o commitments made at the Di spatch B ox — to remove disorder from the G R A and remove the spousal veto. T he ability of a partner to block it h a s been reduced —before I get t old off for using the wrong terminology .
Q19 E lliott Colburn: And t h e progress o n removing disorder from the GR A?
Anna Thompson: T hat is work we continue to plan to do ; it is fair to say that we have not yet started .

Q20 Elliott Colb u rn: T hank you very much for being honest. Th e last question would be around the , sadly cancelled, S afe T o B e M e conference , b ut also it is relevant to reference the fact that last weekend was the 50th anniversary of the first ever Pride m arch in London. Minister, what would your assessment be , given th e conference being cancelled and the anniversary of that march , o n where the Government 's current policies stand in terms of reflecting the priorities of the LGBT+ community in the UK ?

W e are not in a good place. A s I have said several times now, it is a shame we continue to keep having these debates about equality. Q21 Thank you for your candour , M inister. It is very much appreciated . O ne final question f r o m me and I will leave you alone : I can sense the frustration in your answer to that last question. Do you have any optimism that there is an appetite in Government to repair that relationship with the LGBT+ community?

Thank you very much , Minister. Chair , that is all from me.

Q22 Thank you, Chair. My questions, Minister, are about the violence against women and girls strategy. C ould you tell the C ommittee how you a re working with the H ome O ffice to make sure the specific needs of LGBT+ victims are met by this strategy?
Anna will take this because she will have m ore technical information .

W e are working closely with the Home Office and with the Ministry of Justice in particular on a cross - G overnment basis . T here are probably two or three elements I would pull out in particular around better recognition of the support that victims need and the reality for LGBT victims, along with other groups . S pecialist support is really important because otherwise there is no trust and c onfidence in accessing support. T here is an element around recognition and specialisation of support. T here is an increase in funding, and there will be 1,000 specialist sexual violence and domestic violence advisers before too long, which is a big increase. Putting funding on a multi-year basis as well provides a great deal of stability.

T he third element I would point to is a more systematic, co - ordinated approach to the commissioning of support at local level for victims . M y colleagues have been in all those conversations with counterparts in both D epartments articulating the need for LGBT requirements to be taken into account and helping to provide the additional insight as to what i s really required.

If I may, o bviously the issue of women and girls tends to sit in the portfolio held by former Minister Badenoch. The element s that come over to me is in terms of where we ensure hate crime is accurately reported, and we have made progress on that , and w here we see the issue of restorative rape or forced marriage as part of conversion practices, which is something we are addressing. Caroline Nokes may remember that some time ago , when I was not in this position but on the Back Benches , we had conversations about one of things I was working on with the then Home Secretary , Theresa May — same sex domestic violence, because it was n o t understood by police forces . Kemi would have dealt with the broader issue of violence towards women and girls. There is still an awful lot of work to be done—better reporting, better support, and better training for our police forces.

Q23 You have actually pre-empted my question. As we are viewing this issue from the perspective of victims, we are seeing there is a hierarchy of victims, and male victims are missing in this space. Frankly, we can look at recent reporting and see that male victims of sexual vi olence are not treated as seriously , b ut there is a basic issue about how we have treated sexual violence generally . T he services have not been there. For me , we should be talking about male violence as opposed to violence against women and girls ; l et us make it clear where the issue is.

Coming back to Anna’s response, it is reassuring that those discussions are happening, but collectively we need to recognise that support services for victims are pretty rubbish. You mentioned the commissioning. My experience is the Government will say all these nice things about “We must improve support for victims , ” and the NHS publishes its lifetime care pathway for victims of s exual v iolence , b ut when it actually comes to commissioning those services, police and crime commissioners say, “Nothing to do with us , ” and t he NHS says, “No, it's not our problem, it's a victims thing . ” Are you satisfied that the commissioning problems are being dealt with , and that the specific nature of each victim of these crimes will be properly reflected? If we just end up with a commitment to a quantum of spend without a relation to actual outcomes for survivors, it is not going to be worth the paper it is written on , is it?
Shall I respond?
They are all fair criticisms, but you will know more about how this is being addressed across Government, because it does not quite sit in my p ortfolio.

I start by saying I am sure there i s always more that can be done and more informed conversations that can be had . F or the resource s we bring to it , we are pretty impactful in those conversations. I take your point about funding ; it is not always the answer , although it is normally part of the answer. T he focus on those very specialis ed roles and having a better recognition of those specialist adviser roles is critical. I would also point to the existence of the LGBT domestic abuse helpline that the Home Office has on contract with Galop , the LGBT safety specialist charity , funding for which is being increased , along with all the other helplines the Home Office runs , s o the end of things that are closest to the victim, helplines , advisers and so on are getting a lot of attention in this approach .

Q24 Going back to what you said there about male victims in this space , I do n o t want to diminish violence against women and girls strategy because, frankly, female victims have been secon d rate for far too long , b ut I do recognise we do need to do more about male victims , not least to raise awareness , because I think it i s hidden. T here i s stigma for any victim , but it is a different kind of stigma for men . Do you have any long-term projects for actually addressing this , outside and complementary to the VAWG strategy ?
It is not currently in the cross -g overnment work programme, and you have just pointed out the glaring omission, which I wi ll take away.
Thank you, I do n o t want to speak for the rest of the Committee .
It might be in the strategy for other G overnment D epartments, but it i s not something on mine , a nd therefore you have pointed out a big gap, which I will plug.

Q25 The two things do n o t need to be in competition , a ctually you could have a violence against women and girls strategy but raising awareness about male -on-male violence in this space is important .
And w omen on male?

Q26 Y es indeed , b ut it does tend to be a male crime, and when we a re looking at it from the perspective of victim s, w e can miss that pa rt of it. M oving on , we ha ve talked about engaging with the Ministry of Justice on the V ictims B ill to make sure that also meets the needs of LGBT + victims , i s there anything else you woul d like to add to what you ha ve said already on that?

We were quite happy to see in the B ill the work we did on the impact of chemsex in terms of crime and victims. I t was quite refreshing that there was no pushback , and Minister Malt h ouse readily accepted it should be included.

W hat we a re finding goes back to the frustration that there i s a lot of noise that distracts and sometimes blows us off - course, when , in reality, day to day we a re a ctually managing to address issues . B roadly speaking, it has to be a work in progress . I f I can tack back to the Conversion Therapy Bill , we a re actually referring to conversion p racti c es now. O ne of things we are very keen to do is work with the Ministry of Justice and the Policing Minister to ensure there is very clear g uidance to the police on how to handle complaints, particularly when it comes to talking therapy where two people are in a room and the complaint has to be handled with sensitivity . This ensure s those making the complaint are treated correctly , b ut equally those who are on the end of the complaint are also treated fairly . If I can be blunt , I do n o t want to start seeing vicars being dragged down the aisle, so to speak . W e need to ensure that the implementation of how we deal with faith communities and consent is dealt with in a pragmatic and sensitive approach , so that we do n o t end up with the police being heavy-hand ed , whilst ensuring that cases are correctly investigated.

Q27 O ne of the things that gets played back to me from speaking to victims is they find the whole experience very dehumanising —effectively, they are treated like a piece of evidence. T hat is a massive impediment to bringing these offences to justice , because when you a re reliving what has happened to you , you a re re - traumatising yourself. I f you found the actual process of reporting dehumanising, it i s not going to encourage you to a ppear in court. I can see there is a potential issue if people feel th e y are encountering discrimination as well which exacerbates it . I s there any evidence that that i s a material fact or when it comes to LGBT + victims?

Anna Thompson: W e absolutely have evidence in the UK and internationally that LGBT victims are less likely to use reporting mechanisms than others because of concerns about whether their particular circumstances and the impact will be appropriately recognised, and whether there wi ll be a sympathetic hearing at the very least. There is certainly that evidence . I n addition to the B ill work, the actual legislation and the creation of the criminal offence, I would point to our intention to create a system of protection orders on a more preventative basis using civil law , t he guidance th e M inister mentioned to police , and educat i on safeguarding professionals and health professionals . We have mapped the various statutory agencies that w e wi ll need to communicate with, and we ha ve launched the victim support service for victims and those at risk of conversion practices which will be available to anybody who feels they have been or are at risk of that practi c e. T hat sort of support is crucial , alongside the other elements of the strategy.

Q28 M inister , I ha ve witnessed your pain in dealing with some of the se issues, and it strikes me that we seem to have got into a space in all our public discourse that every issue is viewed in a very binary way when actually most of the time the solutions are in the grey area in the middle .
You might say non - binary way.

Q29 Indeed . T here i s a challenge on us all to actually improve the quality of that , a nd I would commend you for the way you ha ve engaged with these discussions , because it has n o t always been easy. W hen we look at the issue of conversion therapy , and I ha ve been first in the queue to give you challenge on that , I wi ll readily say that when it comes down to it, we a re both at one in terms of the outcome we want to achieve —ba sically a law that eliminates harm. W hen we get into these very emotional debates about rights , a nd particularly where there is a potential conflict of rights , which there is in some areas of these discussions , perhaps there is some virtue in start ing from an outcome basis rather than the actual first principle, and we might actually get rid of a lot of this pain. Any reflections on how you have experience d this?

It is very difficult because c learly as a member of the LGBT + community having suffered queer bashing, homophobic abuse and discrimination at work, you feel the pain and the homophobic slurs. C olleagues sometimes make mistakes by just being ill - informed , and there i s no malice behind it . However, when you hear colleagues use phrases or descriptions where there is hurt intended , or it is a depiction of the community that demonises them , th e n I have to check myself because I realise that inevitably I react with passion because of my background and personal experience. I will not always get it right , and what I try to do is understand the positions of those people who have genuine concerns. If some body is coming from a position of “ no ” , then that can be a futile argument , b ut many colleagues I ha ve had discuss ions with have genuine concerns , and that is when you park your fears , and you try to work through those concerns and hopefully achieve a compromise. As you say, most of the engagement you and I have had , and I ha ve had with colleagues , has ended in a much better place.

T here are some people who are seeking to oppose the B ill for a reason I find frustrating and hurtful , which is when someone says, “ Well, how prevalent is it? ”, a nd then question the evidence and the volume of people being hurt as not being true. Then I say, “ Well, what's your threshold ? H ow many people have to be hurt before you think it's an issue we should address ?”, and I find that very painful , because it minimises the hurt and the impact on the victims b ecause one victim is worthy of protection . W e do n o t have thresholds of “ Well, once we get to 1 , 000 victims, then we'll act , ” which is the bit I find the hardest in this job. We a re all human and sometimes I will be very passionate in defending what I want to achieve b ut I sometimes will back off and try to work through people's genuine concerns , to hopefully get us both into a better place. Does that answer y our question ?

Q30 It does . I t is about framing the dialogue and focusing on the outcome. But what I have understood very clearly from you today is there is hurt in the way we sometimes debate these issues. N otwithstanding that we are all here to articulate opinions , this is n o t a g ame, and we need to be cogni s ant of that. We a re all human and w e do n o t always get it right , b ut I do n o t think there are many people who really intend it actually.

M y final question : what assessment have you made of the proposed reservations against the Istanbul c onvention , a nd what impact do you think that might have on LGBT + victims of violence a g ainst women and g irls ?
I turn to my advisor on that one.

Anna Thompson: I t i s really good news that we ha ve reached the point of being able to say the UK has ratified , because that ha s been the intention for a long time. T he reservations in particular, we would probably have to take away and look at any LGBT aspect of that. W ith a different hat on, I also work on international aspects of gender policy , a nd it i s really good news, not least for the standing of the UK in the wider world , that we have been able to announce the ratification.

Q31 W elcome. Minister, I need to first of all shower you with apologies as I was late turning up to this meeting , and I a m going to be leaving early because I am chairing an event about female offenders. I just wanted to put on record my gratitude for your candour and the human way in which you ha ve answered your questions, which is quite refreshing to this C ommittee .

I have been in your shoes before , as beautiful as they are , and one of my core belief s is that the GEO , albeit a small G overnment D epartment , has a superpower in that it has tentacles that, if used effectively, can reach out to every other G overnment D epartment . What you do impacts every other G overnment D epartment and vice versa , and because of that there is a huge symbiotic relationship between the G EO and every other aspect of G overnment , and where G overnment work in silos you have an amazing ability to break through that nonsense .

W ith that in mind, I a m really keen to know to what extent you ha ve been able to break down those barriers between the G EO , the Department of Health and the NHS to look at how we address some of the health issues and health inequalities that have been identified with LGBT + p eople's outcome s?

Personally , I have not found M inisters in the D epartment very difficult at all in e very approach I ha ve made, whether it be on things like trans healthcare, the HIV action plan , or IVF for lesbian couples . O ne of the issues I a m quite keen to address is ensuring that some of the reductions in sexual health clinics made a few years ago are reverse d , because I do no t think you can fulfil your HIV infection eradication programme without having sufficient sexual health clinics that people can go and get checked and tested rapidly. But I have to say that whether it was Sajid Javid , M inister Throup or Minister Caulfield , it ha s been a completely open door . I met no resistance whatsoever.
Q32 That i s really good to hear , a nd to what extent is the G EO able to furnish them with data and information to support their activities ?

W e a re doing a fair amount of that . There is the same relationship at official level — very conducive conversations about what we could do around sexual health and mental health within the D epartment . W e also work really closely with the team that work s on trans healthcare , s o there is really good dialogue both ways. I would additionally point to the role of Dr Michael Brady working with DHS C colleagues . He i s the first ever LGBT NHS adviser —a role which since your time as a Minister has become embedded in the NHS . Your point around data and evidence i s one of his key areas of focus i n ensuring that data is better collected, recognised and used across the system.

Just a very quick comment f rom me is that because of the pandemic, those at the centre of G overnment have spent a huge amount of time working on public health over the last two years, and therefore have much better contacts with not just the Department of H ealth, but the NHS, NHS D igital, NHSX and all the various different agencies in that world. W e do have much better contacts than we did , a nd of course t hose happened because of C ovid, but we can use them for other things.
Q33 Are you happy with the sense of direction in terms of the outcomes for LGBT + people in our health services?

I am certainly happy i n terms of things like the w omen's h ealth s trategy and how that will eradicate , if you like, the imbalance on access to IVF for lesbian couples . I n terms of the work on the HIV strategy, I believe that is world beating . T he access to PEP and Pr EP , although there i s a bit of a battle with elements of the NHS , has been a game changer in how we a re handling HIV , s o I am very comfortable with how that work is g oing . If you ha ve never met Dr Brady , he is a remarkable physician in terms of what is doing to change how we approach LGBT + healthcare.

There are two slightly more difficult issues . O ne is obviously reversing some of the reductions we made in sexual health clinics. Of course, any time money is involved i s a lways a slightly harder conversation , b ut they are genuinely looking to see what they can do to address that .

E qually , on trans healthcare , the NHS , as Hilary Cas s has said and certainly the former Secretary of State accepted, was n o t in a good place , but we ha ve made some steps forward with the new clinics , although there are still too many t rans people opting out of the NHS and then buying crap online to self - medicat e, and we do not know what they are buying or if they a re taking the right dose s. Also, the mental health support s that are there for them as well, all that needs fixing . T he other problem it causes is, because they opt out of the NHS, we do n o t have the data, so it becomes a chicken and egg situation . You say , “W e need to do this , ” but there are not enough people to provide the service . It i s not really a priority, and because they are opting out , we do n o t know how many people there are . But I think there is a genuine willingness in the NH S and the m inisterial t eam to put this issue right.

Q34 That is really h elpful, t hank you. Y ou mentioned equality of access to fertility treatment which leads me on to the question as to whether you a re still working towards fulfilling the commitments that were in the LGBT a ction p lan. One of them was LGBT people with learning disabilities for example , are those still areas you a re working on ?
Before my time , so I will have to seek guidance.

To some extent we are. We undertook some work around recognising inclu sive health practi c es a couple of years ago, and the wider work for people with disabilities t hat i s happening within the Equality Hub, and w e do connect the dots as far as we can. T he role of Dr Brady is probably pretty central on most health issues .

Q35 I s there a plan to publish some sort of assessment tracker of the LGBT action plan ? We know that from time - to - time M inisters change — quite a lot in the last 24 hours — and sometimes pieces of work can get left behind . C ould we do a stock t ake on that action plan?

I a m not particularly keen on action plans. T here i s a cross - G overnment work programme and there are elements I want to put into that that are key measures. I do n o t want to provide a long list of deliverables , because this is a day -to-day issue . O ne of the weaknesses of having an action plan, particularly cross - G overnment , is it can provide a false sense of security because a D epartment can just tick the box , “Y es, I've done that bit — job done , ” and although it is true you can be challenged and pro bed, I think sometimes you are going to just tick the box take your foot off the pedal . I much prefer to say, “ Where do we want to go ? W hat's the objective? ” a nd then measure milestone by milestone , rather than hav ing this long list of de liver able s so that if you only achieve one out of 10, you get beaten up because you ha ve only done 10%. I would much rather have a published work programme with some key deliverables , and those should, of course, change once you ha ve achieved one — what i s the next step —r ather than having just a long list of hopeful items to address .

Q36 N evertheless , It would be somewhat useful, I would suggest , to have done some sort of stocktake on what our aspirations were at one point , to see to what extent we ha ve reached anywhere towards the aims and how far we still have to g o.
If it i s helpful, I can confirm the majority of the commitments in the a ction p lan have seen progress through the wider work we a re doing.
Q37 But is there a plan to publish anything that would kind of reassure us, rather than your very reassuring words ?
Not at the moment. I a m always willing to be quizzed.

Q38 Thank you. Can I just pick up on something that was said there? You made reference to access to fertility services , and y ou mentioned lesbian couples as an example. Apart from the actual access, t here are issues around cost as well, where lesbian couples often have to pick up the cost from day one. Can you tell us if you a re doing anything around that?

My understanding is that there will be parity , but again I am looking for confirmation . T hat is Minister Ca u lfield ’ s policy area , s o I a m not over the detail , b ut I understand that broadly there will be parity now, so there will be no discrimination .
Q39 But a t the moment it is often up to the individual health trust s .
Yes, b asically , my understanding is where we wi ll get to is a heterosexual couple and a lesbian couple living in the same health area will have the same access to IVF treatment s .

With t he current requirement for same - sex female couples and other LGBT couples who would value this service for their family formation , t he costs arise particularly out of the requirement to self - fund several rounds of artificial insemination before IVF services can be accessed. That is the commitment we are fully expecting , assured and have seen will be in the w omen's h ealth s trategy when it i s published, probably before the recess.
Okay, that i s great , t hanks very much .

Q40 The C ommittee has previously expressed concerns about the lack of clarity, capacity , waiting times and waiting lists in gender identity clinics. We put forward a list of recommendations, especially around the long - term prospects of the pilot clinics and how successful they were. The G overnment's response was they would b e making an evaluation of each individual clinic . Has that been done or is it due to be completed? I f so, will it be published , and when ?

I do n o t know how much of it will be published, but my understanding is something will certainly be published , at least one of the evaluations has been completed and is at quality assurance stage, and the evaluation findings are very positive about the community - based clinic model , so I am looking forward to being able to share more of that .

Q41 W e look forward to seeing that . Prior to the pandemic, there were 13 ,500 people on the waiting list in the clinics , and some of those ha d been waiting up to three years for their first appointment. Do you have a breakdown of what the waiting lists are looking like now? How many are actually waiting for their first appointment , and can you give us an idea of the geographical scale of that?

We do n o t have that information to hand , a nd indeed one of the issues is the information is n o t collected centrally — i t i s published on each clinic ’ s website — b ut we can take that away and provide that to the C ommittee .

Q42 We would be grateful to receive that . One more question f rom me : i n May 20 21 the LGBT Foundation argued there were huge issues with the mental health and associated concerns of LGBT people , and the GEO M inisters did not properly consider or research the mental health effect of the pandemic on the LGBT community. Is that a fair criticism , and c an you be specific about w hat steps the G overnment have actually taken to correct that impression?

The other witnesses m ay have more detail, but generally speaking we have accepted that mental health support of the LGBT community is not where it should be , which the NHS has accepted as well. I n terms of the exact numbers and what the NH S are proposing to do about it, we would have to go back to our health colleagues to get a bit more detail for you .

Anna Thompson: We are working with DHS C mental health t eam to see what we can develop together to address the issues. I guess the other thing I would point to is sometimes the value we can add is si g nposting and channelling people a little. W hen the Department of Health and Social Care issued grant opportunity last year for grassroots - based organisations to bid for suicide prevention grants, we were able to get the word out to the LGBT community and to the LGBT grassroots organisations through . for example, the LGBT Consortium , which represents around 1,000 organisations — I cannot remember off the top of my head — of different scale. That would n o t have happened if we had n o t been having the right conversations with Department of Health and Social Care officials at the right time.
Q43 Is it a priority for the D epartment ?
It is for us. W e a re actively looking into what we can do at the moment with the Department of Health and Social Care who are very willing to engage, I should add.
Q44 Thank you. Can I ask Members if they have any further questions? No, o kay . Minister, is there anything you would like to say to the C ommittee ?
I have said enough.

I n that case, can I thank you, Minister , An n a , Marcus, for your time . P articularly M inister F ree r, I would like to thank you for your candour and honesty today. It was certainly refreshing for the C ommittee to have such honest and straightforward answers , t hank you.

sessions.iT: National Shipbuilding Strategy Refresh
sessions.w: Rt Hon Ben Wallace MP, Secretary of State for Defence; Ministry of Defence; Ministry of Defence; Ministry of Defence

segs.tx: Defence Committee
Oral evidence: National shipbuilding strategy refresh, HC 181
Tuesday 5 July 2022
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 5 July 2022.
Watch the meeting
Members present: Mr Tobias Ellwood (Chair); Dave Doogan; Richard Drax; Mr Mark Francois; Gavin Robinson; John Spellar; Derek Twigg .
Scottish Affairs Committee member also present: Pete Wishart.
Questions 41 - 154
Witnesses

I : Rt Hon Ben Wallace MP, Secretary of State for Defence ; Vice Admiral Sir Chris Gardner KBE, Director General (Ships), Defence Equipment & Support, Ministry of Defence ; Rear Admiral Paul Marshall CBE, Director , Navy Acquisition, Senior Responsible Owner – T31 and FSS, Ministry of Defence ; Rear Admiral Rex Cox, CEO, National Shipbuilding Office, Ministry of Defence .
Examination of w itnesses
Witnesses: Ben Wallace, Vice Admiral Sir Chris Gardner, Rear Admiral Marshall and Rear Admiral Cox.

Welcome to this Defence Select Committee hearing on Tuesday 5 July 202 2 . I am delighted to welcome the Secretary of State here this afternoon, along with Vice Admiral S ir Chris Gardner, who is d irector g eneral ( s hips) , d efence e quipment and s upport, Rear A dmiral Paul Marshall, who is d irector of N avy a cquisition and s enior r esponsible o wner for the T ype 31 and the f leet solid s upport, and , finally, Rear Admiral Rex Cox, who is the c hief e xecutive o fficer of the National Shi pb uilding Office. You are all welc ome this afternoon. Thank you very much indeed.
W e will be focusing primarily on the national shipbuilding strategy , and then , towards the end , we will ask about some of the wider issues, as has been agreed.

Q41 Good afternoon, gentlemen. Secretary of State, the role of devolved nations, and particularly Scotland, in supporting shipbuilding and the shipbuilding strategy is key, and we can see the evidence of this in the effort, expenditure and value - add of organ isa tion s such as the FE colleges, University of Strathclyde , Skills Development Scotland, Scottish Enterprise , Glasgow City Council and Fife Council in particular . W hat environment and landscape does the MoD create to allow devolved nations to input to that proce ss, to add value to shipbuilding and to make sure that we continue to build the very best warships that we can?

T he very first contribution that we make is the same that we make to all the nations of the United Kingdom, which is to be , effecti vely , a customer to encourage investment in yards and in skills, because we are the ones buying many of the ships. T hat is the first thing. I would say this, b ecause I am a Unionist : you get a bigger customer because you are part of a big ger union , and s o that is one of the ways.

However, on the other stuff around skills, we have involved the Scottish Government on part of the skills workforce that we have set up , which is one of the committees where we are very keen to make sure that the skills base is stimulated , because it is really important that the skills are there. M ore than taxation , t he thing that companies move very quickly for is skills. If t hey cannot get the skills , like oxygen, t hey will just d ry up and that will be the end of that. C ustomers, whether private or public sector, will move rapidly , s o that is very important.

A lso , we have the National Shipbuilding Office , and I am very happy if Admiral Cox wants to speak to that and the role that he has in involving the Scottish G overnment. We discussed this morning about both we have drafted on—the new head of the Ferguson shipyard is involved in the strategy and, indeed, the work that we do with some of the devolve d A dministrations . If Admiral Cox wants to expand on that , I would be delighted.

Certainly. T he head of Ferguson is a member of the s hipbuilding e nterprise for g rowth. Ferguson is a nationalised yard, so we have really good input there . F undamentally , the strategy is for the whole of the United Kingdom. There are s pecific elements for Scotland and the other devolved A dministrations, but it is a strategy for the whole of the United Kingdom. Scotland plays a significant part with the w est c oast and e ast c oast shipbuilding enterprise.

On skills, the Department for Education has launched the UK s hipbuilding s kills taskforce, which is chaired by Dr Paul Little , who is the c hair of the University of Strathclyde . [1] T here is a really good input fr om Scot land .

There is another thing that is in the pipeline. The role that I have as shipbuilding tsar and that our shipbuilding office has is to help other D epartments and A dministrations to find their way through procuring vessels , which the y do not routinely do. If you think about the Ministry of Defence , we nearly always have a submarine or a ship in the pipeline. We are always building ships . S ome would say that we should build more than others, but we are always doing it , s o we have a residual knowledge base . F or some D epartments , such as the Home Office, which only occasionally replace s its B order F orce , or the Scottish Government , with its fisheries protection vessels and , indeed, its ferries, i t is not a constant.

T he idea of the Nat ional Shipbuilding Office and me as the tsar is that we are there to try to help facilitate those procurements when they happen. T here is definitely a sense here that we are here to help . With one other G overnment Department, I am very keen to encourage Br itish manufacturing, British supply chains, British build and British investment in yards . T herefore , we can often help them to find a way of doing that , if t hey are not used to it. W hat I would press on the Scottish G overnment is that you have some ships coming up . Y ou can build them. There are many ways of trying to get them built , or partly built , or supply chain into those yards in Scotland .

Come and ask us, a nd we will try to help you do that. As you know from the political rows th at happen both in the Scottish Parliament and elsewhere , i t is too late after the event to say , “We wanted to build it in Scotland but had to build it in Romania”. It is too late after the event. We are genuinely in the spirit of collaboration . What is goo d for Scottish shipbuilding is good for British shipbuilding , and I would be delighted to continue to make sure that we try to deliver that.

Q42 I n terms of specifications, I do not want you to go into FSS in detail , because that will come later o n . I n terms of specifying in terms of a tender for what we need, operations and operational requirements dictate what the vessel or any other piece of equipment can do in terms of its performance. W hat procedures do you have to ensure that the specificatio n required of any vessel is consistent with the capability that exists in Scottish yards, or yards elsewhere in these islands?

I can ask both Admiral Chris and Admiral Rex to expand, but, fundamentally, when the bidders respond to a tender, they have to demonstrate that they have the capacity or the capability to build or respond to that tender, otherwise you end up placing a contract with someone who cannot deli ver and we all end up with messes that we have sometimes seen in the past. They have to demonstrate that they have a track record and the technical requirements that will meet it. That is the start point of the process and it is why getting investment in y ards is really important.

The public sector, whether it is devolved or UK Government, is a big player in placing contracts. We should be insisting on what you get in exchange for that from those yards. What are the yards going to invest in the skill base i n exchange for that? What are the yards going to invest in machinery? It is very telling when you go to a yard abroad—in some cases entirely private yards—how much investment has gone into the machinery and the capabilities that allow them to compete.

Q43 Dave Doogan: Let me just gently push back on that. I hear what you are saying—as the client, you hold the whip hand, and that is kind of the case, but it is a mutual dependency. The UK does not want to be without shipyards, and shipyards need orders to come fr om the UK and other customers, so it is a mutual dependency. The question that I am trying to get it as how we ensure that we do not specify an element that is a “ nice to have ” but not essential to the mission and which, in so doing, precludes it from bein g satisfied from a yard on these islands.

There is never one single factor that breaks the camel ’ s back. It is fundamentally whether they can deliver something on time and on budget. Whatever your politics are, you want to manage a public proc urement process that comes in on budget—that is just the reality of it. You have an obligation in Scotland to your taxpayers, the same as I do—and on time, because otherwise the N avy does not get a ship that it needs to meet the threat.

Under all Governmen ts, there are key targets. It is the least that we can expect. You will no doubt criticise me about a delay to a Type 26 programme sometime in this sitting, because we all know that—
Mr Francois Yes, I have that one.

Those are two key targets . The second one is security of supply chain. It is incredibly important to make sure that we are not overdependent on another country, should a war happen. The skills base is really important to helping it compete. It is a mixture of long-term funding and security, but I cannot avoid the fact that, on a number of occasions, the Scottish Government had a chance to place orders in Scottish yards but went to Romania.
Q44 The Scottish Government is not here giving evidence. It is the UK Government tha t are here giving evidence.
But you are in control of the same levers as I am, like skills base, investment in yards and capital grants.
I do not want to get into a constitutional debate .
No, I bet you do not.
Q45 T he Scottish Government is not in control of the same levers that you are , and that is my question.

Here is the thing. If you think that is the case, you are wrong. Y ou need to understand what goes into maki ng a shipyard viable . I t is things like skills, capital investment in equipment and making sure you have a ready workforce and good management. All of that is in the gift of the Scottish Government, in the same way that some of it is in the gift of my Government. If you do not have the skill base, you cannot build your ships. When I last looked, that is devolved. It certainly was when I was in the Scottish Parliament.
Q46 To get back to my original point, would you like to amend—
I t is called the national shipbuilding strategy. I am here to talk about the national shipbuilding strategy. That means both devolved and reserved, thank you very much.

Q47 In terms of the impact and value - add that the Scottish Government ha ve in m aking sure that the skills are available in Scotland to provide that technical expertise and labour for the production of warships for the UK, that is a very positive thing, is it not?
It is a positive thing, if the skills are delivered, not i n the management, as we can tell from Ferguson and the management of your ferries, which did damage the reputation of Scottish shipbuilding.
Q48 Rear Admiral Cox, I was pleased to hear you talk of the National Shipbuilding Office being represen tative of the entirety of the United Kingdom. How are we getting on in Northern Ireland?

We have reached out to the Northern Ireland Government and to officials. We have Harland & Wolff in your constituency—a great shipyard under new mana gement and looking to do great things going into the future. Baroness Goldie, representing devolved issues within the Ministry of Defence, has been in contact with Members of the Assembly to bring them up to speed and to discuss the strategy with them. We have a relationship. I would be very keen to strengthen that relationship and we will continue to do that.

Q49 I do not want to put you on the spot, Secretary of State, and I have walked this path for quite a while with your predecessors as wel l. I was reminding Committee colleagues that I found it quite frustrating when a pr edecessor , Sir Michael Fallon , came to Northern Ireland and stood in the shipyard in my city to name a ship after my city, which was going to be built in Glasgow. That has b een a frustrating path to tread. The national shipbuilding strategy was written by Sir John Parker [2] to try to encourage economic diversion across the United Kingdom, and this modular approach was going to see a re-energising around yards outside of Scotla nd and outside of the south of England. Aside from warm words and engagement with the Northern Ireland Executive or with Members of the Legislative Assembly in Northern Ireland, what pipeline do we have for Northern Ireland yards to ensure that this nation al shipbuilding strategy is delivering on its core aims?

First of all, the Northern Ireland Executive alone has four, and potentially five or six, ships starting in 2022-23 within its powers. What Admiral Cox is saying, and what my point is ab out the National Shipbuilding Office , is that we are to help. I am not going to overrule the devolution settlement, but if they want help to try to find a way of building those ships in a Northern Irish yard, or to make it feasible to do so, they should co me and engage with us. As you say, we want more than warm words. They have the budget, and let us see what we can do on it.

The plus side for your industry in Northern Ireland is that Harland & Wolff is now joined with Appledore and Methil, which is good n ews, because that consolidation into a bigger group gives it all sorts of capacity to share work around that conglomerate of yards, which is in the right direction. I noticed very recently one refurbishment of a big cruise ship that came in on budget and u nder time, which has to be a good thing for the reputation of the Belfast yard.

On N avy contracts, subject to the completions that are going on, Harland & Wolff are active and bidding in a number of contracts there , not just in the N avy but in a number of other contracts. I am very happy, without fear or favour, to help make sure that, if they are successful, these things come back to Northern Ireland or anywhere else. Harland & Wolff ’ s changes have been really positive just from outside looking in. I went to visit Appledore recently. It is in a good place to be winning both private and public contracts. The investment that the chief executive has now started to make in the skill base in Northern Ireland is very welcome. As you will know, one of the worries early on was that it had a big dry dock, but the skill base had dissipated. It has come back, which has been really good.

Q50 Good afternoon, gentlemen. It is good to see you again, Secretary of State. Who knows what could become of Members of the Scottish Parliament in their future political career, but it is good to see you.
It is all d ownhill after that.

Q51 Pete Wis hart: Could I thank you, Chair, for the very kind invitation to come along this afternoon? The Secretary of State will know, of course, of our very keen interest in shipbuilding in Scotland. This is the second of our current range of inquiries. On Monday a nd Tuesday, we will be visiting Govan and Rosyth for ourselves, just to see, first hand, how progress is being made on the Type 26s and Type 31s.

I hope that I am not going to get as tetchy an exchange as you did with Mr Doogan . I want to be positive and h elpful, because we are in a good place just now in Scotland. We are all encouraged by the drumbeat of orders. There is confidence in the yards. There seems to be security of employment going forward. Secretary of State, shipbuilding in Scotland seems to be characterised by a process of feast and famine. We have been through the bad times and are currently going through the good times, which is great for the skills that Mr Doogan outlined in his question to you. How do we assure and have certainty that that drumbeat will keep beating and that jobs will be protected and maintained in Scotland?

One of the ways is a consistently above real - term s defence budget. We heard the announcement at NATO of a defence budget that is committed and not falling b ut growing over a period of time, which is one of the ways, because it is absolutely the case that I want to continue building, not feast or famine. It is also why the onus is often on me and the Department to make sure that we come in on budget, which is why the budget point is really important.

If the Type 26, for example, went really over budget, history shows that you end up with fewer ships ; instead of nine, you get six or whatever. That means that I often have quite tough conversations with the two me n left and right, because I want them to make decisions. I had a discussion yesterday about the weapons fit on the Type 26, because every time you do not make a decision, we all know that the cost goes up. First of all, there is a strong defence budget.

Se condly, it is publishing, which we did for the first time , a 30- year pipeline. That is a really good document . I t is not a free lunch. S ome of these D epartments are buying small vessels once every few years or decades, and our shipbuilding office is there to help them with how to do that. I t gives some sense of the British Government and devolved A dministrations’ shopping list. If you are an investor in the City or in industry, you can finally get a sense of the scale of it, which is 150 ships in 30 years, and that is a good start point.

T he other bit is how we make sure that we prepare the yards for the day that there is not always a N avy contract . I have to commend the c hief e xecutive of Babcock . I used to meet members of B ritish s hipbuilding who did not r eally want to talk about it . T hey would not tell everyone in the City that one of the things that they did was build ships . T hey would rather talk about their other engineering businesses. He has been brilliant at saying, “N o, I am a shipbuild er. Babcock is leading in s hipbuilding ” . They have won contracts in Indonesia, Qatar, Oman and the UK. T hat atmosphere that you talk about is partly driven from the top about a belief and an ambition, and we can all have a role in that. T hat helps unlock i nvestors and do that.

W e should not be left behind. That is the other thing . C ompared to other European yards — and I do not mean state - owned yards, but just other European yards — we have not been keeping pace over the last 30 years , for lots of reasons. Some might be feast and famine, some might be that the owners have not invested, and some might have been productivity challenges . Sir John Parker and this iteration is a really positive step .

T here are cultural issues around FE coll eges and skills, which we really have to cross . I n some parts of our country , i t is really positive. If you are a west of Scotland or Lancashire MP, apprenticeships and FE colleges are embraced. They are part of the fabric and the culture of what we get. I t is how we recruit people and how we grow it. In o ther parts of the country, there is still a snobbery around FE colleges and apprenticeships that does not help in the very important skills that we need. I t is palpable. In parts of Scotland , it is embraced , and , in other parts, just like parts of England, it is not. T hat is some of the work that we all need to do

Q52 I am grateful for that. I am not entirely sure about the character isa tion of the FE offer in Scotland. I know persona lly j ust how good and superb that is, and the assistance that it gives . I understand all of that . I like the document and the refresh strategy. T hey are very helpful and outline a way forward , but c ould I suggest maybe two things —one that could have been d one and one that you could maybe assure me of as we go forward ?

First, would it not have been better not to have split the Type 26 contracts , and that we got all eight ships at once? Would that not have given better security and confidence to the contract or ? S econdly, could you see something positive about the delivery of the Type 32s and Type 83s—that they will be built in the UK and, i f they are built in the UK, that the yards in Scotland will have first look in for the construction of these vessels ?

The yards of the United Kingdom will be able to respond to the social value weighting in our contracts, which recogni s es things like level l ing up and economic disparity , etc . M y father was brought up in sight of the yards in Fife, so I understand .
I am from W est Fife and my father worked at Rosyth. We have that common background.

You and I are probably the only East Fife supporters left , although my father is in Leven. It is an impor tant document . I could ask Chris Gardner to explain why they split the original contract for the Type 26 . Again, as the Secretary of State, we have to also guard against complacency , so that people do not get the single contract and then just sit back and let an overrun or an overc o st happen. W e do want, even within British yards, some sense of competition to make sure —and it is not lost on me that some of the excellent progress in Rosyth on the T ype 3 1 already is slightly driven by a sense of competition w ith the Clyde shipyards about who can invest, who can moderni s e and who can deliver on target to set them up for the next set of contracts. T here is no harm in that and that is a good thing.

I went to see the cut steel on the T ype 3 1 in Rosyth . A s you say, if the Scottish Committee and , indeed , this Committee go to visit some shipyards, it is really fascinating , w hen you go to enough of them, how every single one has a different culture and attitude, which absolutely can make the difference.
Q53 Pete Wishar t: Any reassurance that the Type 32s and Type 83s will be —

T hey are way into the mid- 2030s , if you and I are still around at that stage . T hey are definitely a key part of the N avy’s war fight and the need to have them . We are talking about 203 0s, but we will need to start the process towards the end of the 2020 s.
Q54 I would like to hear the drumbeat in the future .

The drumbeat is there. It is in the pipeline. We will need to replace the T ype 4 5s and the other ships that are currently floating around , and so far , so good , T ype 26 and T ype 3 1 . I f Rosyth is churning out as it is , that is all good omens.

The only thing I would add is that, if we had ordered all eight ships straightaway, we would not have got as keen a price as we are going to get on batch two . B uilding a new ship that has never been built before , when the level of risk , complexity and engineering is not well understood, means that the company would , understandably , price in a significant margin for that. What we have now, of course, is the evidence, good and bad, about how well the batch one program me is doing, and we have used that as part of our negotiations on batch two.
Thank you. I look forward, Secretary of State, to you coming to our Committee in the next few months.

Q55 Secretary of State, you have referenced a couple of times the work being done in support of other D epartments , and y et , as our colleague the r ight h onourable Member for North Durham has been raising several times, for the Border Force vessels, they bypass ed British yards and went straight to a Dutch provider. Was that helpful to British shipbuilding ?
I do not think that any contract has b een placed yet, ha s it?

F or the record , I can categorically state that that is not the case. The S enior R esponsible Owner (SRO) joined on 1 June, taking over from the interim S RO , and is reviewing the program me and examining the procurement strategy . I can categorically reassure the Committee that that is not the case.

Q56 Secretary of State and gentlemen, good afternoon . It is always a pleasure to see members of the R oyal N avy. As m y father and grandfather continually reminded me , you are members of the senior service . A s a former guards officer, we did not quite rate that highly . A nyway, it is very nice to see you all.

Can I read the question and then perhaps just raise a couple of points that I have from t he information that I have had that perhaps the Secretary of State and others can comment on? The work in the pipeline is concentrated in the early decades. What are you doing to flatten out these peaks and troughs?

I am tempted to go down the fleet solid support ships , but that is the next question, so I will not, other than to say that it is seen by the shipbuilding industry as the block on which they would like to build further. On m y specific question , c an I just mention, for example, Francis Tusa, a ve ry respected commentator who I am sure you are all aware of ? He says that there is insufficient yard space and skills for the first decade , and insufficient work for the latter two . P erhaps you could comment on that.

There is a concern that , if you give st ate aid to foreign yards in order to dump prices, that might play a role in shipbuilding going abroad. Several people have commented that t here are no guarantees that all vessels, despite the fact that there are many in the pipeline, will be built in the U K. Secretary of State, you have already hinted that it might be the case that not all are guarantee d, depend ing on the size of the yard, the ability of it to do the work and , of course, the skills that are so important.
The final point is on exports. A s we know, some of our vessels will be exported. The view there is that that will help with the peaks and troughs. Where do you see that fitting in?

On the peaks and troughs, on the N avy pipeline, depending on the guarantees of the budgets and the long - term future, the Type 31s, Type 32s and Type 83s, and the replacement of Albion and Bulwark—the amphibious assault ships— towards the end of the decade , are all a pipeline that goes well into the 2030s as well, so both decades are fairl y well catered for in the purely N avy space. Admiral Rex could probably talk about whether he agrees with the peaks and troughs in that thing.

I am glad that you brought out the issue about yard space , because it is not always the case that you choose not to build or construct or part - build abroad because you do not want to do it in a British yard, but sometimes because , at that moment in time , either the British yards have not bid or , indeed , there is no capacity in that yard. F or example, Scotsto u n and Go van will not have much capacity, if at all, in the next 10 years, because it is building the Type 26. W hen HMS Glasgow sa ils up the Clyde, hopefully sooner rather later , she will go to Scotstoun . T he second ship is already starting to be constructed . Third , Rosyth does have space at the moment , b ut it is absolutely the case —and I agree with you —that we are trying to do is stop feast and famine, but it would be a lovely problem to have that all the yards are full for a very long time.

The second part of that is the skills question . I f I could ask Admiral C ox on the skills thing, it is a really good piece of work that we are doing. It was really telling w hen I went to the south - west of England . T here are 19 , 000 jobs in the maritime industry in the south - west, ranging from Sunseek e r and Princess Yachts all the way through to A&P yards in Falmouth, Pendennis and Appledore. There are huge amounts of people in the whole industry , from building a metal box to carpets and furniture for superyachts and all of those sorts of things. It is really good industry.

My point about the FE colleges was that one of their chall enges is getting into schools to persuade people that there is a great career in shipbuilding or the maritime industry, let us call it, and some schools being less keen to allow FE colleges to come and advertise their wares, and much keener to divert them to higher education somewhere else, not always necessarily helpful to our industry, but also not necessarily the right thing. That i s a really interesting thing.

T hat is exactly what we need to get after and exactly what the United Kingdo m s hipbuilding s kills t ask f orce is designed to get after . It meets this week for the first time . It has 18 months to map out what the problem is and to come up with some recommendations.

This is not about ditching everything that is going on at the moment, because there is so much really good work on apprenticeships and skills going around across the country by the main primes, for example. We have over 800 apprentices and graduates being employed by the shipbuilding industry at the moment, and that is growing year by year, but we need to make sure that is co-ordinated, because what is right for one part of the country may not be right for the rest of United Kingdom. We need to understand the problem and then make recommendations. We should be under no illusions here. We are not going to solve this overnight, but we must set the conditions now, as soon as we can, to begin to address the problem.
