Q57 Admiral, if we are going to build all these ships in the UK, would that be po ssible, for example, by expanding port facilities and getting all the skills ? Is it your long - term ambition to try to have a shipbuilding industry in this country that caters for everything, or is that an unachievable aim ? A re trying to get 7 5% ? Is there a target that you are trying to achieve ? I s it realistic that you can get anywhere near ?

As the Secretary of State mentioned, t he n ational shipbuilding strategy refresh sets out a 30- year pipeline of work. T ogether with commercial opportun ities, that gives British yards every opportunity to compete on a like - for - like basis, but this is also about increasing productivity and investment in the yards , not just in skills but in the infrastructure . P rocurement contracts are written in order to t ry to facilitate and encourage that.

The point that I make to everyone who I talk to about the strategy is that this is a whole - of - enterprise approach . This is G overnment, the NSO, the Royal Navy and industry. We are all in this together and we have a moment in time where we can change this , and we really need to grasp that . I am very optimistic .
Q58 What about foreign yards dumping prices? Is it going to be tempting, if money is short, to maybe send one or two ships over to wherever it may be?

W e need to combat that, and the way that we do that is through the UK home shipbuilding c redit guarantee scheme, which incentivi s es owners and operators to build in the United Kingdom, and we are look ing forward to announcing that very shortly. T hat will be a real fillip for the enterprise.

Richard, you talk about exports, so part of the paraphernalia that we have put in place is the m aritime c apability c ampaign o ffice to try to win export s. This is the balance . I know that colleagues are often keen on t he total UK build model. We are trying to develop a shipbuilding industry that exports , as it does. That is important. W e are in competitions in Poland and in Greece . W e have sold the Type 3 1 design and more than that to Indonesia, which is building two ships to begin with f rom that . T he Type 26 in Canada and Australia is one of the biggest shipbuilding products.

A ll of that is partly because we are an open economy. I f we shut the doors, do not be surprised if there is a reciprocal response . A ll shipbuilding industries need to maintain some form of export market. That is just really important to do. T here will be more competitions coming up . Norway ’s anti- submarine - typ e frigate will be coming up, and so we need to be in that business.

W hat really struck me, going around all those different yards, is how some are ready for the future and some are not . What we have done, which is really good , through the shipbuilding ente rprise for growth is to start a program me called S hipyard of the F uture . I am conscious that in Europe there are some totally private ly owned companies. You see super yacht after superyacht being ch urned out of German and Dutch yards. There is no state dump ing there. I went to one yard — I will not mention which one it was — a nd I said to them , “W hat would I expect if I walked into the German yard? What would it look like? What is the difference? What is the difference in machinery? ”

W e have started a programme , Shipyard of the Future , which will set out what we think and would, hopefully, sometimes when placing a N avy contract, expect the yard to invest in —“ If you want our contract for £2 billion worth of ships, we expect you to invest in th ese things that your competitors have and you do not have ”, and make the management work a bit harder for the long - term future of their yard as well .

We have a productivity challenge. That is a fact. We also had a competitive problem, some of which we have changed by those export credit guarantees in home. We did a productivity study, and one of the things that our competitors had in Europe was access to export finance and domestic export home finance. We have done both of those, which is why we have now se en a number of foreign yards buying or investing in British yards. I think that Damen has invested in a site on the Isle of Wight? Have they done that yet? It is not done yet. It is OCEA France, sorry. Foreign yards are looking at now investing in Britain in the infrastructure of British yards in order to either potentially win contracts or because they see a capacity opportunity. It is looking positive.

People were definitely discouraged from building ships in British yards through the lack of a home guara ntee scheme for the financing. It seemed to me odd that you could get some infrastructure support, but, when it came to a ship, you could not , s o we have fixed that as well , and I am really looking forward to that .

Q59 I j ust have two very quick p oints, Secretary of State. One is on a point that you were making j ust a second about the productivity that you see exhibited in foreign yards. Babcock producing 3 1 at £ 250 million a unit for the floating moving vessel , ex of GF E , is an extraordinary price. I s it your understanding that is being achieved because of the investments that it has made in Rosyth and the world - leading advanced manufacturing facility that it has there ?
I hear what you are s ay ing about capacity . A re you aw are fully of BAE’s exceptional ambition for the build hall at Govan and the effect that will have on its available capacity ?

G o ing back to my point about Rosyth and the Clyde , the Babcock leadership came along, invested in the build hall , got on with it and said, “If we can build these ships inside, we can increase our productivity. We do not have to stop when it is bad weather and everything else ” . BAE, which is now doing it, first of all wanted us to pay for it . T o my point about getting the management to invest in the yard s , it is in their interest , as much as it is in the customer ’ s. I am delighted that BAE is going to put a covered build hall in place. We will be contributing to it as the MoD and the customer , b ut that is the sort of thing that is about the cultural shift and investing in the yard , so that when , whatever happens one day — there is not a naval contract or it wins another contract to build a civil ship—it can show that productivity.

When I went to Pendennis yard recently down in Falmouth , it was awarded a regional development grant, which it immediately spent on a new lift. I n doing so , it probably saved itself a lot of money and cut production by six weeks. B ecause it is an entirely private yard, it knew that its superyacht customers , who are basically its customers , will go somewhere else at the drop of a hat if you do not deliver on time. There is a really pressing demand .

I nvesting in the yard and its capital really can make a diff erence. Some companies are up for that , s ome have to be prompted and some do not do it at all. A s an enterprise, we have to really be quite direct about it.

Q60 Just following that, when we were at the BAE yard in Adelaide, that covered facility has been built with very considerable investment from both the South Australian and the Federal Commonwealth Government of Australia. What you are saying, Secretary of State, is welcome, but, for a long while, Treasury has just insisted on everybody going on the lowest price, as long as they can meet quality. T hat has put British yards at a disadvantage, which brings us on to the fleet solid support vessels, which, as you know, are huge ships . The award of the contract for those has been pushed back for years, and industry has told us that it sees this order as a litmus test for the credibility of the shipbuilding strategy. What reassurance can you give us and them that this order will go to a UK yard?

F irst of all, John, you will know that i t is in the middle of a competition. I do not want to be sued if I pre - empt the result of the tendering process. I cannot give you certain guarantees in the middle of this process. What I can say is that the reason it was delayed last time was the competit ion collapsed. It collapsed because a number of yards pulled out of the bidding and , therefore , it became an untenable competition . W e thought we would recast the competition , which was the right thing to do.

I would hope, John, that you would also support the fact that, when anyone is bidding, whether it is a British or a foreign yard, they bid at price. It is not just a blank chequebook. No Secretary of State, Labour or Conservative, is going to sit here and do blank chequebook contracts. If we say, “Here is the contract for a group or a class of ships”, there is a contract put out to price, and that is part of the process. I hope that people agree with that. You just cannot do it any other way.
Q61 Is it on ly on price ?

N o, it is not only price, which is why we have social value in there. It is a minimum of 20 % . [3] T he social value includes a whole number of factors , but those that are most important to me are the factors of economic disparity and , indeed , social, economic and levellin g up factors that allow us to put a weighting into those contracts , where the bidders must answer some of those , and i t is really important that they do.
Q62 W ould you let us know the breakdown of that 20 % ?
W e will write in, but I can tell you that all bidders have to meet that in that price .

On the solid support ship, it is, of course, incredibly important. We have already insisted that the ship is constructed or integrated in the UK. That is important. We have also talke d about the supply chain, the build of the ship and the proportion of the build. I do not know if it is a percentage or just a build proportion that has to be in the UK. We are very keen to make sure that we get a competition.

What I am keen to do in our B ritish shipbuilding is to do the same thing that we had with Nissan and Honda . Nissan and Honda brought their skills, their management and their modern methods into UK car manufacturing and basically saved the car industry in the 1980s . N o one ha s looked b ack on that. The Sunderland car factory is the most productive car factory in Europe , if I am not mistaken , s o we need to sometimes access the winning formula that some of the other yards have had, and that is important.

W e cannot rely purely on the perman ent . A s I talked about earlier, I want to access leverage on skills, on productivity and on investment and capital investment in yard s . It is really important to make sure that we produce the best yards in the world , and I think we can do that , b ut if we pull up the drawbridge, I do not think that we will get there, because we have pulled up the drawbridge for the last 50 years, John, and our productivity is well behind European yards in both cost and time, which is w hy we are not winning enough private contracts .
Q63 P artly also because of feast and famine .
There are plenty of private yards in Europe that are not based on public contracts and that still winning more bids than we are, and that is not satisfactory.
Q64 They get Government subsidy in many cases .
N ot all of them.

Q65 You talked about integrating. I could say, “I integrate my piece of IKEA furniture by just putting a few bolts in” . W hen you say “ integr ated ” , how many of the blocks that are going to be integrated are going to be built in British yards, or will they all be built in foreign yards and then welded together in a yard in this country?

As you know, I worked aerospace, John , so you will understand that there are lots of ways in which a contract is valuable. In terms of Govan and Scotstoun, probably the most valuable part of the contract for the Type 26 is Scot stoun , where we put on radars , sensors , steering gears and engines . Britain sometimes leads the world in things other than just the metal box. It leads the world in the integration , the weapon systems and the electronic warfare .

Q66 We are talking about a support ship that will have s ome of that but not primarily. Will those blocks for those ships be built in British yards , or will they be built in foreign yards and just welded together?

I will ask Admiral C ox to tell you , to the extent that we can in the middle of a compe tition which we are in, but when the competition is decided, we can answer many of those questions for you . F undamentally , the majority of that ship project, whether it is build , integration or supply chain, will be UK. How much — 100 % , 60 % or 70 % ? W e will s ee what the bidders are putting in, but it is important, as I have said earlier, that we are trying to access both export markets and productivity investment into yards.

For example, if a British bid said, “ I would like your contract, but I am not going to invest in the capital of the yard”, and a foreign bid said, “W e will invest in some of your British yards, but some of the build will be in our country”, which would you accept—the one that does not want to put any investment in machinery and capital, or the one that does want to improve the yard at the same time? Which would you accept, John? T hat is often the choices that I have. Which would you accept?
Q67 Not necessarily, because if you had not brought in the foreign yards, you could have had, as you know, a NAPNOC negotiation—
You could answer my question, John.
Q68 You could have a NAPNOC negotiation. I am very happy to change roles. I would be quite happy to go back anytime you want.
You had my role once, John. I did not see a shipbuilding pipeline under your role.

Q69 Essentially, it is abou t what the industry, both the workforce and the companies , are looking for . Y ou talk about exports. One of the key questions, if you are trying to export, is that, if you are not good enough for the Royal Navy , the British Army or the Royal Air Force, you are not good enough for us , and that is absolutely right . One of the bestselling points is that you are good enough for the Royal Navy. Industry, this Committee and the workforce do not understand this prejudice against British yards , which no other major naval power undertakes. France and Italy are giving orders, and we used to have loads of excuses about EU regulations. Now , we are told it is WTO regulations . I t is garbage. The United States is a founder member of the WTO and absolutely ensures that it s orders go into its own yards. Why do we not?

I am sorry, but there is no prejudice from me or this team against British yards. You can keep repeating it and , in doing so, by the way, you will undermine British yards, be cause there is no preju dice against British yards. W e are also trying to produce the best N avy that we can in the world , to give our people the best ships and the capability. We are trying to do it on time and on budget, which is incredibly important. We are trying to make sure that, at the same time that we do that , we improve productivity . U nder the old system, they just got a cheque and it did not improve productivity, it did not improve the skill base and we had all sorts of other problems .

Q70 Mr Francois Secretary of State, we will come on to productivity when we get to Type 26. Just with regard to the fleet solid ship, these are crucial to fully exploiting the capability of the carrier strike group, as we all know. Can you confirm the intention is still to procure three rather than two?
That is right.

Q71 Mr Francois S econdly, if you look at T ype 3 1 , the D epartment set quite a tight indicative cost of a £250 million per vessel, and it is broadly accepted that that worked well in terms of limiting the cost of the ships, which , indeed , have then gone on to w in further exports, for instance , in Poland. H ave you set, as it were, a firm indicative limit for the cost of th e fleet solid support ships à la the Type 31?
T he answer to that question is that we have given the bidders the cost envelope in which we are expecting them to be able to deliver three ships against the requirement that we h ave set.
Q72 Mr Francois You made the cost envelope for T ype 3 1 very public , deliberately. Are you planning to do the same for FSS and , if not, why not?
It is in the public domain. The contract price will be £ 1.617 billion .
Mr Francois A maximum of.
That is the contract price .
We have given inflation relief.
This is for all three vessels.
Q73 Mr Francois That is based on three, not two.
That is three , and we have given inflation relief . I n other words, since it started , inflation has gone up, so we have put into that an inflation relief —
Q74 Mr Francois Lastly, just quickly, before I hand back, is there any slippage in the IOC ? I f not, what is the IOC for each of the three vessels ?

Rear Admi ral Marshall: We have put a high premium on incentivi s ing the delivery of the first ship in 202 8 to meet our out of service date for Fort Victoria , with a contract target of delivering all three ships by 203 2. [4]
Mr Francois So 2028, twenty- whatever and the n 2032.

Q75 The reason why we are raising this is because it ha s been around for a long time. This is not the first time that we have raised this with you , Secretary of State . I know that you said that the competition was not running well , which is why you then started again. I think y ou also were the Secretary of State —correct me if I am wrong — who dedicated these as warships. Therefore , that obliged the ship to be completed , if nothing else, here in the UK. Is that correct?

Yes . I n the past, before we refreshed the strategy, there was this thing that , if you called them a warship , you had more freedom of manoeuvre if they were designated not, so I changed that to make sure that it was a warship in order to give us more freedom of man o euvr e in the new competition. Now, we have got rid of that definition and done it on a case by case basis .
It took us a while for us to get that.
Q76 What we are trying to get to is the pace of decision-making. You are saying that you are still open to competition. When will the decision be made now?
The final bids will be received at the end of July this year.
Q77 The end of this month , and then the contract will be awarded and then when will the first ceremonial cutting of steel be ?
T he target to be on contract i s quarter 1 next year. We are aiming to go as fast as we can to contract, given the current economic conditions, but we start the evaluation in July.
Q78 Forgive me ; you are starting the evaluation—
Vice Admiral Gardner : W e will get the bids in this month , and then we will go through the evaluation process to down - select the fin al preferred bid der .
Q79 But y ou will not make a decision until, did you say, the end of the year?
We are aiming to place the contract by the end of the first quarter next year .

Q80 Next year —i t is the time that is going along. T here is a pressure here . A m I right in saying that the Fort Victoria i s the single ship that is having to do all the support ? Does that not need to go into refit at some point?
We have factored in the run - on cost s for Victoria out to 2028 a s part of the program me.
Q81 So you have led the lifetime of the Fort Victoria deliberately to cover this , b ut this is a single ship, is not it?
It is a single ship, yes , being replaced by three.
Q82 Mr Fran cois Sorry, Admiral, t he Chair’s question was specific. Will she not have to go into refit ? Will she be available operationally throughout that time until 2028?
The current plan is that she will remain available out to 2028.
Q83 Mr Franc ois She has given very loyal service . No disrespect, but she is a pretty old ship already, is she not ?
She will require some work, but we can meet the operational outputs with Fort Victoria until 202 8 .
So we are going to need a support ship for the support ship.

Q84 Just listening to the comparisons with international benchmarks, I may be wrong but I am detecting a lack of credit for the steps that primes have made, being Babcock, in terms of the work that they are doing just now. T hat is evident in the fact that very serious navies around the world are buying the rights to these ships. O ther navies, p articularly in the case of the Type 3 1 , were buying the ships built in the UK and in Rosyth . C an you think, Secretary of State, of a time in the past when navies were buying UK warship designs in the way that they are now ?

No, but if you listen ed to my evidence , there has been no shortage of praise for Babcock at Rosyth . Yo u characterise it that you are detecting a lack of it. I have congratulated them on the shipbuilding hall, the sense of delivering on time and doing incredibly well with t he T ype 3 1 , the fact that they won in Indonesia, the design that they are building in—and I think I listed everything, including contracts in Oman. Y ou could not accuse me of that at all.
Q85 I did say that I might be wrong, so I am happy that I have given you the opportunity to underline your esteem for Babcock and BAE.
Ben Wal lace: If you would like me to get on the record how well Fife and Babcock is doing, it is doing very well and it has great leadership.

Q86 W e are engaged , of course, in some very challenging conflicts in Europe just now, in Ukraine, and this has had a very significant impact on stock levels of allied nations as they support Ukraine to seek to defend and liberate its country. This has presented significant c hallenges for skills in restocking . W ith particular reference to a conflict of that nature, or even more significant a conflict , w hat if the demand for vessels increased as a result of global tensions , and increased quickly? G iven that 31 and 26 are being manufactured in relative , in naval terms, peace time, and it is already a challenge with skills , w hat is the plan , if things got very difficult very quickly , to ramp up production of naval warships ?

W hether it is shipbuilding or complex munitio ns , I said earlier on that the skills are more important than the tax. It is like oxygen , and I totally agree with you that it is a really important thing to have a plan for, which is why we have already set up —and Admiral Cox can expand on it —a skills forum to see what more we can do. It is why we are seeking investment around the UK on that skill base. BAE has an academy in Barrow -in-Furness, which I have been to visit , for shipbuilding skills. Babcock does a lot on its skills as well . A gain in the south - west, a number of apprenticeships are really important for building that.

Rapidly expanding skills is the place that everyone fears. You cannot just grow a very good welder on a tree. You have to invest in them, and they take time, and that is wh y one of the lessons of Ukraine, whether it is weapons, complex weapons or any type of engineering or technology skills, is that we really have to, as the United Kingdom, invest in those skill bases and to get people wherever we can from school, from FE an d from higher education into that area of growth.

I was hearing today about how Amazon , in many parts of the country , ha s, effectively , sucked up lots and lots of other jobs and caused quite big challenges, because , locally , lots of people are opting for t he Amazon m assive d istribution centre and, in doing so , the battle over scarce young people and resources is greater . T hat is a challenge for us all in terms of how we are going to encourage people to go into w hat I would say are the skill bases that reall y build the difference for the long ter m— STEM, cyber, IT and engineering skills that are so important. Admiral Cox can expand on the skills work that we have already done.

I referred earlier to the s kills t askforce , so I will not rehearse that, but I would say that your potentially hypothetical scenario, which I recogni s e, would require a change in the national effort , which would then require other elements of the industrial base to be focused towards that and prioriti s e that . To your question of whether we could scale up to match events , y es, but that would be a national effort. As the Secretary of State rightly points out , we need that skill s base, and that is what the taskforce is getting after over the next 18 months.

Q87 Dave Doo gan: T here is a second part to that . I say this against the backdrop of FSS, because some of us find enduring a term of “ significant UK content ” difficult as opposed to “total UK content ” , accepting , of course , that the engines will almost certainly , and t he gearboxes might, come from somewhere else. The shipbuild ing part of it, many of us believe, should be entirely on these islands . P erhaps if there was already greater synergy between yards in the United Kingdom on these islands, there would not even be a conversation about building blocks abroad and having them welded up together in yards in the UK.

W hat does the strategy do to facilitate greater synergy between Scottish yards that are centres of excellence for this element of shipbuilding and that element of shipbuilding , blocks and final construction , and all the rest of it ? Where is that synergy that defies changes in Government , constitutional changes and whatever threat that we face ? W here is that synergy being encouraged?

In terms of t he shipbuilding enterprise for g rowth, which I co- chair with the p resident of the Society of Maritime Industries, Mr John Howie, w e are getting after two task and finish groups. One is, as th e Secretary of State mentioned earlier, the S hipyard of the F uture, and the second is centres of excellence. W e are working really closely with industry and many colleagues in Scotland, as well as across the rest of the United Kingdom, to define what those centres of excellence could look like and how they could dovetail with a shipyard of the future to make the shipbuilding enterprise better. I entirely recognise your question and we are absolutely determined to get after that.

Q88 J ust on that skills element, Secretary of State , when the Committee went to both Scottish yards , we heard evidence from people who work there that, when you take in apprentices , there is a tendency to get the very best candidates that you can —and w hy would not you do that? M aybe an unintended consequence of that is that people then ping - pong up the ir career progression, which is great and , if that is what they want to do , that is fine, b ut it does leave you with a constant cycle of renewal at the skills end on the shop floor, where you are plating and welding and all the rest of it.

Do we need to have an intelligence - led step change to having a dual stream recruitment process for apprentices , where we have those who are pursuing a career that might go somewhere , and others who are looking for a vocation that might go somewhere but also might stay on the shopfloor for 3 5 or 40 years ?

I can tell you only about my experience from Lancashire and my part of the world, where you have BAE Aerospace, and then I l ive only about an hour and a half from Barrow. Part of that is in the gift of the employer and the regional educational piece. In Lancashire, BAE manages that very well, because it has so many ways into its shopfloor and so many different types of apprenti ceships. There is a healthy group of skilled and semi-skilled workers and degree-led apprenticeships in a very healthy way. That is to the credit of BAE rather than any Government or whatever. That is something to reflect on, in one sense, in this inquiry and to ask the employers about that.

I do not disagree. Not everyone can be managers. I suppose it goes back to my point on FE and things like that. A good welder is worth their weight in gold. They are incredibly important. I have seen highly complex piec es of equipment, either for America or made in America, or made in Britain for abroad, or made abroad and brought in here, where one welding mistake can cost tens of millions of pounds in rectifying it. They are worth their weight in gold.

When we talk abo ut the future skill base, one of the challenges is finding the future instructors, never mind the future pupils. We need to make sure that, if we do need to bring in workforce from abroad, we consider whether it is the instructors rather than the mass. I h ad one defence prime ask me to lobby to bring in a whole load of workforce from abroad at mass, and I said, “No, but I would support you bringing in 10 or 20 instructors or people who could teach our British citizens how to be the welders of the future”.

V ice Admiral Sir Chris Gardner: If I may, you will see that in evidence at Rosyth in terms of the apprentices that Babcock is bringing on to the shopfloor. The truth is that we need both types—those who want a long-term career and see themselves moving up t hrough the company, and those who want to stay on the shopfloor. The point that I would make is that the skill base is changing as well, because the welders who we need for tomorrow are people who are trained on operating robotic welding machines, not doin g the welding themselves. That is a fundamental change in the way in which our shipbuilding industry needs to evolve.
Q89 Rear Admiral Cox, in answer to Richard Drax’s earlier question, you mentioned 800 apprenticeships.
And graduates, yes.
Q90 Does that meet the requirement? Is it above or below that requirement at the moment?
Th e answer is that we do not know, and we set up the skills taskforce to get after that answer.
Q91 In that case, how do you plan if you do not know? I get the skills taskforce. Why has this not been done before?

Work has been done by various primes, but it has not necessarily been coherent or co-ordinated on a national basis. That is what the task force is a bou t. Through its visits, it will be visiting shipyards, the supply chain and FE colleges, and using the experience of the tas kforce that has been carefully selected for that experience to map this out.

Q92 Do you have any data or information on the retention of apprentices—the young people who go through an apprenticeship and stay , leave and go elsewhere, or even do not complete the apprenticeship? Do you have any figures on that?
I do not have that to hand.
It would be useful to know.
The taskforce will report to the shipbuilding enterprise for growth and upwards to the inter-ministerial group, and so, once it has been analysed, that data will be publicly available.
Q93 But at the moment, we do not know what the wastage is in terms of the people who go through an apprenticeship—
At the moment, I do not. My colleagues in the Department for Education may have an idea on those numbers.
Q94 But this taskforce will get to the bottom of that.

Rear Admiral C ox: Absolutely, and the taskforce is a joint endeavour between the Department for Education and the National Shipbuilding Office to deliver the skills issues identified in the strategy refresh.

Q95 Just before we move on to the next class of ships, I ju st wanted to ask about Sir John Parker’s review when he talked about virtual shipyards. This was a concept that was used quite efficiently and impressively with the Queen Elizabeth class, where chunks of this ship were built in different parts of the UK an d then all put together up in Scotland. It seems to have been dropped from the shipbuilding strategy. Is that not one method through which we could distribute the work across different shipyards across the country?

One of th e things that we are trying not to do is to dictate to the bidders how to build the ship. It is for them to come back to us and tell us how they intend to do it, but there is absolutely no reason why they cannot and would not necessarily adopt a distribute d build strategy as part and parcel of that. We do not yet know on FSS, for example, what the exact build strategies are going to be for each of the current bidders, but all of those options are open to them.
Q96 But you seem to have dropped it as somet hing to encourage. I thought that this would be something particularly with the skill sets.

It is encouraged in at least two or three different ways. First of all, the construct of the contract. On the f uture solid support ship, I deliberately chose to change the contracts construct. I separated the design and priming from the yard, because, in the past, it has been an all - or - nothing event, and I took the view that what we want to see is that there is a design/priming contract, and then the win ner of that gets to have access to all the yards.

To the point that Richard Drax made about yards being full, the way that we are going to maximise and flatten out the peaks and troughs is that, when we place our contracts, we should not be held to, “You u se our yards or nothing”. If, let us say, Company A that owns a yard in the west of Scotland wins, but its yard is full, why should Company A not be free to place the build in another yard that might be a competitor but, nevertheless, is empty? It is a really important way of maximising our productivity and our yard space in the build process, because that was often not how it was done in the p ast.
Q97 But I simply flag up that Sir John Parker’s review recommended the virtual shipyard concept and, as a concept, it seems to have been—

No one has abandoned that concept. In fact, we have put in place things that will encourage more use of it, so my point about the construct of different contracts. Secondly, there is the issue around investing in the capital in all the yards and in the yard of the future that will allow people to do that. No one has abandoned that sense. Just because it is maybe not explicit, no one has abandoned it. In fact, our actions are louder than just an aspiration. Our actions, by the redesign of our contracts and by trying to encourage an all - of - UK enterprise and social weighting value, are actions rather than aspirations.
Q98 I hear the actions but the words themselves which—
The words in his first one were an aspiration. This is action.

Q99 But in the document that you just pointed to, those words have been dropped; t hat is all I was saying . It is a concept that would certainly help the smaller shipyards, because they are the ones that would benefit from it.
Yes, absolutely.
Q100 We have made that point. Can we now move on to, first, HMS Alb ion , HMS Bulwark and RFA Arg u s? Can you tell me what is happening to these multirole ships?
As you know, one goes in and is having its deep maintenance.
“Mothballed”, I think, is the term.
No.
Q101 So where is Bulwark right now?

One of them has just come out or been on service and she has come back in. The other one came out of deep maintenance last year or the year before when I went to visit her in Falmouth, and she has come out. They are not mothballed. One is on R 5 [5] —is that right? 180 days’ notice to move, and the other one is on R0 or R1.
We have one of the LPDs currently in service, and the other one is undergoing deep maintenance and upkeep.
Q102 Deep maintenance and upkeep. We will use that phrase. RFA A rg u s has been given another lease of life. This is 1970s engineering. Is that right?
She is an old ship. There is absolutely no doubt about that, but we have just extended her in - service life in order to maintain our access to a role 3 medical capability for the foreseeable future.

It is a superb ship. There is no doubt about it. Many of us have visited it and it is also used for a lot of decking and a lot of the N avy doing its flight training and so forth. It is extremely versatile ; t here is no doubt about it. Its simplicity and mo dularity is what gives it such great flexibility. It is curious, though, that it is still kicking around since the 1970s, and it just shows you that perhaps, if you look after these ships, they can last a long time. What caused you to make the decision to then elongate its life again?

Maybe I could just talk about the LPDs. As you know, the f uture c ommando f orce is redesigning itself to have a future commando force north and a future commando force south, which will require, effectively, two LPDs. Of the current fleet that we have, there are a range of vessels that could provide that function. Bulwark and Albion are not due to go out of service until roughly 2030 and a bit later, so we have, effectively, a funding stream, whic h has not started yet, to pay out. We will seek to replace Bulwark and Albion at the end of the decade.
Then you have the Bay class, which, again, have an internal dock. They have a single dock well and a dual dock, but they have the same versatility and a re incredibly versatile.
Q103 Just remind us how many of those you have left?

Four. [6] One is almost permanently down in Kipion, which is the minesweeping mothership. We have seen them used in the Caribbean. They provide a support role. They were used as an LPD recently in one of the future commando force operations. They are versatile, and Argus can do a similar thing. They are all landing pads with C2 nodes, and a number of them have internal docks that all fit the use that the Marines would wish to have.

Your question about why Arg u s is absolutely correct, because, right now, there is a debate within the N avy about what ships should provide the littoral strike group north and south support until we get to the end of the decade when we will b e replacing Albion and Bulwark. That is a live, unresolved debate by the N avy. Two years ago, it was of the view that it would convert a Bay class to give it a better capability to store helicopters. That has currently changed and I am expecting a proposal , although it has not been signed off, that RFA Argus may fulfil that function.

As Secretary of State, I am quite pressing on the N avy to settle its mind about what it wants. I am confident that whatever ship they choose — Bay class, Argus or, indeed, Albion or Bulwark—can do the function, but the key here is how they wish to fulfil that. They all have strengths and weaknesses. Argus ’ s weakness is that it has a massive crew, because it is an old ship. Bulwark and Albion are fantastic, but they again require a big crew, although they have some real strengths. Bay class has a small crew—about 67, if my memory serves me right—but does not necessarily have the hangar space that you might want for helicopters.

They all have strengths and weaknesses. I have asked th e N avy to make sure that it settles on an option. Come 2030, we may be working with another country to see if we can share a cycle of design for the next generation.

Q104 Secretary of State, for many years, the Royal Navy has had a surface escort f orce of 19 frigates and destroyers. The Type 23 HMS Monmouth retired in the summer of last year, so that takes us down to 18. The Type 23 HMS Montrose will retire in the summer of 2023, so that takes us down to 17. That leaves us something of an escort gap until the Type 31s come in, I believe, in 2027. This Committee has been told that this juggling of escort numbers is akin to alchemy. We regard it as fool’s gold. Why will we next year be down to 17 frigates and destroyers and then have to wait another fo ur years before we go back up.

The good news is that we are committed to funding to go above that by whatever it is—2028 or 2030. The Government have committed to funding the replacements and getting online. As you say, there is a dip that cle arly takes place in the middle of the decade before we can start generating out.

One of the ways that we sought to solve that—and I do not think it is alchemy—is better availability. While I recognise that you cannot have one hull in two places, you can ha ve a ship more at sea than it used to be, because availability is sometimes just as important as location. We have seen very significant improvements in availability of our ships. Montrose is an interesting example where we forward-based the ship and we ar e rotating the crews through, which has been better for its availability, because she is no longer spending x number of weeks just going back to the Britain and changing over , et c .

Q105 But in war, Secretary of State—and it is not fantasy to talk a bout a general conflagration now. Last week at RUSI, the C hief of the G eneral S taff was talking about mobilising the British Army in order to deter. We might come on to whether the F irst S ea L ord plans to mobilise the Royal Navy. All your ships need to be available and there is no reserve. The Royal Navy has no war reserve of surface escorts. You have to fight with what you have. As they say in the jargon, you would have to fight tonight. Are you not concerned that we would have fewer ships with which to fi ght?

Let me put it another way. For a very long time, we have not had the availability that we are going to have now. You say that all our ships have been available. All our ships have not been available for decades.
We know that.

If availability is part of the premium, that has gone up, so the number of days at sea. It might be hulls in the water, but they have to be hulls in the water that are available. The stuff that we have been doing in rectifying the Type 45 is a really good example. It is all very well having £6 billion ships on paper ; if three or four of them are wrapped in bubble wrap and not going anywhere , it is totally pointless.
Q106 Secretary of State, not a single ship has come out of PIP. The fi rst Type 45 to go in has been in there for two years.
Dauntless is out and she is doing well.
Q107 Sir, she has not re - joined the fleet. She is still doing trials, so she has been out of action for two years.
Most of them have been out of action for 10 years.

Q108 Secretary of State, is to your credit that you have accelerated PIP from one ship to two, so you are doing them in parallel, but there is still not a lot of point having a £1 billion air defence destroyer tied up alongside. If you drive her too fast in the water, she breaks.

Let us stick with Type 31. We visited Babcock at Rosyth, and then went to Scotstoun at Glasgow, as a Committee. We saw HMS Venturer, the first of class of the Type 31, in the very early stages of build. She comes in in 2027. In the meantime, the Type 23 s , which have given loyal service and been the workhorses of the fleet for decades, are very old. The most modern, HMS St Albans, was commissioned 20 years ago. The oldest, HMS Norfolk, wa s commissioned 32 years ago. These ships are tired and are increasingly expensive to keep in service. How can you be confident that we can continue to maintain their availability when the first replacement, Venturer, does not enter service for another five years?

You are absolutely right, Mr Francois , that the ships are old. They are obsolescent and are suffering from a degraded material state, which is why we are having to spend a significant amount of money on maintaining a nd extending their lives.
Q109 You said “obsolescent”.
No, they are suffering from obsolescence.
Q110 So if we had to fight the Russians next week, would you want to go to war in an obsolescent warship?
I did not say that the ships were obsolescent, but that they are suffering from obsolescence because of the age of the equ ipment.
What is the difference?
That is sophistry.
Q111 Could you just explain the difference between a ship being obsolescent and the equipment that they use being obsolescent? Surely that makes a ship obsolescent.

Vice Admiral Sir C hris Gardner: My point is that, fundamentally, we can still get the operational outputs that we need out of the platforms as currently configured, but it is the maintenance of those platforms that is suffering from increasing obsolescence challenges, becau se we just find it harder to source the spare parts for them.

Yes, and when they go into refit, they take longer and longer to come out. It is analogous to taking an old car to a garage and you have to work harder every year to get it through its MOT. The Secretary of State understands this. That is the problem with Type 23 availability, and there is no war reserve. You have the R&R, but, in terms of warships, there is no war reserve. You can fight only with those ships that you have, and it ta kes far too long and too many years to build a complex warship. Let us come on to that.

We also went to Scotstoun in Glasgow and visited the Type 26 in construction, HMS Glasgow. Make no mistakes—the design is world - beating, and that is why we sold it to A ustralia and Canada. She will, when she is in service, be the absolute peer anti-submarine warfare frigate in the world. There is little argument about that, but her IOC has now been delayed again—we got this from BAE Systems—until late 2028, so the gap ge ts even longer and the Type 23s have to work even harder.

The Japanese have just introduced a new class frigate, the Mogami class, which took three years from lay down to commission. It is taking BAE Systems 11 years to build and commission a warship. Why can the Japanese build a modern, complex worship three and a half times or nearly four times faster than BAE Systems at Glasgow? Who wants to take that one?
I will. It goes back to the points that we have been making about the productive utilisation of the yards in which we are building our ships.
Q112 Is that a euphemism for saying that they are not very good at building very quickly?

I am saying that there is a need for significant i nvestment in the yards in order to increase the rate of productive utility that we can get out of the yards themselves. You see a world class frigate factory now, having been built in Rosyth on the back of £60 million worth of joint investment in infrastru cture and facilities, which is going to be churning out the Type 31 in a decent timeframe.

Q113 We went to Glasgow. We were shown the old Victorian shed where its new “frigate factory” is going to be built. We have been hearing about this factory f or years. We were told that, apparently, it is all held up because it has a unique Victorian roof, and someone in Scotland has objected to that on heritage grounds. I am sure that Vladimir Putin is killing himself laughing. I put it to you again. Why does it take 11 years to build a modern frigate, and why has it slipped by one more year and is now over a decade? You are the man in charge of this, so what is the answer?
In terms of why HMS Glasgow has slipped, there are, fundamentally, three root causes to the problem. The first of those is Covid .
Q114 Sorry, Covid affected Japan and they still did it in three years. Did the Japanese not get Covid ?
I have no idea how they managed t he Covid challenge in Japan.
Q115 They did it somehow and they are knocking out the Maya class, which are their Aegis-capable destroyers, three years, start to finish. Are the Japanese immune from Covid ?
I did not sa y that they were immune from Covid .
Q116 In terms of that excuse, I am sorry but the Japanese managed to get around it. What are your other two?

The other two were that we had significant challenges over engineering maturity in the Type 26 ; BAE would acknowledge that fact itself. The other one is that the supply chain performance has not been as good as we would have wished it to be. The consequences of all of that have been the delay to HMS Glasgow by 12 months.

Q117 Mr F rancois: But you do accept that, with modern naval warfare, if you had to go to war against the Russians within the next few months, you can go only with what you have, and what we have is tired or has engine problems. These ships are world - beaters, but th ey are years late, so what are you doing to speed the programme up and recover that year that you have lost?

In terms of HMS Glasgow, we will not recover the time. I will be completely honest about that. What we are doing is we are working with BAE to ensure that we minimise the delay on ship two, and I am holding their feet to the fire to deliver ship three against the original contracted vessel acceptance date.

I do not know anything about the Japanese spec for ships. I have no idea what the different ship specification was. Before we compare apples and pears rather than apples and apples, I will write to the Committee saying, if there was a difference, why there is a difference. Some of it is maybe in productiv ity and production, but some of it may be the Type 26. One of the reasons it has been bought by Australia and Canada is that it is a unique submarine warfare ship with a very unique design that makes it incredibly quiet and, therefore, able to listen. As a first in class of a world - beating new design, they are always going to take longer, because they are always going to be complex.

However, that does not excuse the supply chain problem. I went to visit the supplier, because I was told only at month 20 when this thing was late. I went to visit it to, effectively, read them the riot act about why I thought it was unacceptable, and I said to BAE, the Navy and the subcontractor, “There is too much fragility in this supply chain. It is all a bit late telling me now at month whatever. Do not underestimate that the Canadians and Australians are watching and, if you do not start fixing that, they will be off and you will become an embarrassment to the United Kingdom, and I am not prepared to have that”. W e have fixe d some of that. We have already shortened that initial delay. Glasgow is going to be, as you say, about 12 months late. However, the overall class of all of them will, I have been told, come in on time.
Q118 Just quickly, Secretary of State, that d epends on them sorting out this issue about the Victorian roof and building the “frigate factory” to catch up on the delay.

We are all very happy to talk to the Scottish Government about accelerating that. I know that the Scottish Government and the SNP have been campaigning on the frigate factory, so it is absolutely something that they support. I am sure that, together, we c an fix any of those problems, if there are those types of problems, but I can assure you that the issue will be the complexity of the system.

A bit like my thing on the future commando force, I have said to the Navy, “Start making decisions on the Governme nt fixtures, because delay and dither about whether you are going to have this type of missile or that type of missile costs money in the long run”.

Q119 On that, I have one more question on obsolescence. We produced our report , We’re going to need a bigger Navy , in December, before the Russian invasion of Ukraine. I will just read very quickly from the summary: “When ships do get to sea, they act like porcupines—well defended herbivores with limited offensive capabilities. This is a result of decisions by success ive Governments to limit budgets and prioritise defensive capabilities. What offensive capabilities these ships do have will be reduced even further in three years’ time”—this came out last year—“when the Government retires the Harpoon anti-ship missile wi thout a planned replacement. More money must be found to upgrade the Navy’s lethality and allow our ships to take the fight to the enemy”.

If we take out Harpoon, our only surface-to-surface weapon on the ship, not the helicopter, is a 4.5-inch gun, whereas the Russian and Chinese equivalents have missiles that can destroy our surface escorts from very many miles away. What is the plan to replace Harpoon?

There is a plan to replace Harpoon. There is an interim plan in between what we might settle on in the long term. I do not know if I can announce the details of that yet, because I am not even sure if it has been put out to a tender 1 , but there is absolutely a plan to do so, because, like you, I agree there.

B en Wallace: There is a plan to replace Harpoon. There is an interim plan in between what we might sett le on in the long term. I do not know if I can announce the details of that yet, because I am not even sure if it has been put out to a n agreement , but there is absolutely a plan to do so, because, like you, I agree there.

Q120 Secretary of State, the long-term solution is an Anglo-French cruise missile that, at the earliest, would enter service a decade from now. The weapon does not exist. It is a theoretical construct.

With all due respect, Mark, that is not the case. The Type 26 will be fitted with a Mark 41 launcher, which gives us access to a whole range of missile systems from around the world, predominantly United States ones, but certainly the requirement on MBDA is to start making missiles that can be fired from that, and that i s being fitted to the Type 26 as it is being manufactured.
Q121 Secretary of State, Type 26 will have the Mark 41, and it is the old story : it is fitted for but not with. It will have the launcher, but we have not decided what goes in it. It is a b ox.
My point is that we have time to decide what goes in it before the first one becomes in service.
Q122 My point is that the Russians are shelling Mariupol as we speak and we do not have time, so what is the interim weapon and when does that enter service, with respect ?
I do not know whether it has been contracted 2 . I am being slightly careful. The Navy has decided on an interim weapon and we have to —
We are in negotiation now, so it would be inappropria te to comment.
Q123 Lastly, the C hief of the G eneral S taff said very powerfully at RUSI that he is going to mobilise the A rmy to deter war with Russia. Is there any plan to mobilise the Royal Navy?

The Chief of the General Staff ’s defi nition of mobilising the A rmy is to make it ready and focused on the threat of Russia. It is not mobilising as in we are going to empty the barracks and send everyone out into the field.
We all know what he meant.

Mobilisation is making it ready and relevant. Is there a plan to make the Royal Navy ready and relevant? Yes, a bsolutely—Type 26, Type 31, investments in the next generation of attack submarines. Have our deployments been absolutely in places that they have not been befor e since the C old W ar? We have been in Barents Sea.
Q124 In other words, we are going to mobilise in five years.
No.
Q125 You just mentioned the 26 and the 31. They are five or six years away.

Yes, but we still have a current surface fleet. Right now, we have an Astute in the Mediterranean and another somewhere else. We have our surface fleet active, working in joint exercises. In the last few months, we have been in the Barents Sea, the Baltic Sea and the North Sea. They are not Type 26s and Type 31s, and I cannot magic them if Russia goes to war with us, but I can absolutely make sure that we have the availabil ity, so that we have as many Type 23s and Type 45s out and active as possible, and that is what is happening right now.

I have a point of clarification. My understanding from BAE is that the new build hall is not going to be in that location, so there are no heritage planning issues with the site of its new build hall.
That is what they told us when we went there.
They did tell us that.
We stood in front of it ; sorry, we stood inside it.
I heard it too and I was there, but things have moved on at the site.

Q126 It does not take away from the fact, if I may, that we went to Govan and we saw a Type 26—a state of the art frigate, one of the best in the world—being built under canvas and sc affolding. Whether it is Japan or elsewhere, other countries around the world have state of the art hangars inside which these things are then built. Whether it is at Govan or somewhere else, that is what we need. Perhaps that is the starting point when we give out contracts to shipyards, where we say, “Do you have a locality indoors to build these things?” which means that the pace—

Tobias, you and I totally agree. What I have been seeking to do with these contracts is to put some form of cond itionality. I do not know if you remember, but when Gordon Brown encouraged BAE to take on Scotstoun and Govan — VT or whoever had owned it— one of the deals was that it would get a 15-year work programme and throughput of ships to encourage BAE to take that on. That was part of the deal. The question is that it had at least 15 years and has not built a covered thing.
We made the point. It was a great visit, and thank you for allowing us to visit.
Q127 My supplementary is very brief. Admiral, wh en a Type 26 finds a submarine in a war environment and seeks to dispatch that submarine as a threat, how does it do that?
It uses either the Merlin helicopter that it has on the back of the ship, or it will cue other assets that can do that, like P-8 Poseidon.
Or a sub.
Or another submarine.
Or the Mark 41 launcher—my point about having access to a whole range. There is a n anti- submarine missile that can be fired u p .
An a nti-submarine rocket.
The point that Mark was making is that you have a version of this in the Type 45s, and they are just tubes. We do not put a lot in them at the moment. Moving forward, the Type 26 will be welc ome.
Do not misunderstand us. She is a world - beating ship. That is why we want it sooner rather than later.
I am the same. I wanted to be holistic .

Q128 We are running out of time. I want to draw this piece to a conclusion and then move on wider things. I do not know if the Secretary of State had an opportunity to read a recommendation by the House of Commons Defence Select Committee in our report on the Navy , “ We’re going to need a bigger Navy ” . Did you have time to do that?
I did read it.

Q129 With that in mind, you were just talking about the availability of surface fleets. You mentioned that the numbers are going up, which is good to see , but I would just remind the Secretary of State that, during the C old W ar, we had 13 destroyers in 35 frigates. Given the threats that are coming over the horizon, are there any plans for us to look at increasing the size of the Navy ?

Overall , there is a plan. It is early days, but you heard the Prime Minister’s 2.5% of GDP by 2030, and I have always been clear that, as the threat changes, so must our investment and, indeed, our plans. I know that 2.5% does not match your 3% or 4%, but, nevert heless, on today’s predictions, it would equate to £55 billion extra . It is absolutely the case that what we need to press more and more into service is more availability and w here we think it is the best way to meet the threat ; if it turns out to be more vessels, it is more vessels. It may not be. It may be more subsea or more air delivered.

Q130 I just said the Navy , but I would just remind the Secretary of State of what Professor Andrew Lambert said at the RUSI conference only a few days ago, where he suggested that a country’s industrial capacity for a major conflict must be built before the war starts, and that is the message that we would like to pass on.
You do not have to be a professor to observe that, to be honest.
Q131 But you do need to be a Secretary of State to action it, though, and that is what we are saying today.
We are actioning it.
Q132 If that is the case, sir, if we are actioning it, there is a delay in replacing the Type 23s with Type 26s. There is a dela y in repairing the Type 45s. There is a delay in building—
Actually—

Q133 Let me finish, please, sir. There is a delay in building the fleet solid support, there is a delay in replacing the Vanguard submarines, and there is a delay in purcha sing all the F-35 requirement. Is the Navy not going to need a bigger budget?

First of all, let us deal with the delays, because you started this, Chair, and I can help finish it. The delay in the Type 26 is nothing to do with me. Since I have taken office, I have managed to shorten the delay by at least 12 months, so we now no longer have a 22 - month delay .

On the Type 45, it was me who accelerated the PIP replacement. It was long before I even started that the floor design of the Type 45, which was 2005 or 2006, where I stood in Scotstoun on the deck of that ship, was put in place that caused the PIP problem . Since I have come into office as Secretary of State for Defence, I have put in place the accelerating of PIP. We are now on bo at three of PIP, so, hopefully, we can get those ships out and running and increased.

On the issues around the Type 26 delay in the supply chain, we have, as I have already said, managed to sort out the problems that happened in supply chain, which were mainly around the gearbox, and put that in place.

On the future solid support ship, the competition collapsed. That was nothing to do with this office or, indeed, the MoD . When the bidders withdrew, I took immediate steps to de-spec the thing from having a six-tonne lift to a three-tonne lift, which was a standard off the shelf lift, which meant that it was both affordable and able t o be delivered on time. I am pretty confident that the future solid support ship will be delivering the capacity that we need and, as you rightly pointed out, HMS Victoria is a very well - versed ship.

On top of that, you will find that, when we provide the Committee with the details, availability of the ships that we have are at the highest availability that we have had for probably the last 15 to 20 years, which means more ships at sea at the same time, dealing with the threat. I cannot do anything about ac celerating ships in build immediately, and I cannot do anything about the emerging threat of Russia, given that most people have underplayed Russia’s threat for far too long, and that is not just across this country but the whole of NATO, including the Uni ted States, which is finding that they too have stockpile problems.

Q134 To be fair, Secretary of State, that needs an answer. A year ago, in a report on armoured vehicles, which you may well recall, we said that, if you matched a British division against a peer division—and let us not talk in euphemisms. We mean Russia. This Committee, one way or another, has been warning about the Russian threat for quite some time.
I disagree with you on that.
We have a lot more questions to g et through and we are running out.

Q135 We have the new medium-lift helicopter programme, which has just been launched. We have the Merlin fleet, which has come down from 72 platforms to 55 platforms, roughly a third of which will be engaged in tra ining or unserviceable in maintenance. Then you have the remaining Merlins that will need to be on station at RNAS Culdrose. From that, you will need to have some hanging off the back of 31s and 26s, once they come off 23s. I know that we have Wildcats in the mix as well.

Does that sound like enough medium-lift capability in the Royal Navy? Would it not have been prudent to get a marinised version of whatever the new medium-lift helicopter is going to be to future - proof rotary wing platforms for the Royal N avy going forward?

On the overall availability of the fleet, I am not sure about the Merlin Force, but I can certainly write to the Committee with the detail its availability. We have already committed to extending the life of the Merlin for n ow on a number of issues. I do not know if anyone wants to take this here, or shall we write the Committee on rotary craft of the Royal Navy?
Q136 With specific reference to the strategic decision that said new medium-lift would be for the land dom ain only, and that there was no maritime requirement for new medium-lift.
It was fundamentally to replace the Puma.

Q137 Secretary of State, in light of Ukraine and the decisions in Madrid, it would probably be wrong not to take the op portunity to ask you a question around the size of the A rmy. Do you and the Prime Minister both agree that there is no need to stop the reductions planned in the army and to increase the size of the A rmy?

The current size of the A rmy is about 78,000. [7] If you take into account people in training, it is about 81,000 . That is the current si z e. We have not reduced the A rmy as yet. We have already gone up from what we said we would. We were going to go down to 72,500. We have gone up to 73,000 beca use, as I have said, as the threat or the requirement changes, we should look at that.

I can tell the Committee that I asked the Treasury a few months ago if I could look at a challenge around the salary rather than the numbers, to see whether there is a w ay of reducing the overall salary bill of the A rmed F orces. I do mean cutting people’s pay, but , fundamentally , the Navy has done a huge amount of work of reducing onshore Navy people to get them out into ships and asking itself why so many of its personnel are onshore and not at ship. If you asked some traditional questions of the A rmy, like why the A rmy is structured the way it is, there has not really been much challenge or t hought about that.

The first issue, secondary to this threat, is whether we can get away from the arbitrary numbers game that we have all been in for 30 or 40 years, where someone just picks a number and you reduce it. If the Treasury is keen on reducing t he costs of anything in a Department, whether it is the C ivil S ervice or the military, we should be asking the question of whether there is a way of doing it separately, because you could have a lot more people for less.
Q138 Are you and the Prime Minister still in agreement that the planned reduction in the Armed F orces set out in the command paper and Future Soldier is correct?
At the moment, we are still in the position where we are working towards reducing to 73,000.
Q139 Ar e you in agreement?

Can I deliver the effect that is required in the defence command paper with a force of 73,000 plus the reserves? The answer is yes, but as the threat has changed—and that command paper was done before the threat—we should a bsolutely be looking at all things, including the size of all our A rmed F orces. It is not just the A rmy, because what we may see—
Q140 So you are looking at whether to change the size of the A rmy.
Across the whole of the A rmed F orces.
You are looking at that.

I would say across the whole of the A rmed F orces, because it may be that one of the ways that we want to get more littoral strike group commando force out is by increasing the size of the Navy to get more crews. It may be that you need to recruit—
Q141 We understand that, but we have it on record now that you are looking at the size of the A rmed F orces.
Armed F orces, yes.
Q142 That includes the Army.

Yes, it does, but could I just say one thing? I said this at the RUSI conference, so people are not surprised. If the decision was to be made to increase the size of the A rmy, do not be surprised if it is not in the cavalry or the infantry.
Derek Twigg: W e know a little bit about the A rmed F orces on this Committee.

It is quite interesting how attached people are to platforms, almost in a historical way. The lessons of Ukraine are that our deep fires, our air defence and our electronic warfare are deeply inadequate, and we need to invest in those areas. We got that slightly right in the command paper, because that is where we did increase.

Q143 I am just conscious of time, but we have that on record now. You mentioned looking at salaries. Again for the record, have you made or are you making any representations about increasing the size of the defence budget? You mentioned 2.5 % before. Are you in any discussions or are you in agreement with N o. 10 that there should not be any incr ease in the defence budget over and above what is planned?
Within my spending period, which finishes in 2024-25, I have not sought to increase that budget because—
That is not t he question I asked .

Let me finish the a nswer. I have made it perfectly clear that, before Russia invaded Ukraine, we took a decision that there would be a dip—a sort of sunset and sunrise, as the former C hief of the D efence S taff used to talk about—in capabilities. While the 26s, 31s and the Bo xers came on stream in the A rmy, for example, we were going to take that dip. The threat has changed, so I take a view that some of those areas we were prepared to take a risk in are areas where we should not be prepared to take that risk and, therefore, I have made no secret of the fact that that is a place where we would look for more money or more investment. I wanted to continue, because the PM was really the first to reverse taking the peace dividend and putting an investment in, and I want that to con tinue.

Q144 So despite the comments coming from N o. 10 and the Prime Minister last week, you are looking at the size of the A rmed F orces and the budget, so let me just put one final question to you. In that case, let us just keep on the budget. Bas ed on the lessons and experience that we have all seen or had in Ukraine, is there anything that you can see that has happened there that in any way suggests that we can provide a credible response at whatever level with the current budget?

Ou r response against Russia has always been as part of an alliance. It goes right to the heart of our debates about how 360 our frigates should be . S hould they be completely equipped with everything, or do we plug into a wider Navy ? If you look at the C old W ar, Britain had some real strengths but also some real inadequacies in its surface fleet, because it always took the assumption that it would be part of an American/NATO umbrella. It is absolutely the case that, if we were engaged in a conflict with Russia today and yesterday and tomorrow, we will always be reliant on the alliance. On the plus side, which slightly goes to the availability of ships and things like that, we now have Sweden and Finland coming into NATO to protect the north Atlantic.

Q145 Derek Twig g: I accept all of that, but that is not the question. Given the lessons and experience, and the threat that you have talked about coming from what is happening in Ukraine, is there anything there that suggests that we do not need an increase in the defenc e budget?
I have said I would like an increase in the defence budget. Maybe I could read out what the Prime Minister said at NATO.
Q146 Is he listening in and giving you lines to take here?

No, it is really important that you understand the context of what he said, but also what he said and why it is important. He said, “The truth is that we, as an alliance”—that is NATO—“are compensating for years of underinvestment in defence”. I do not think that anyone on this Committee would disagree with that statement. “We need to invest in the long term in vital capabilities like combat air, while simultaneously adapting to a more dangerous and competitive world. The logical conclusion of the decision is 2.5% at the end of a decade, remembering that goals set in Wales in 2014 were for a different era”, so that is, like you said, a recognition that the threat has changed, that we need to invest, and that, in 2030, by the end of the decade, it is 2.5% of GDP.

Q147 À propos that, Secretary of State, the integrated review and the defence command paper were published before the invasion of Ukraine, which we all know, in security terms, is a 9/11. It is a complete game - changer. That has been evident already today.

We are an all-party Committee, but my colleagues were happy for me to read out one paragraph from the conclusions of a paper that was released a couple of weeks ago by the Conservative Back - Bench d efence c ommittee, of which you were given an advanced copy as a courtesy, where they concluded, “It is recommended most strongly that the conclusions of the integrated re view and the defence command paper be revisited and the associated military cuts to both manpower and capabilities be halted immediately and a th reat-based review carried out, post Ukraine, supported by increased defence spending in real terms”.

That is the view on the Conservative Back Benches , but I suspect that most of this Committee would not disagree with it one jot. Is it likely that there wi ll be some new chapter to the integrated review? There was a previous review a few years ago that was slightly overtaken by events. Will there be a further document or a new analysis in light of new events?

I cannot speak for the integrated re view. It is a Cabinet Office/N o. 10 document. What I can say is that I re-read the defence command paper the other day. A lot of the assumptions are absolutely in the right place—resilience matters, investing in EW and SIGINT, and all the extra stuff in Ar my 2030, which we were looking at. They absolutely turned out to be exactly the areas we need, such as around unmanned subsea , et c .

Do I think that we should do a piece of work looking at the threat and the lessons learned, which should infuse into the Dep artment and change, if necessary, some of the things? Yes, we should, and we will. Of course, we are doing it right now in an ongoing process, but there is definitely a time when we will have to absolutely look at Ukraine and learn the lessons. We are lear ning s ome lessons as we speak—supply chain on. In the old days, you would not have viewed them as complex weapons, but they are now, like the NLAWs and things like that. Richard, in our day, they were viewed as pretty basic and did not have a complex suppl y chain. Now, they are as complex as a w a rship, which leads to big problems when you are no longer buying them.

Those are absolutely really important things that we are learning right now. The use of the ability to provide resilience to your allies in trai ning. We sent the Ranger battalion to train on the NLAWs literally a few weeks before the invasion, which showed that, if you could—
Q148 We are tight for time, but , to be clear, you are not talking about a full-blown review of the review, but you are talking about a lessons learned exercise.

Absolutely, and we will be happy to share as much of that when it happens. There are two parts to this—when we do a fixed lessons learned and whether you do that at the end of the conflict, and whe n we can do a running commentary that is so important that we have to get on with it.
The plus side is that we have been given more money. Some of that £2.3 billion of military aid and support is to refurbish our stocks, because we have given some away.

Q149 Ch air: Just to expand that further, though, if the Prime Minister is saying he is going to increase the defence budget by 2030, there is a recognition that we are going to need more money. The world is getting more dangerous, so we need to invest more in def ence. You have articulated that now, with a recognition that you are going to have to look at aspects of the integrated review.

What I do not understand is that, when you look at the library’s own figures—and they have crunched the numbers here—they have put in the impact of inflation on what is going to happen to the defence budget over the next few years. The defence budget decreases in 2023-24 by £1 billion. It goes down by a full £1 billion, because of inflation. The reality check of tha t anyway is the cost of fuel and of all these other things that have gone up, which we are all experiencing. The same applies to the A rmy, the A ir F orce and, indeed, the Navy as well.

When I read this list of equipment that we are having to delay, because we do not have the money to repair or maintain them, or, indeed, purchase and replace, you are going to need an increased defence budget to meet the minimum requirements that we have today, let alone the threats that are coming over the horizon that you un derstand, more so than potentially others that are around the Cabinet table.

First of all, our defence budget is in a four-year chunk. Over that period, we had significant rises in years one and two. It was flat in three and drops off in four, so , if you want to take it in a chunk as a four-year thing , t he Treasury would say to me, as it would say to you over the four-year average, that it is an increase.

As I have been clear about, when we had our defence settlement, inflation was running at 1.5% or whatever it is. We are a capital-heavy Department and, therefore, more vulnerable to inflation than some other Departments, because £14 billion o r £15 billion of procurement is subject to inflation. It is very important to recognise that we have to find measures. Indeed, the Government are looking at the impacts of inflation.

For me, as I said earlier, the start point of worry is the middle of the decade. It is not here and now. I have, on paper, a theoretical unders pend of £800 million o f capital in this financial year, because of the way that the profiling of the money of our budget was given. That is why it is really important that we work through the four-year period. I can assure you that I make sure that I get the money out the door and that I will be talking publicly about, in the middle of this decade and onwards, why there is a requirement for more defence budget.

It is really welcome news that you are looking at aspects of the integrated review, given the threats that are c oming over and that you are looking at the composition of our A rmed F orces. That is something that we can take away.

Q150 Secretary of State, you referenced supply chains and finding that there were severe problems and inadequacies. By the way, t hat is not just a British problem but an international situation. In the past, d efence d epartments around the world have tended to leave this to primes to manage these supply chains and are now finding a whole number of problems, partly, of course, in term s of unsatisfactory suppliers and those who may be potential enemies, but also a lack of skills, a lack of production capacity, and very long timelines. This is now almost the major topic of international discussion within the alliance. What are we going t o do about it?

First and foremost, skills are important. Secondly, we are going to place orders because, as I have said on numerous occasions, the hollowing out of our A rmed F orces that happened under my Government, your Government and previou s Governments often took place in the unseen space—the ammunition stocks, the fixed maintenance, the yards. It was all the stuff that was unsexy and unglamorous and that no one knew about. That has been going on since I was in the A rmy in 1991. It is not a party - political point ; it is a fact that you can track where people took money out of defence in order to pay for maybe a new platform, but it went to war unequipped or un-bombed up , et c .

One of the reasons that I am reticent to over-speculate on the size of the A rmy or the Navy is because I have to properly equip the young men and women who we are sending on our behalf right now as quickly as possible, because the lesson of the Russian invasion of Ukraine so far is that you can have all the mass you like on that road to Kyiv, but, if you do not have the right comms, the right anti-UAV and the right ammunition, you are dead in large masses. That is a really important lesson.

You are right. The first thing that we are going to do is to place orders with some of those guys. Hand in hand with the order is, “What are you now going to do to expand the production line?” Everyone loves the NLAW, which is made in Belfast. You can imagine how many countries are now interested in buying the United Kingdom NLAW. Even t hough it is a joint venture between Sweden, Thales and everything else, it is made in Belfast.
